## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: message-driven processor | A processing node whose "controller is driven by the incoming message stream". Each arrival schedules a code sequence. | pp. 189, 191 |
| new: direct execution of messages | Overhead is reduced "by directly executing messages rather than interpreting them with sequences of instructions". "no instructions are required to receive or buffer the message". | pp. 189, 191 |
| new: single primitive message (EXECUTE) | Only EXECUTE <priority> <opcode> <arg>… is hard-wired. Richer messages are ROM macrocode, and the paper says they run "almost as efficiently" as hard-wired ones. | p. 191 |
| new: message unit / instruction unit split | The MU receives, buffers and vectors. The IU "simply executes instructions". | pp. 189, 192, 195 |
| new: memory-based architecture for fast context switches | Instructions read or write on-chip memory in one cycle. With four general registers, a context saves or restores in under 10 cycles. | pp. 189, 191, 196 |
| new: priority register sets | Two register sets, one per priority level, so a low-priority message is preempted "without saving state". | pp. 189, 191 |
| new: associative (set-associative) memory | The same on-chip memory is accessed by address or by content. It is used to translate object IDs to node and address, and class+selector to a method address (a method cache). | pp. 189, 193 |
| new: global name space / object identifiers | Global object IDs are translated at run time. Code is kept as one distributed copy. Local and non-local objects are handled uniformly through tags and traps. | pp. 189, 194, 196 |
| new: futures via tags | A reply target is tagged "context future". Use before the reply suspends the context. | pp. 190, 194–195 |
| new: fine-grain concurrency (grain size) | The natural grain is "about 20 instruction times". The MDP aims at about 10 instructions, against several hundred on existing machines. | pp. 190, 195 |
| new: congestion as governor (no send queue) | With no send queue, network congestion blocks producing objects. | p. 191 |

## Notes
- **Source and version:** ACM Digital Library publisher PDF of the ISCA '87 paper (© 1987 ACM, pp. 189–196), not the 1998 reprint (10.1145/285930.285993). dl.acm.org returned HTTP 403 to direct download, so the identical PDF was taken from the Internet Archive snapshot of https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/30350.30372 (timestamp 20240413161934) and saved as `papers/P69.pdf`. It is a scan with an OCR text layer. Table 1 (p. 195) was checked on the rendered page image.
- **Criterion:** screening's I1 is confirmed: the message-transmit instruction (I1(a), p. 192) and hardware message buffering and dispatch (I1(b), pp. 191–192). No exclusion criterion applies. It is not X3: the message mechanism is in the processor itself, not only in the network interface (pp. 189, 191). It is not X4: the node is for general concurrent programs and is described as an emulator for "other programming models" (p. 196). I2 is not met, because this is a design proposal, not a retrospective or evaluation of an existing architecture.
- **Relation to P12:** this paper is the 1987 architecture proposal of the MDP. From this paper alone, the design read here (single EXECUTE message, two priority levels, 4K-word memory-based node, expected 100 ns clock; pp. 189–191, 195) is a design stage with simulated results only. Whether the results overlap P12's (X8) is for the gate. This record was written from P69 alone.
- The comparison figure of "about 300µs" for Cosmic Cube, iPSC and S-NET (p. 190) carries no citation or measurement setup in the text.

# Quality assessment checklist

`n/a` is used only when the source was not read (abstract-only record) or the question cannot apply to the paper's kind, and always with the reason. `no` means the paper fails the question.

| ID | Question asked of each paper | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Does the paper state its aim or contribution explicitly (in the abstract or introduction)? yes: stated in one place as a goal or contribution list; partly: has to be inferred from several places; no: not stated. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q2 | Is the system's communication mechanism described in enough detail to reimplement it: message format, naming or addressing of the receiver, delivery and ordering guarantees, and what happens when the receiver is busy? yes: all four; partly: one to three; no: none. For papers with no system (I3 studies), the studied programs and their communication mechanisms count instead. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q3 | Does the evidence come from a working artefact? yes: silicon, FPGA, or a kernel or system that runs real programs; partly: simulator or emulator; no: design or argument only. For I3 studies: yes: defects taken from real bug trackers or commit histories; partly: from benchmark suites; no: from examples only. Analytical models count as no (design or argument). | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q4 | Is every performance or defect claim measured against a named baseline? yes: each claim names its baseline (system, version, configuration); partly: some claims do; no: none do, or no measured claim is made. A hypothetical baseline counts as partly. For I3 studies: yes if the counts are compared with another named study or population; partly if only some are. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q5 | Is the measurement setup reported: workloads or programs used and why they were chosen, hardware or simulator configuration, number of runs or sample size? yes: all three; partly: one or two; no: none, or nothing measured. For I3 studies: the sampling procedure (sources, search terms, screening) replaces the hardware or simulator configuration. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q6 | Does every quantitative claim in the abstract and conclusions have a table, figure or text passage in the body that reports it? yes: all; partly: some; no: none, or no data in the body. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q7 | Are causes attributed to results (e.g. "the slowdown comes from X") supported by a measurement that isolates that cause, such as an ablation or a breakdown? yes: every attributed cause; partly: some; no: none, or causes only asserted. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q8 | Does the paper discuss limitations or threats to validity? yes: a section or paragraph dedicated to them; partly: mentioned in passing; no: not discussed. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q9 | Is the evaluation independent of the system's designers? yes: no author is listed as a designer or builder of the evaluated system in the paper or its cited design papers; partly: some authors are; no: all authors are, or the paper does not evaluate a system. For I3 studies: yes if no author developed the studied programs. | yes / partly / no / n/a |

# Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. Programs whose defects are reported as accesses to shared variables count as shared-memory programs even if the paper does not use that term. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |
===

# Protocol change: reading-pilot

Saved as `sls/1-protocol/changes/2026-10-06-reading-pilot.md`.

## What changed
- `extraction-form.md`:
  - New *Applies to* column (I1–I4 per field); a field outside the paper's criteria is `n/a (I3)`, and `not stated` means the field applies but the paper is silent.
  - Values in *Cost of message primitives*, *Performance results* and *Scaling* are tagged measured / simulated / design figure / analytical / read off.
  - *Reference*: pages are those printed on `papers/P*.pdf` (else its PDF page), with the version (publisher, preprint, manuscript, reprint), the publisher's page range and any offset; abstract-only content cites `abstract`. Criteria I1–I4.
  - *Paper type*: one or more types, plus "position or analytical argument".
  - *Levels with message semantics*: adds `partly` (a message is a primitive at the level but other paths exist, naming the message-only operations), and for kernels and multicomputers separate answers between cores or nodes and within a core.
- `quality.md`:
  - Scale adds `n/a`, only for a source not read or a question that cannot apply, with the reason.
  - Q3: analytical models count as no.
  - Q4: a hypothetical baseline counts as partly. For I3, yes if the counts are compared with another named study.
  - Q5: for I3, the sampling procedure replaces the hardware setup.
  - Q9: for I3, yes if no author developed the studied programs.
- `criteria.md`, I3: adds "Programs whose defects are reported as accesses to shared variables count as shared-memory programs even if the paper does not use that term."

## Why
The reading pilot (P5, P8, P9, P10, P12, P13, P22, P33) showed the form and the checklist did not fit most papers:
- most fields did not apply to bug studies or analytical papers;
- readers cited five different kinds of page numbers;
- the strict yes/no on levels hid the differences the review is about;
- abstract-only and I3 records could only answer "no" to quality questions that could not apply.

Lu et al. (2008) met I3 only by inference, because it speaks of shared variables, not shared memory.

## Papers affected
The pilot records P5, P8, P9, P10, P12, P13, P22 and P33 were written under the previous form and are not re-read. Their fields are mapped to the new form at synthesis (4a). P5 meets I3 as changed. Every later record uses the new form.

# P53

## Reference
Alan C. Bomberger, A. Peri Frantz, William S. Frantz, Ann C. Hardy, Norman Hardy, Charles R. Landau, Jonathan S. Shapiro (1992). *The KeyKOS Nanokernel Architecture*. Proceedings of the USENIX Workshop on Micro-Kernels and Other Kernel Architectures, USENIX Association, April 1992, pp. 95-112 (venue and page range from the HTML reprint at cap-lore.com; not on the PDF). P53, round-file row R0-072, screened include (I1); full text confirms I1(c).

Version: author manuscript reformatted from Word (`KEYPAP4.DOC`, PDF made in 2007), 18 pages, hosted at http://css.csail.mit.edu/6.858/2014/readings/keykos.pdf; not the USENIX publisher layout. The PDF has no printed page numbers, so every page below is the PDF page (p. 1-18). Publisher pages 95-112 are also 18 pages, so publisher page = PDF page + 94 is likely, but the line breaks may differ (inferred, not checked against the publisher copy).

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** design description of a running commercial capability-based operating system kernel (KeyKOS nanokernel), plus implementation and a "limited performance comparison" (p. 14) of a UNIX built on it (KeyNIX) against Omron MACH 2.5 (p. 1, 2, 14).
- **Context:** microkernels; compares itself with Mach ports (p. 3), MACH 2.5 / MACH 3 and CHORUS (p. 13, 15, 17), Multics/80x86 ring security (p. 4); cites Hydra/C.mmp, Levy's capability systems, Lampson's confinement (p. 18).
- **Correctness:** the design claims rest on the authors' production experience ("in production use since 1983", p. 1); the performance claims rest on one small benchmark table with no stated number of runs and an explicit caveat: "A more careful analysis would be required for any serious evaluation" (p. 14). Several claims (transaction performance, >90% disk utilisation, task switch "several times lower than in competing microkernels") have no data in the paper (p. 8, 9, 13).
- **Contributions:** a kernel where "KeyKOS entities call upon the services of other entities by sending messages via a key" with "total reliance on capabilities without any other mechanisms" (p. 3); a stateless kernel with no dynamic allocation and no message buffering (p. 2, 7); keepers that turn exceptions into messages (p. 9); a binary-compatible UNIX with one UNIX keeper per process (p. 9-11) and its measured costs (p. 14-16).
- **Clarity:** clearly written; the kernel implementation itself is deliberately omitted ("we have omitted a description of the underlying kernel implementation", p. 2); measurement setup is thin.

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | Stated in one place: "This paper presents the architecture and design of the KeyKOS nanokernel, and the UNIX system that runs on top of it" (p. 2; also abstract, p. 1). |
| Q2 | partly | Message format (parameter word, up to 4096 bytes, four keys, p. 7), naming (keys with an 8-bit field, p. 3-4) and busy receiver (invocation "deferred until the recipient is ready", p. 7; "no mechanism for stacking messages", p. 12) are given; ordering guarantees are not stated. |
| Q3 | yes | Running kernel: production since 1983 on IBM 4341 (p. 2); KeyNIX runs unmodified BSD binaries including X11 on the Omron Luna/88K (p. 14). |
| Q4 | partly | The benchmark table names its baseline, "the Omron MACH 2.5 implementation" (p. 14); other performance claims (transactions vs "competing transaction facilities", p. 9; disk utilisation, p. 8; task-switch cost vs MACH and Chorus, p. 13) give no measured baseline. |
| Q5 | partly | Workloads and iteration counts are given (p. 14-16) and the purpose of the decomposition tests is stated (p. 10, 15); the machine is not stated in the measurement section (Luna/88K inferred from p. 9) and the number of runs is not stated. |
| Q6 | partly | Code size and memory (p. 2, 4) and "competitive" performance (table p. 14) are reported in the body; "intervals between failures in excess of one year" (p. 1) and restart "typically less than 30 seconds" (p. 1) rest on anecdotes (p. 3), not reported data. |

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** design description of a running commercial capability-based operating system kernel (KeyKOS nanokernel), plus implementation and a "limited performance comparison" (p. 14) of a UNIX built on it (KeyNIX) against Omron MACH 2.5 (p. 1, 2, 14).
- **Context:** microkernels; compares itself with Mach ports (p. 3), MACH 2.5 / MACH 3 and CHORUS (p. 13, 15, 17), Multics/80x86 ring security (p. 4); cites Hydra/C.mmp, Levy's capability systems, Lampson's confinement (p. 18).
- **Correctness:** the design claims rest on the authors' production experience ("in production use since 1983", p. 1); the performance claims rest on one small benchmark table with no stated number of runs and an explicit caveat: "A more careful analysis would be required for any serious evaluation" (p. 14). Several claims (transaction performance, >90% disk utilisation, task switch "several times lower than in competing microkernels") have no data in the paper (p. 8, 9, 13).
- **Contributions:** a kernel where "KeyKOS entities call upon the services of other entities by sending messages via a key" with "total reliance on capabilities without any other mechanisms" (p. 3); a stateless kernel with no dynamic allocation and no message buffering (p. 2, 7); keepers that turn exceptions into messages (p. 9); a binary-compatible UNIX with one UNIX keeper per process (p. 9-11) and its measured costs (p. 14-16).
- **Clarity:** clearly written; the kernel implementation itself is deliberately omitted ("we have omitted a description of the underlying kernel implementation", p. 2); measurement setup is thin.

- **Category:** Descriptive book chapter on one architecture, followed by a short evaluative discussion of it (pp. 159–186; "9.8 Discussion", pp. 184–186).
- **Context:** One of a series of chapters on capability-based systems; compares the 432 with the IBM System/38 (p. 159), Carnegie-Mellon's Hydra (p. 159, p. 167), STAROS (p. 185) and the Dennis and Van Horn model (p. 185). Describes the 432 "as of revision 3 [Intel 82]" (p. 160).
- **Correctness:** Based on Intel's manuals and Organick (1983), cited (p. 159, p. 186). The one performance figure (CALL time, p. 185) and the installed-base figure (p. 186) have no stated source or method.
- **Contributions:** A structured account of the 432's object addressing, program execution, type managers, storage resources and instruction encoding (pp. 161–184), and a third-party assessment of its strengths, limits and commercial fate (pp. 184–186). Interprocess communication by messages to ports is mentioned only briefly (p. 159, p. 162, p. 171).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well illustrated (15 figures, 3 tables); the scan's OCR text has errors but the page images are legible.

| new: type definition object (TDO) | The "representative 'type'" of a programmer-defined object; its AD is stored in each object's descriptor | 177–178 |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: Processor Coupling | A method for exploiting instruction-level parallelism across clusters [18]; the M–Machine relaxes its lock-step implicit synchronization to explicit register-based synchronization. | p. 2, 6 |
| new: H–Thread | A 3-wide, statically scheduled instruction stream on one cluster; H–Threads of a V–Thread communicate and synchronize "via registers". | p. 3–4 |
| new: V–Thread | "similar to a standard process", composed of up to four H–Threads; six resident V–Threads are interleaved cycle by cycle. | p. 3–4 |
| new: event V–Thread (asynchronous event handling) | A dedicated thread slot whose H–Threads handle events (LTLB misses, block status and synchronization faults, message arrivals) asynchronously, "without stopping the thread". | p. 4–6 |
| new: user-level protected message passing substrate | User code sends messages with an atomic SEND instruction, protected by virtual-address destinations and restricted DIPs, without operating-system invocation. | p. 6–8 |
| new: Global Translation Lookaside Buffer / Global Destination Table | Hardware cache of a software table mapping virtual address regions (page-groups) to nodes, used to name message destinations. | p. 7 |
| new: dispatch instruction pointer (DIP) | The first word of a message; the receiving handler jumps to it to run the specific action. | p. 7 |
| new: return-to-sender throttling | Flow control in which unconsumed messages are returned to a reserved buffer at the sender and resent later; SEND stalls when no buffer is reserved. | p. 7 |
| new: register-mapped message queue | The head of the hardware message queue is a register, so messages are not copied to or from memory. | p. 7–8 |
| new: shared memory layered on message passing | "a coherent shared memory system layered on the message-passing substrate", via trap handlers that send messages. | p. 6 |
| new: block status bits | Two bits per 8-word block in LTLB and page-table entries (invalid, read-only, read/write, dirty) enabling software caching of remote data in local DRAM. | p. 9 |
| new: guarded pointers | The M–Machine's light-weight capability system for protection [5]. | p. 2–3 |
| new: incremental parallelization | An unmodified sequential program runs on one node using local and remote memory and is parallelized step by step. | p. 1–2, 9–10 |

# Protocol change: reading-pilot

Saved as `sls/1-protocol/changes/2026-10-06-reading-pilot.md`.

## What changed
- `extraction-form.md`:
  - New *Applies to* column (I1–I4 per field); a field outside the paper's criteria is `n/a (I3)`, and `not stated` means the field applies but the paper is silent.
  - Values in *Cost of message primitives*, *Performance results* and *Scaling* are tagged measured / simulated / design figure / analytical / read off.
  - *Reference*: pages are those printed on `papers/P*.pdf` (else its PDF page), with the version (publisher, preprint, manuscript, reprint), the publisher's page range and any offset; abstract-only content cites `abstract`. Criteria I1–I4.
  - *Paper type*: one or more types, plus "position or analytical argument".
  - *Levels with message semantics*: adds `partly` (a message is a primitive at the level but other paths exist, naming the message-only operations), and for kernels and multicomputers separate answers between cores or nodes and within a core.
- `quality.md`:
  - Scale adds `n/a`, only for a source not read or a question that cannot apply, with the reason.
  - Q3: analytical models count as no.
  - Q4: a hypothetical baseline counts as partly. For I3, yes if the counts are compared with another named study.
  - Q5: for I3, the sampling procedure replaces the hardware setup.
  - Q9: for I3, yes if no author developed the studied programs.
- `criteria.md`, I3: adds "Programs whose defects are reported as accesses to shared variables count as shared-memory programs even if the paper does not use that term."

## Why
The reading pilot (P5, P8, P9, P10, P12, P13, P22, P33) showed the form and the checklist did not fit most papers:
- most fields did not apply to bug studies or analytical papers;
- readers cited five different kinds of page numbers;
- the strict yes/no on levels hid the differences the review is about;
- abstract-only and I3 records could only answer "no" to quality questions that could not apply.

Lu et al. (2008) met I3 only by inference, because it speaks of shared variables, not shared memory.

## Papers affected
The pilot records P5, P8, P9, P10, P12, P13, P22 and P33 were written under the previous form and are not re-read. Their fields are mapped to the new form at synthesis (4a). P5 meets I3 as changed. Every later record uses the new form.

# Quality assessment checklist

`n/a` is used only when the source was not read (abstract-only record) or the question cannot apply to the paper's kind, and always with the reason. `no` means the paper fails the question.

| ID | Question asked of each paper | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Does the paper state its aim or contribution explicitly (in the abstract or introduction)? yes: stated in one place as a goal or contribution list; partly: has to be inferred from several places; no: not stated. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q2 | Is the system's communication mechanism described in enough detail to reimplement it: message format, naming or addressing of the receiver, delivery and ordering guarantees, and what happens when the receiver is busy? yes: all four; partly: one to three; no: none. For papers with no system (I3 studies), the studied programs and their communication mechanisms count instead. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q3 | Does the evidence come from a working artefact? yes: silicon, FPGA, or a kernel or system that runs real programs; partly: simulator or emulator; no: design or argument only. For I3 studies: yes: defects taken from real bug trackers or commit histories; partly: from benchmark suites; no: from examples only. Analytical models count as no (design or argument). | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q4 | Is every performance or defect claim measured against a named baseline? yes: each claim names its baseline (system, version, configuration); partly: some claims do; no: none do, or no measured claim is made. A hypothetical baseline counts as partly. For I3 studies: yes if the counts are compared with another named study or population; partly if only some are. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q5 | Is the measurement setup reported: workloads or programs used and why they were chosen, hardware or simulator configuration, number of runs or sample size? yes: all three; partly: one or two; no: none, or nothing measured. For I3 studies: the sampling procedure (sources, search terms, screening) replaces the hardware or simulator configuration. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q6 | Does every quantitative claim in the abstract and conclusions have a table, figure or text passage in the body that reports it? yes: all; partly: some; no: none, or no data in the body. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q7 | Are causes attributed to results (e.g. "the slowdown comes from X") supported by a measurement that isolates that cause, such as an ablation or a breakdown? yes: every attributed cause; partly: some; no: none, or causes only asserted. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q8 | Does the paper discuss limitations or threats to validity? yes: a section or paragraph dedicated to them; partly: mentioned in passing; no: not discussed. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q9 | Is the evaluation independent of the system's designers? yes: no author is listed as a designer or builder of the evaluated system in the paper or its cited design papers; partly: some authors are; no: all authors are, or the paper does not evaluate a system. For I3 studies: yes if no author developed the studied programs. | yes / partly / no / n/a |

# Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. Programs whose defects are reported as accesses to shared variables count as shared-memory programs even if the paper does not use that term. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

+- **Context:** VLSI technology trend that chip area is now dominated by memory, not processing (p. 1, citing [14]). Builds on the authors' Processor Coupling [18] and guarded-pointer capability addressing [5] (p. 2), and on the J–Machine [8, 25] (p. 7–8). +- **Contributions:** (1) Relaxed Processor Coupling with H–Threads and V–Threads, register-based synchronization and asynchronous event handling in dedicated thread slots (p. 3–6); (2) a "fast, protected, user-level message passing substrate" with an atomic SEND instruction, virtual-address destinations translated by a GTLB, register-mapped receive queue and DIP dispatch, and return-to-sender throttling (p. 6–8); (3) coherent shared memory layered on that substrate through software trap handlers and block status bits (p. 6, 8–9); (4) preliminary simulated latencies for local and remote access (Table 1, p. 9).

| Many-core scaling | Per node: 4 clusters of 3-issue units (12 function units) on one chip; across nodes: 3–D mesh multicomputer. Shared memory: yes, a global virtual address space; coherence is in software handlers with block status bits, not hardware (p. 3, 9). Inter-core (cluster) communication: register writes over the C-Switch and global CC registers (p. 4–5); inter-node: user-level messages (p. 6–7). Scaling result: not measured (p. 8). Limits named: superscalars "do not scale well with increasing number of function units" (register file ports) (p. 6); remote latency "still large compared to local memory references" (p. 9); memory bandwidth and capacity "the dominant factor in the cost and performance of systems of all scales" (p. 11). | p. 2–6, 8–9, 11 |
| Adoption factors | n/a (I1) | — |
| Quality | See the Quality table: Q1 yes, Q2 partly, Q3 partly, Q4 partly, Q5 partly, Q6 partly, Q7 partly, Q8 partly, Q9 no. | p. 1–10 |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: Processor Coupling | A method for exploiting instruction-level parallelism across clusters [18]; the M–Machine relaxes its lock-step implicit synchronization to explicit register-based synchronization. | p. 2, 6 |
| new: H–Thread | A 3-wide, statically scheduled instruction stream on one cluster; H–Threads of a V–Thread communicate and synchronize "via registers". | p. 3–4 |
| new: V–Thread | "similar to a standard process", composed of up to four H–Threads; six resident V–Threads are interleaved cycle by cycle. | p. 3–4 |
| new: event V–Thread (asynchronous event handling) | A dedicated thread slot whose H–Threads handle events (LTLB misses, block status and synchronization faults, message arrivals) asynchronously, "without stopping the thread". | p. 4–6 |
| new: user-level protected message passing substrate | User code sends messages with an atomic SEND instruction, protected by virtual-address destinations and restricted DIPs, without operating-system invocation. | p. 6–8 |
| new: Global Translation Lookaside Buffer / Global Destination Table | Hardware cache of a software table mapping virtual address regions (page-groups) to nodes, used to name message destinations. | p. 7 |
| new: dispatch instruction pointer (DIP) | The first word of a message; the receiving handler jumps to it to run the specific action. | p. 7 |
| new: return-to-sender throttling | Flow control in which unconsumed messages are returned to a reserved buffer at the sender and resent later; SEND stalls when no buffer is reserved. | p. 7 |
| new: register-mapped message queue | The head of the hardware message queue is a register, so messages are not copied to or from memory. | p. 7–8 |
| new: shared memory layered on message passing | "a coherent shared memory system layered on the message-passing substrate", via trap handlers that send messages. | p. 6 |
| new: block status bits | Two bits per 8-word block in LTLB and page-table entries (invalid, read-only, read/write, dirty) enabling software caching of remote data in local DRAM. | p. 9 |
| new: guarded pointers | The M–Machine's light-weight capability system for protection [5]. | p. 2–3 |
| new: incremental parallelization | An unmodified sequential program runs on one node using local and remote memory and is parallelized step by step. | p. 1–2, 9–10 |

- **Source:** author preprint PDF, https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~skeckler/pubs/micro95.pdf (11 pages, headed "Appears in the Proceedings of MICRO-28", PDF created Dec 1995), saved as `papers/P66.pdf`. The publisher (IEEE) version was not read; the journal version (10.1007/bf02700035, Int. J. Parallel Programming, pp. 183–212 per Crossref) was not read. Section headings are garbled in the PDF text layer; the body text is intact.
- **Criterion (X8, for gate 3c):** the journal version reports the same system and, by Crossref, has 30 pages against 11 here. Under X8 "The one with more pages is kept"; this MICRO paper would be excluded unless it reports something absent from the journal version. I did not read the journal version, so I cannot check.
- **Criterion (possible I4):** besides I1, the paper builds "a coherent shared memory system layered on the message-passing substrate" (p. 6) with simulated costs (Table 1, p. 9), which bears on *Model equivalence* (messages as base, shared memory on top; what is kept: transparency to user programs, p. 6; cost: remote read 138 vs local 3–61 cycles, p. 9). Whether this meets I4 for SQ10 is for gate 3c; under I1 alone the field is n/a.
- **Inconsistencies:** the remote-read step list sums to 132 cycles (2+2+48+5+29+5+41, computed) against 138 in Table 1 (p. 8–9). Figure 6's caption says "Sending a 3 word remote store message" while the code comment says "send a 1 word remote store message" (p. 7); the text explains a 1-word body in a 3-word message (p. 7). "only a twice as large" compares 138 with 61 cycles, a ratio of about 2.3 (computed, p. 8–9).
- **Metadata:** Semantic Scholar maps DOI 10.1109/micro.1995.476822 to a different paper (Norris and Pollock, register allocation); Crossref gives the correct title and pages 146–156.
- The paper contrasts the M–Machine with the J–Machine, where user access "without atomicity must temporarily disable interrupts to allow the sending process to complete the message", and claims no earlier register-mapped interface protected user-level messages (p. 8).

# P29

## Reference
Paul M. Hansen, Mark A. Linton, Robert N. Mayo, Marguerite Murphy, David A. Patterson (1982). *A Performance Evaluation of the Intel iAPX 432*. ACM SIGARCH Computer Architecture News 10(4), 17–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/641542.641545. P29, included under I2 (row R0-033). Pages below are the page numbers printed on `papers/P29.pdf` (pp. 17–26), which match the publisher's page range (Crossref: 17–26). PDF page n = printed page n + 16. Version: a scanned photocopy of the published issue (see Notes).

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Third-party measurement study (benchmark evaluation) of one processor against three contemporaries; a short report of 7 pages of text and tables plus 2 figure pages (pp. 17–26).
- **Context:** Intel's own claims for the 432 [Intel 81] and its project goals [Mazor 81] (p. 17); benchmark programs from EDN [Grappel and Hemmenway 81], Byte [Gilbreath 81], Baskett's puzzle and Wichmann's Ackermann study (p. 18); procedure-call frequency studies [Clark and Levy 82], [Ditzel and McLellan 82], [McDaniel 82] (p. 18).
- **Correctness:** The premise is that an object-oriented architecture with "software-transparent multiprocessing and fault tolerance" may cost performance, posed as "An interesting question is how much performance is degraded" (p. 17). The authors hedge that "a high-level language system consists of the compiler and the machine, so we are not measuring just the architecture and hardware implementation" (p. 17). Four programs only, limited by "The time allotted to our visit at Intel" (p. 18). Several 1983 figures are forecasts, not measurements (p. 22).
- **Contributions:** Execution time and code size of four integer and character programs on the iAPX 432 (Ada, release 2 hardware and release 3 simulator) against the 8086, 68000 and VAX-11/780 (Pascal, C) (pp. 20–22). Headline: "A single 4 MHz, release 2 432 is currently about 1/20th of a VAX-11/780" (p. 23).
- **Clarity:** Clear and short; every machine configuration (clock, wait states, compiler version, who ran it) is listed (pp. 18–19). Weak points: the Table 2(a) header labels the search column "484" (p. 21); how the 432 release 2 times were normalised to 8 MHz in Table 3 is not explained (p. 22); the y-axis of Figure 2 is not evenly spaced (p. 26).

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The abstract states the aim: "an experiment to test the 432 as a high-level language uniprocessor" (p. 17). |
| Q2 | no | The paper describes no communication mechanism of the 432; it excludes "object-oriented programming, ... multiple processes, and multiple processors" from the study (p. 17). |
| Q3 | yes | Table 1 is "measured on real hardware", a release 2 432 system at Intel (pp. 19–20). The release 3 timings come from a simulator (p. 19), and the 1983 figures are forecasts (p. 22). |
| Q4 | partly | The measured results name their baselines (VAX-11/780 VMS Pascal, 8086, 68000 with clock, wait states and compiler; pp. 19–21). The 1983 claim ("1/5th the speed of Pascal programs on the 1983 VAX", p. 23) uses a hypothetical baseline. |
| Q5 | partly | Programs and the reason for each are given (p. 18) and the hardware configurations (pp. 18–19). The number of runs is not stated. |
| Q6 | partly | "about 1/20th of a VAX-11/780" matches Table 1(b) (.05–.07; p. 20). "1/5th" in 1983 rests on Figure 2 forecasts (p. 26). "5 processors may perform as well as a VAX" has no table or figure behind it (p. 23). The abstract has no quantitative claim. |
| Q7 | partly | The cost of parameter and global access is isolated by running modified programs (* rows, Table 1, p. 20). The code-size causes (no immediates, 16-bit addresses; p. 21) are only asserted. |
| Q8 | partly | Limits are mentioned in passing: compiler and machine measured together (p. 17), only four programs (p. 18), "we can not compare completely equal systems" (p. 23). There is no dedicated section. |
| Q9 | yes | All five authors are at UC Berkeley (p. 17), and none is named as a 432 designer. Intel's Konrad Lai ran the 32-bit release 2 and all release 3 runs (p. 19). |

| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: high-level language uniprocessor | The 432 is tested "as a high-level language uniprocessor" for integer and character programs. | pp. 17, 23 |
| new: high-level language system = compiler + machine | "a high-level language system consists of the compiler and the machine, so we are not measuring just the architecture and hardware implementation". | p. 17 |

- **Source and version:** Internet Archive item `PerformanceEvaluationOfTheIntelAPX432` (uploaded 2019, scanned 2013 with a ScanSnap; the archive also offers an OCR text file). It is a 10-page photocopy whose printed page numbers 17–26 match the SIGARCH CAN 10(4) page range on Crossref. Page 17 carries a "THIS MATERIAL MAY BE PROTECTED BY COPYRIGHT LAW (TITLE 17 U.S. CODE)" stamp, so it is likely a library copy of the published issue (inferred). The paper is dated "May 17, 1982" (p. 17). The ACM full text (dl.acm.org) was blocked by a Cloudflare challenge, and Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar list no open copy. Saved as `papers/P29.pdf` (the image scan). Table values were read from the page images, not the OCR text, which garbles digits (8 → B).

- **Criterion:** consistent with screening (I2; pp. 17, 20). The paper does not meet I1 on its own text: it never uses message, send, port, IPC or method invocation (checked over the full text). Whatever message mechanism the 432 has is outside this paper.
- **Scope:** uniprocessor, integer and character programs only. Object-oriented programming, floating point, multiple processes and multiple processors were excluded (p. 17), so none of the 432's object or inter-process mechanisms were measured.
- **Call frequency context:** "1 out of every 20 instructions executed is a procedure call or return" in other studies. Acker is "certainly on the high side with 1/7", and the others are low: puzzle 1/235, search 1/245, sieve 1/125000 (p. 18).

# P29

## Reference
Paul M. Hansen, Mark A. Linton, Robert N. Mayo, Marguerite Murphy, David A. Patterson (1982). *A Performance Evaluation of the Intel iAPX 432*. ACM SIGARCH Computer Architecture News 10(4), 17–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/641542.641545. P29, included under I2 (row R0-033). Pages below are the page numbers printed on `papers/P29.pdf` (pp. 17–26), which match the publisher's page range (Crossref: 17–26). PDF page n = printed page n + 16. Version: a scanned photocopy of the published issue (see Notes).

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Third-party measurement study (benchmark evaluation) of one processor against three contemporaries; a short report of 7 pages of text and tables plus 2 figure pages (pp. 17–26).
- **Context:** Intel's own claims for the 432 [Intel 81] and its project goals [Mazor 81] (p. 17); benchmark programs from EDN [Grappel and Hemmenway 81], Byte [Gilbreath 81], Baskett's puzzle and Wichmann's Ackermann study (p. 18); procedure-call frequency studies [Clark and Levy 82], [Ditzel and McLellan 82], [McDaniel 82] (p. 18).
- **Correctness:** The premise is that an object-oriented architecture with "software-transparent multiprocessing and fault tolerance" may cost performance, posed as "An interesting question is how much performance is degraded" (p. 17). The authors hedge that "a high-level language system consists of the compiler and the machine, so we are not measuring just the architecture and hardware implementation" (p. 17). Four programs only, limited by "The time allotted to our visit at Intel" (p. 18). Several 1983 figures are forecasts, not measurements (p. 22).
- **Contributions:** Execution time and code size of four integer and character programs on the iAPX 432 (Ada, release 2 hardware and release 3 simulator) against the 8086, 68000 and VAX-11/780 (Pascal, C) (pp. 20–22). Headline: "A single 4 MHz, release 2 432 is currently about 1/20th of a VAX-11/780" (p. 23).
- **Clarity:** Clear and short; every machine configuration (clock, wait states, compiler version, who ran it) is listed (pp. 18–19). Weak points: the Table 2(a) header labels the search column "484" (p. 21); how the 432 release 2 times were normalised to 8 MHz in Table 3 is not explained (p. 22); the y-axis of Figure 2 is not evenly spaced (p. 26).

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The abstract states the aim: "an experiment to test the 432 as a high-level language uniprocessor" (p. 17). |
| Q2 | no | The paper describes no communication mechanism of the 432; it excludes "object-oriented programming, ... multiple processes, and multiple processors" from the study (p. 17). |
| Q3 | yes | Table 1 is "measured on real hardware", a release 2 432 system at Intel (pp. 19–20). The release 3 timings come from a simulator (p. 19), and the 1983 figures are forecasts (p. 22). |
| Q4 | partly | The measured results name their baselines (VAX-11/780 VMS Pascal, 8086, 68000 with clock, wait states and compiler; pp. 19–21). The 1983 claim ("1/5th the speed of Pascal programs on the 1983 VAX", p. 23) uses a hypothetical baseline. |
| Q5 | partly | Programs and the reason for each are given (p. 18) and the hardware configurations (pp. 18–19). The number of runs is not stated. |
| Q6 | partly | "about 1/20th of a VAX-11/780" matches Table 1(b) (.05–.07; p. 20). "1/5th" in 1983 rests on Figure 2 forecasts (p. 26). "5 processors may perform as well as a VAX" has no table or figure behind it (p. 23). The abstract has no quantitative claim. |
| Q7 | partly | The cost of parameter and global access is isolated by running modified programs (* rows, Table 1, p. 20). The code-size causes (no immediates, 16-bit addresses; p. 21) are only asserted. |
| Q8 | partly | Limits are mentioned in passing: compiler and machine measured together (p. 17), only four programs (p. 18), "we can not compare completely equal systems" (p. 23). There is no dedicated section. |
| Q9 | yes | All five authors are at UC Berkeley (p. 17), and none is named as a 432 designer. Intel's Konrad Lai ran the 32-bit release 2 and all release 3 runs (p. 19). |

## Extracted fields
| Field | Value | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | See Reference above. I2: the authors refer to "the object-oriented architecture" of the 432 and test it "as a high-level language uniprocessor", and they report measured performance (Tables 1–3). | pp. 17, 20–22 |
| Paper type | evaluation (third-party benchmark measurement, with forecasts) | pp. 17, 22–23 |
| System | Intel iAPX 432: a "32-bit VLSI microprocessor" announced by Intel in 1981, from a project "that started in 1975". Built by Intel. | p. 17 |
| System | Status: silicon. A release 2 system "running with a 4 MHz clock and 12 wait states", "a half-speed prototype of an 8 MHz system"; the experiments are called "432/670" experiments. Release 3 was planned to ship in December, and its timings "were obtained from a simulator" (simulated). 432/800 systems (release 3, 4 wait states) and 10 MHz chips were planned for the first quarter of 1983. | pp. 19, 22 |
| Levels with message semantics | not stated for every level. The paper does not describe messages, ports or any send operation. It quotes Intel that the 432 supports "an object-oriented programming methodology" and "true software-transparent, multiprocessor operation", but describes no mechanism behind either. | p. 17 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | not stated | — |
| Message mechanism | not stated. The only call mechanism measured is the Ada procedure call, through Ackermann's function (no message semantics are claimed for it). | p. 18 |
| Non-message primitives | not stated. The paper notes only that the 432 systems "support virtual memory and provide error correcting memory", without saying how. | p. 19 |
| Self-definition | not stated. The paper quotes Intel that the 432 "is designed to be programmed entirely in high-level languages". | p. 17 |
| Interposition | not stated | — |
| Operating system functions | n/a (I2) | — |
| Cost of message primitives | not stated. Nearest proxy: Ackermann(3,6), "more than 170,000 procedure calls", "useful in measuring the cost of a procedure call", takes 260,000 ms on the 432 (4 MHz, release 2, Ada). That is at most about 1.5 ms per call including the work of the function (inferred). The 432 time for acker(3,6) was itself extrapolated from acker(1,2) by the VAX ratio. | pp. 18–20 |
| Performance results | Execution time, ms (measured), 432 4 MHz release 2, Ada 16-bit, unmodified. search 35; sieve 3200; puzzle 350,000; acker 260,000. Baseline VAX-11/780 VMS Pascal 32-bit: 1.4; 259; 11,530; 9850. Ratio to VMS Pascal: .04; .08; .03; .04; average .05±.02. | p. 20 |
| Performance results | 432 Ada programs modified to avoid expensive parameter and global access (*, measured): 16-bit search 14.2, puzzle 165,000; 32-bit search 16.1, puzzle 180,000 (ms). Ratio to VMS Pascal: average .07±.02 for both word sizes. | pp. 18, 20 |
| Performance results | Other machines (measured, ratio to VMS Pascal, average±sd): VAX C 1.3±.4; VAX UNIX Pascal 1.1±.2; 68000 8 MHz C .6±.4; 68000 8 MHz Pascal 16-bit .5±.2, 32-bit .4±.2; 68000 16 MHz Pascal 16-bit 1.8±1.0, 32-bit 1.6±.9; 8086 5 MHz Pascal .4±.3. | p. 20 |
| Performance results | Code size, bytes of object code and constants, excluding libraries and OS (measured from compiler output). 432 release 3 Ada 16-bit: search 612, sieve 180, puzzle 2443, acker 144. Baseline VMS Pascal: 636, 411, 2904, 340. Ratio .6±.2. 68000 Pascal 16-bit .5±.2; VAX C .5±.2; 8086 Pascal .9±.1. | pp. 19, 21 |
| Performance results | Normalised 8 MHz, 16-bit time, ms, 4 wait states. 68000 Pascal (measured on EXORMACS): 5.3; 810; 32,470; 11,480. 432 rel. 2 Ada: 17.5; 1600; 175,000; 130,000. 432 rel. 2 Ada modified: 7.1; 1600; 82,500; 130,000. These rel. 2 values are exactly half of the 4 MHz times (inferred); the method is not stated. 432 rel. 3 Ada (simulated): 4.4; 978; 45,700; 47,800. | pp. 19, 22 |
| Performance results | Normalised 8 MHz, 0 wait states (analytical). 8086 Pascal, "predicted from the 5 MHz measurements": 4.6; 448; 27,500; 6938. 68000 Pascal, "computed by doubling the times for the 16 MHz 68000": 2.6; 392; 18,360; 5500. A 0-wait-state 432 is "expected to be about 25% faster" (no data). | p. 22 |
| Performance results | Figure 1, average performance relative to the 4-wait-state 68000 at 8 MHz (read off): 432 rel. 2 ≈ 0.28; 432 rel. 2 modified ≈ 0.44; 432 rel. 3 ≈ 0.77; 8086 0 ws ≈ 1.47; 68000 0 ws ≈ 2.0. | p. 25 |
| Performance results | Figure 2, relative to the VAX-11/780 (read off; the axis spacing is uneven). Measured: 432 4 MHz R2 and R2* below 0.1. Predicted: 432 10 MHz R3 4 ws ≈ 0.3; 8086 5 MHz ≈ 0.4 measured and 8 MHz ≈ 0.65 predicted; 68000 8 MHz 4 ws ≈ 0.5 measured, 0 ws ≈ 0.9 predicted, 16 MHz ≈ 1.8 measured; VAX 1.0 measured, ≈ 1.35 predicted. | p. 26 |
| Performance results | Conclusion: "A single 4 MHz, release 2 432 is currently about 1/20th of a VAX-11/780, and we expect Ada programs on the 1983 version to run about 1/5th the speed of Pascal programs on the 1983 VAX." The 1983 baselines are forecasts: DEC Pascal "1.2 to 1.4 times faster", 68000 systems "1.5 to 3 times faster", the 8086 "at least 3 times faster" (analytical). | pp. 22–23 |
| Scaling | Not measured; uniprocessor only ("We limited ourselves to studying uniprocessor performance"). Hedged estimate: "For some applications a 432 system consisting of 5 processors may perform as well as a VAX-11/780. We need multiprocessing benchmarks that could assess such systems." | pp. 17, 23 |
| Attributed causes | "Accessing parameters and global variables is very expensive inside a procedure in release 2 of the 432 and will be much less expensive in release 3. This overhead can be avoided by either changing the compiler or modifying the program source". Third party. Due to the implementation (release 2 and its compiler). Isolated: the modified (*) programs measure it (search 35 → 14.2 ms, puzzle 350,000 → 165,000 ms at 16 bits). | pp. 18, 20 |
| Attributed causes | Code size: "Although the 432 has bit-variable length instructions, it requires more space than either the 68000 in Pascal or the VAX in C. Reasons include the lack of immediates and the inability to refer to a local variable or constant using fewer than 16 bits of address." Third party. Inherent to the instruction set (inferred). Not isolated. | p. 21 |
| Attributed causes | The 432 being smaller than VAX Pascal: "Nothing simple explains this seeming contradiction; perhaps a VAX Pascal system requires more sophisticated compiler technology than is currently available." Third party; hedged; not isolated. | p. 21 |
| Attributed causes | Release 3 is "the first version in which they have attacked the problem of performance". Third party, about Intel's plans. Due to the implementation (inferred). Isolated only by the simulator comparison of rel. 3 against rel. 2 (Table 3). | pp. 19, 22 |
| Attributed causes | Cost of the object-oriented architecture itself: posed as a question ("how much performance is degraded because of the object-oriented architecture with software-transparent multiprocessing and fault tolerance"), but not answered by an isolating measurement. The authors say they "are not measuring just the architecture and hardware implementation" and "can not compare completely equal systems". | pp. 17, 23 |
| Fate and reasons | not stated (the paper predates any outcome). It reports only Intel's plans: release 3 to ship in December, and 432/800 systems and 10 MHz chips in the first quarter of 1983. | pp. 19, 22 |
| Concurrency defects | n/a (I2) | — |
| What shapes programs | n/a (I2) | — |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Cost in performance (measured): about 1/20 of a VAX-11/780 for the release 2 432 on integer and character programs, and 1/5 forecast for 1983. | p. 23 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Cost in code size (measured): larger than 68000 Pascal and VAX C, smaller than VAX Pascal. | p. 21 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Benefits argued, not measured: "we should not disregard the potential 432 benefits of programmer productivity, transparent multiprocessing, and data security". On cost: "If performance were the only measure of system cost, then software development would always be done in assembly language." | p. 23 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Alternative named: "One could attempt to build these 432 functions into software around a 8086, 68000, or VAX, but until then we can not compare completely equal systems." | p. 23 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Whether it applies to a message send as the primitive: not stated. The object, process and multiprocessor features were explicitly outside the study. | p. 17 |

| Quality | See Quality above. | pp. 17–23 |
| Notes | See Notes below. | — |

| new: high-level language system = compiler + machine | "a high-level language system consists of the compiler and the machine, so we are not measuring just the architecture and hardware implementation". | p. 17 |

# P102

## Reference
David Wentzlaff, Anant Agarwal (2009). *Factored Operating Systems (fos): The Case for a Scalable Operating System for Multicores*. ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 43(2), pp. 76–85. https://doi.org/10.1145/1531793.1531805

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** A position and design paper with motivating measurements. It argues that SMP operating systems cannot scale to "1000+ core systems" (p. 2), measures two Linux scaling problems (p. 3–4), and describes the design of a new message-passing OS (fos) whose prototype is "under active development" (p. 2, p. 8). fos itself is not evaluated.
- **Context:** Microkernels (Mach, L3, L4; p. 2, p. 8), scalable shared-memory kernels (Tornado/K42, Hive, Disco/Cellular Disco, Corey; p. 9), distributed OSes (Amoeba, Sprite, Clouds; p. 9) and distributed Internet services (DNS, BitTorrent, Chord, AFS, GFS; p. 9–10). The authors' own Raw and Tilera on-chip networks are cited for message costs (p. 8).
- **Correctness:** The Linux measurements are on real hardware (p. 3), and the cache study runs in a QEMU-based simulator (p. 4). The case for fos rests on argument, for example "We believe that the shared nothing, message passing only, approach will encourage OS developers to think very carefully about exactly what data is being shared, which will lead to more scalability" (p. 5). The paper names its own open questions in Section 3.4 (p. 8).
- **Contributions:** (1) A measurement showing that the Linux 2.6.24.7 physical page allocator "does not scale beyond 8 cores under heavy load" (p. 2, Fig. 1 p. 3). (2) A simulated measurement of OS/application cache interference on Apache2 (p. 4). (3) Three recommendations: avoid hardware locks, separate OS from application cores, and avoid global cache-coherent shared memory (p. 5). (4) The fos design: a microkernel with mailbox messaging, OS services split into fleets of servers bound to cores, a name server, and space multiplexing instead of time multiplexing (p. 5–7).
- **Clarity:** Well structured and readable. The figure labels in the author PDF use an odd font encoding (the text cannot be extracted), but the rendered figures are legible. The message format is not described.

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The abstract and introduction say so in one place: "This work investigates why simply scaling up traditional symmetric multiprocessor operating systems is not sufficient ... and proposes how to build a factored operating system (fos)" (p. 1). |
| Q2 | partly | Receiver naming (symbolic mailbox names, name cache, name server; p. 6), delivery ("reliable messaging layer", p. 6) and busy receiver ("If a receive mailbox is full, the sending client send call returns an error", p. 6) are described. Message format and ordering are not. |
| Q3 | no | The claims about fos rest on design and argument. The prototype is only said to boot (p. 8). The Linux studies used to motivate it are measured on hardware (p. 3) and simulated (p. 4), but they do not evaluate fos. |
| Q4 | partly | The Linux allocator scaling is judged against a hypothetical baseline ("perfect scaling would be bars all the same height", p. 3). The fos claims against Mach, L4 and K42 (p. 8–9) are not measured. |
| Q5 | partly | Workloads and hardware or simulator configurations are given (p. 3, p. 4), and the allocator workload is partly justified (p. 4). The number of runs is not reported. |
| Q6 | yes | The only quantitative claims in the abstract and conclusion are core-count projections ("100's to 1,000's of cores", "double every 18 months"). Body text reports them with citations (p. 1–2). |
| Q7 | partly | Lock contention is isolated by an oprofile breakdown by function (Fig. 1, p. 3). Interference misses are isolated by simulating separate OS-only and application-only caches (p. 4). The architectural overhead is only "believed to be caused by contention in the hardware memory system" (p. 3). The causes of fos's expected benefits are asserted only (p. 7–9). |
| Q8 | yes | Section 3.4 *Challenges* (p. 8) is dedicated to open questions and costs, such as core-to-core latency, shared structures like the buffer cache, lock servers, and multi-sequence operations. |
| Q9 | no | Both authors design fos (p. 1–2), and the paper does not evaluate fos. The Linux systems measured are third-party, but they are only motivating baselines. |

David Wentzlaff, Anant Agarwal (2009). *Factored Operating Systems (fos): The Case for a Scalable Operating System for Multicores*. ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 43(2), pp. 76–85. https://doi.org/10.1145/1531793.1531805

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** A position and design paper with motivating measurements. It argues that SMP operating systems cannot scale to "1000+ core systems" (p. 2), measures two Linux scaling problems (p. 3–4), and describes the design of a new message-passing OS (fos) whose prototype is "under active development" (p. 2, p. 8). fos itself is not evaluated.
- **Context:** Microkernels (Mach, L3, L4; p. 2, p. 8), scalable shared-memory kernels (Tornado/K42, Hive, Disco/Cellular Disco, Corey; p. 9), distributed OSes (Amoeba, Sprite, Clouds; p. 9) and distributed Internet services (DNS, BitTorrent, Chord, AFS, GFS; p. 9–10). The authors' own Raw and Tilera on-chip networks are cited for message costs (p. 8).
- **Correctness:** The Linux measurements are on real hardware (p. 3), and the cache study runs in a QEMU-based simulator (p. 4). The case for fos rests on argument, for example "We believe that the shared nothing, message passing only, approach will encourage OS developers to think very carefully about exactly what data is being shared, which will lead to more scalability" (p. 5). The paper names its own open questions in Section 3.4 (p. 8).
- **Contributions:** (1) A measurement showing that the Linux 2.6.24.7 physical page allocator "does not scale beyond 8 cores under heavy load" (p. 2, Fig. 1 p. 3). (2) A simulated measurement of OS/application cache interference on Apache2 (p. 4). (3) Three recommendations: avoid hardware locks, separate OS from application cores, and avoid global cache-coherent shared memory (p. 5). (4) The fos design: a microkernel with mailbox messaging, OS services split into fleets of servers bound to cores, a name server, and space multiplexing instead of time multiplexing (p. 5–7).
- **Clarity:** Well structured and readable. The figure labels in the author PDF use an odd font encoding (the text cannot be extracted), but the rendered figures are legible. The message format is not described.

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| factored operating system (fos) (new) | An OS "factored into function specific services", each "distributed into spatially distributed servers" that "collaborate and communicate only via message passing" | p. 5 |
| space multiplexing replaces time multiplexing (new) | "Scheduling becomes a layout problem not a time multiplexing problem"; the OS "runs on distinct cores from applications" | p. 5 |
| fleet (new) | The set of servers of one type that together provide one OS function, e.g. physical memory allocation, file system, scheduling | p. 6 |
| fos client (new) | "The code executing on a single core under the fos-microkernel"; applications and OS servers "act as peers" | p. 6 |
| receive mailbox (new) | A named, protected endpoint owned by a client, with a large buffer in the receiver's address space; a send to a full mailbox returns an error | p. 6, 8 |
| message proxy library / translation library (new) | Turns a traditional system call into a message to an OS-layer server and unpacks the reply | p. 6 |
| microkernel to OS layer delegation (new) | The microkernel delegates naming and privilege to OS-layer fleets, caches their answers, and avoids cycles by knowing the delegates' locations and granting static privileges ("privilege fixed point") | p. 7 |
| stateless, transaction-oriented server with continuations (new) | A server processes each transaction to completion without preemption, stores a continuation for long-latency operations, and needs no local locking | p. 7 |
| notional lock / lock server (new) | A lock held by a server and acquired by message; "the cost of software-based lock management may dwarf the performance wins of removing traditional locks" | p. 8 |
| OS-application and OS-OS locality aliasing (new) | OS and application working sets competing for implicitly shared caches and TLBs on one core, including "anti-locality cache collisions" | p. 4 |
| best-effort OS interfaces (new) | Interfaces that return information "which may be slightly out of date" for higher performance, with an accurate but slower alternative | p. 2 |

April 2009", p. 1). The ACM PDF returned 403, and Unpaywall lists no open-access copy. The publisher page range 76–85 is from Crossref. Read in full, figures included (second pass).
- **Criterion:** the full text meets I1(c) as screened. The OS layer's servers "communicate only via the messaging interface provided by the microkernel layer" (p. 6), the paper uses the terms "message passing", "send" and "mailbox" (p. 5–6), and fos runs without an underlying conventional kernel (p. 5). No exclusion applies. X2 does not: messaging is the kernel's own mechanism, not a library on a conventional kernel. X3 does not: the target is a single multicore chip (p. 9). X5 does not: a 10-page journal article. The paper may also answer SQ13/SQ14 under I4 (inferred), through its Linux scaling measurements and its named limits of cache-coherent shared memory (p. 3, p. 5). That would not change the include verdict.
- **For SQ10 (model equivalence, I4 field):** fos messages may be carried on shared memory: "The fos-microkernels transport the message to the destination via on-chip networks or shared memory" (p. 6). The cost of doing so is not reported.
- **For SQ11 (model mixing):** "Within an application, communication can be achieved via shared memory communication or messaging", and fos keeps shared memory for applications "if the underlying hardware supports it" (p. 6).
- **For SQ7/SQ8 (defects, what shapes programs):** the paper argues, without counts, that "Adding locks into an operating system is time consuming and error prone" and that locks "can introduce circular dependencies and hence cause deadlocks" (p. 3). It also argues that "global shared memory easily allows the introduction of data races which can be difficult to detect at test time" (p. 5). It expects that "the shared nothing, message passing only, approach will encourage OS developers to think very carefully about exactly what data is being shared" (p. 5). It says "the message passing nature of fos discourages this usage model [lock managers] by making programming in this manner difficult" (p. 7). All of these are argument, not measurement.
- **Open questions the authors name:** whether shared OS structures (virtual memory, buffer cache) "can be accessed with good performance" (p. 8); whether all multi-sequence operations can be written without local locks: "it is not certain that all cases can be handled" (p. 8); whether "a hardware solution or the software solution explored by fos proves more scalable" (p. 8).

+## Reference

+David Wentzlaff, Anant Agarwal (2009). *Factored Operating Systems (fos): The Case for a Scalable Operating System for Multicores*. ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 43(2), pp. 76–85. https://doi.org/10.1145/1531793.1531805
+## Deepest pass
+## First pass: the five Cs

+- **Category:** A position and design paper with motivating measurements. It argues that SMP operating systems cannot scale to "1000+ core systems" (p. 2), measures two Linux scaling problems (p. 3–4), and describes the design of a new message-passing OS (fos) whose prototype is "under active development" (p. 2, p. 8). fos itself is not evaluated.

+- **Context:** Microkernels (Mach, L3, L4; p. 2, p. 8), scalable shared-memory kernels (Tornado/K42, Hive, Disco/Cellular Disco, Corey; p. 9), distributed OSes (Amoeba, Sprite, Clouds; p. 9) and distributed Internet services (DNS, BitTorrent, Chord, AFS, GFS; p. 9–10). The authors' own Raw and Tilera on-chip networks are cited for message costs (p. 8).

+- **Correctness:** The Linux measurements are on real hardware (p. 3), and the cache study runs in a QEMU-based simulator (p. 4). The case for fos rests on argument, for example "We believe that the shared nothing, message passing only, approach will encourage OS developers to think very carefully about exactly what data is being shared, which will lead to more scalability" (p. 5). The paper names its own open questions in Section 3.4 (p. 8).

+- **Contributions:** (1) A measurement showing that the Linux 2.6.24.7 physical page allocator "does not scale beyond 8 cores under heavy load" (p. 2, Fig. 1 p. 3). (2) A simulated measurement of OS/application cache interference on Apache2 (p. 4). (3) Three recommendations: avoid hardware locks, separate OS from application cores, and avoid global cache-coherent shared memory (p. 5). (4) The fos design: a microkernel with mailbox messaging, OS services split into fleets of servers bound to cores, a name server, and space multiplexing instead of time multiplexing (p. 5–7).

+- **Clarity:** Well structured and readable. The figure labels in the author PDF use an odd font encoding (the text cannot be extracted), but the rendered figures are legible. The message format is not described.

+| Q3 | no | The claims about fos rest on design and argument. The prototype is only said to boot (p. 8). The Linux studies used to motivate it are measured on hardware (p. 3) and simulated (p. 4), but they do not evaluate fos. |

+| Q4 | partly | The Linux allocator scaling is judged against a hypothetical baseline ("perfect scaling would be bars all the same height", p. 3). The fos claims against Mach, L4 and K42 (p. 8–9) are not measured. |
+| Q5 | partly | Workloads and hardware or simulator configurations are given (p. 3, p. 4), and the allocator workload is partly justified (p. 4). The number of runs is not reported. |

+| Q6 | yes | The only quantitative claims in the abstract and conclusion are core-count projections ("100's to 1,000's of cores", "double every 18 months"). Body text reports them with citations (p. 1–2). |

+| Q7 | partly | Lock contention is isolated by an oprofile breakdown by function (Fig. 1, p. 3). Interference misses are isolated by simulating separate OS-only and application-only caches (p. 4). The architectural overhead is only "believed to be caused by contention in the hardware memory system" (p. 3). The causes of fos's expected benefits are asserted only (p. 7–9). |

+| Q8 | yes | Section 3.4 *Challenges* (p. 8) is dedicated to open questions and costs, such as core-to-core latency, shared structures like the buffer cache, lock servers, and multi-sequence operations. |
+| Q9 | no | Both authors design fos (p. 1–2), and the paper does not evaluate fos. The Linux systems measured are third-party, but they are only motivating baselines. |
