+## Concepts
+| Concept | What the paper says | Page |

+| factored operating system (fos) (new) | An OS "factored into function specific services", each "distributed into spatially distributed servers" that "collaborate and communicate only via message passing" | p. 5 |
+| space multiplexing replaces time multiplexing (new) | "Scheduling becomes a layout problem not a time multiplexing problem"; the OS "runs on distinct cores from applications" | p. 5 |
+| fleet (new) | The set of servers of one type that together provide one OS function, e.g. physical memory allocation, file system, scheduling | p. 6 |
+| fos client (new) | "The code executing on a single core under the fos-microkernel"; applications and OS servers "act as peers" | p. 6 |
+| receive mailbox (new) | A named, protected endpoint owned by a client, with a large buffer in the receiver's address space; a send to a full mailbox returns an error | p. 6, 8 |
+| message proxy library / translation library (new) | Turns a traditional system call into a message to an OS-layer server and unpacks the reply | p. 6 |

+| microkernel to OS layer delegation (new) | The microkernel delegates naming and privilege to OS-layer fleets, caches their answers, and avoids cycles by knowing the delegates' locations and granting static privileges ("privilege fixed point") | p. 7 |

+| stateless, transaction-oriented server with continuations (new) | A server processes each transaction to completion without preemption, stores a continuation for long-latency operations, and needs no local locking | p. 7 |

+| notional lock / lock server (new) | A lock held by a server and acquired by message; "the cost of software-based lock management may dwarf the performance wins of removing traditional locks" | p. 8 |
+| OS-application and OS-OS locality aliasing (new) | OS and application working sets competing for implicitly shared caches and TLBs on one core, including "anti-locality cache collisions" | p. 4 |
+| best-effort OS interfaces (new) | Interfaces that return information "which may be slightly out of date" for higher performance, with an accurate but slower alternative | p. 2 |
+## Notes

+- **Source and version:** author preprint PDF, downloaded on 2026-10-07 from https://www.princeton.edu/~wentzlaf/documents/Wentzlaff.2009.OSR.fos.pdf and saved as `papers/P102.pdf` (11 pages, created 2009-03-02, marked "To appear in ACM SIGOPS Operating System Review ... April 2009", p. 1). The ACM PDF returned 403, and Unpaywall lists no open-access copy. The publisher page range 76–85 is from Crossref. Read in full, figures included (second pass).

+- **Criterion:** the full text meets I1(c) as screened. The OS layer's servers "communicate only via the messaging interface provided by the microkernel layer" (p. 6), the paper uses the terms "message passing", "send" and "mailbox" (p. 5–6), and fos runs without an underlying conventional kernel (p. 5). No exclusion applies. X2 does not: messaging is the kernel's own mechanism, not a library on a conventional kernel. X3 does not: the target is a single multicore chip (p. 9). X5 does not: a 10-page journal article. The paper may also answer SQ13/SQ14 under I4 (inferred), through its Linux scaling measurements and its named limits of cache-coherent shared memory (p. 3, p. 5). That would not change the include verdict.

+- **For SQ10 (model equivalence, I4 field):** fos messages may be carried on shared memory: "The fos-microkernels transport the message to the destination via on-chip networks or shared memory" (p. 6). The cost of doing so is not reported.

+- **For SQ11 (model mixing):** "Within an application, communication can be achieved via shared memory communication or messaging", and fos keeps shared memory for applications "if the underlying hardware supports it" (p. 6).

+- **For SQ7/SQ8 (defects, what shapes programs):** the paper argues, without counts, that "Adding locks into an operating system is time consuming and error prone" and that locks "can introduce circular dependencies and hence cause deadlocks" (p. 3). It also argues that "global shared memory easily allows the introduction of data races which can be difficult to detect at test time" (p. 5). It expects that "the shared nothing, message passing only, approach will encourage OS developers to think very carefully about exactly what data is being shared" (p. 5). It says "the message passing nature of fos discourages this usage model [lock managers] by making programming in this manner difficult" (p. 7). All of these are argument, not measurement.

+- **Open questions the authors name:** whether shared OS structures (virtual memory, buffer cache) "can be accessed with good performance" (p. 8); whether all multi-sequence operations can be written without local locks: "it is not certain that all cases can be handled" (p. 8); whether "a hardware solution or the software solution explored by fos proves more scalable" (p. 8).

The Intel iAPX 432     l   an accessselector for the segment containing the array,
                       l   the displacement of the array in the segment,
                       l   an accessselector for a possibly different segment containing
                           the array index, and
                       l   a displacement of the index in this second segment.

                        Many options are provided for each part of the specification
                     and, in general, commonly occurring options can be efficiently
                     encoded. Stack operands save the most instruction space be-
                     cause they require no reference field bits. Space can also be
                     saved in the reference field if operands are located at the start
                     of a segment because this requires no offset. There is a large
                     variance in instruction size-a three-operand instruction can
                     take from 10 to more than 300 bits, depending on where the
                     operands are to be found.

                     9.8 Discussion
                         The Intel iAPX 432 is certainly one of the most sophisti-
                     cated architectures in existence. By using the object-oriented
                     approach throughout the development effort, the Intel 432
                     designers have produced an extremely uniform and tightly-in-
                     tegrated hardware/software system. This uniformity of hard-
                     ware and software systems is due to the use of a consistent
                     philosophy. Everything in the Intel 432 is an object. All objects
                     have associated types that specify the operations that can be
                     performed on those objects. Some objects have hardware-de-
                     fined operations while others do not. However, from a lan-
                     guage viewpoint, all objects are accessedin the same way.
                         All objects, whether hardware-supported or not, are con-
                     trolled by type manager modules. Programmers can freely add
                     new types to the system by creating new type managers. The
                     mechanisms of domain refinement and type definition object
                     provide a way for type managersto exhibit privilege over their
                     objects and the environments in which their procedures exe-
                     cute. A type manager can restrict and later amplify privileges
                     in ADS for its objects by using a privately held type control
                     object. By permitting client accessto type management proce-
                      dures through a refinement, an executing type management
                      procedure can obtain accessto a richer environment than its
                      caller.
                         There are no special privileges in the Intel 432 system. The
                      mechanisms used by programmer-defined type managers are
     184              identical to those used by operating system type managers.

  **Deepest pass:** 3.
  
  **Criteria**
  - **I1 holds.** I1(a) is met by the "user-level SEND instruction", which launches a message atomically (p. 3, 6–7). X2, X3 and X4 do not apply: the message mechanism is in the processor's instruction set and hardware, and the machine runs general programs.
  - **X8, your call:** the journal version (10.1007/bf02700035, Int. J. Parallel Programming, pp. 183–212, so 30 pages) covers the same system. X8 keeps the version with more pages, so this MICRO paper would be excluded unless it reports something the journal version lacks. I did not read the journal version.
    - Options:
      - (a) Keep P66 as is (your brief said to prefer the MICRO paper). No edit.
      - (b) Exclude P66 under X8 and read the journal version as a new record. P66's status becomes excluded (X8).
      - (c) Have someone read the journal version first, then decide.
    - I recommend (c), because X8 depends on what the journal version contains.
  - **Possible I4, your call:** the paper builds "a coherent shared memory system layered on the message-passing substrate" (p. 6), with simulated costs (Table 1, p. 9). That is evidence for *Model equivalence* (SQ10). I did not read the SQ files because they were not among my inputs, so I can't say whether this "directly answers" SQ10.
    - Options:
      - (a) Leave it at I1 only. The field stays `n/a (I1)` and the evidence stays in Notes.
      - (b) Add I4 for SQ10. Change the Reference line to "I1, I4" and fill the *Model equivalence* field from the Notes bullet.
    - I recommend (b).
  
  **Open issues**
  - **Quality:**
    - Q9 is no: all the authors designed the system.
    - Q3 is partly: the only measurements come from the simulator, and the chip was not yet built (p. 8, 10).
    - Q2 is partly: the paper never states an ordering guarantee, only "dimension order" routing (p. 3).
  - **Fields the paper is silent on:** fate (the machine was "currently under development", with tapeout expected in 1996, p. 10), the kernel level, and any central component in OS functions. All are marked `not stated`.
  - **Inconsistencies in the paper (in Notes):**
    - The remote-read step list adds up to 132 cycles, but Table 1 gives 138 (p. 8–9).
    - The caption of Figure 6 says "3 word" message, while the code comment says "1 word" (p. 7).
    - "only a twice as large" compares 138 with 61 cycles, a ratio of about 2.3 (p. 8–9).

# P15

## Reference
Steele, G. L., Jr., Gabriel, R. P. (1993). *The Evolution of Lisp*. HOPL-II (History of Programming Languages II), ACM, pp. 231–270. https://doi.org/10.1145/154766.155373 (other records: 10.1145/155360.155373; 10.1145/234286.1057818). Included under I2 (R0-017). Pages below are the printed page numbers (1–77) of the authors' manuscript saved as `papers/P15.pdf`, not the publisher's pages; see Notes.

## Deepest pass
2 (first pass of the whole paper: title, abstract, contents, introduction, section headings, section 5 scanned; second pass of every passage on Lisp machines and stock hardware: sections 2.5, 2.6, 2.9, 2.10.1–2.10.2, 2.11–2.12, pp. 10–35. Sections 3 and 4, on language features and Lisp as a language laboratory, were only searched for Lisp machine passages.)

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Historical account of a programming language (a HOPL paper), organised as "a series of slices through the subject matter" (p. 2): projects and people, technical themes, Lisp as a language laboratory, and why Lisp evolved as it did. It includes a history of the "ascension and decline of special purpose Lisp machines" (p. 1, abstract).
- **Context:** Picks up "where McCarthy's paper in the first HOPL conference left off" (p. 1, abstract; p. 2). Sources are mostly the authors' own participation, mailing lists and manuals; the reference list includes Lisp machine papers and manuals (Deutsch 1973, Greenblatt 1974, Moon 1984, Weinreb and Moon 1978/1981) (pp. 12–13).
- **Correctness:** The Lisp machine claims are narrative and qualitative, with no measurement reported; reasons are often hedged ("perhaps", "probably", "possibly") (pp. 15, 27, 28). The authors were participants: both in the Common Lisp Group (p. 21), and Gabriel a founder of Lucid, which became "the primary stock-hardware Lisp company" (pp. 30–31), i.e. a competitor of the Lisp machine companies (inferred). The manuscript read has unresolved citations shown as "[?]" (e.g. p. 13, p. 27).
- **Contributions:** A chronology of Lisp dialects and implementations from Lisp 1.5 to the ANSI and ISO standards; the technical evolution of selected features (NIL and T, iteration, macros, numerical facilities, notable failures); Lisp as a language laboratory; "some reflections on the forces that have driven the evolution of Lisp" (p. 1, abstract).
- **Clarity:** Clearly written and well organised; the authors warn the slice-by-slice organisation "inevitably leads to some redundancy" (p. 2). Lisp machine material is spread over several sections (2.5, 2.6, 2.9, 2.10, 2.11.2, 2.12).

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The abstract states in one place what the paper traces, examines and discusses (p. 1), and the introduction gives the section plan (p. 2). |
| Q2 | no | No communication mechanism is described; Flavors is named "a multiple inheritance, message-passing system" (p. 26) but its format, naming, ordering and busy-receiver behaviour are not described. |
| Q3 | no | The Lisp machines were built and sold (pp. 13, 26–28), but the paper's evidence is historical narrative; it reports no measurement taken from them (design or argument only, as far as the evidence goes). |
| Q4 | no | No measured claim is made: comparisons name a baseline in words (Dorado "faster than a KL-10 running single-user Interlisp", p. 14; Le Lisp on Vax 780's "about as well as Symbolics 3600's", p. 25) but give no values, version or configuration. |
| Q5 | no | Nothing is measured; no workload, hardware configuration or number of runs is reported. |
| Q6 | n/a | The abstract and the conclusions (section 5) make no quantitative claim, so the question cannot apply. |
| Q7 | no | Causes are only asserted, e.g. the Dolphin lost "primarily because it was a slow machine that ran the Interlisp virtual machine" (p. 24); the 3600 incremental collector's "relatively bad performance, possibly due to paging problems" (p. 27); none is isolated by a measurement. |
| Q8 | partly | Limits are mentioned in passing: the organisation "inevitably leads to some redundancy" (p. 2); "we do not want to claim that the other companies did not have strong significance" (p. 27). No section on limitations or on the authors' own role. |
| Q9 | yes | No author is listed as a designer or builder of the Lisp machines discussed (pp. 12–15, 26–28); but Gabriel co-founded Lucid, a stock-hardware Lisp company (p. 30), and both were in the Common Lisp Group (p. 21), so they were interested parties. |

## Extracted fields
| Field | Value | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | Steele, Gabriel (1993), *The Evolution of Lisp*, HOPL-II, ACM, pp. 231–270; P15; I2. Version read: authors' manuscript (77 pp., letter size), not the publisher's typeset version; pages are the manuscript's printed page numbers; no fixed offset to pp. 231–270 can be given (different layout) | p. 1; publisher range from the OpenAlex record |
| Paper type | retrospective (historical account): "We trace the development chronologically ... past the ascension and decline of special purpose Lisp machines" | p. 1 (abstract) |
| System | (1) Deutsch's proposed Lisp machine, 1973: a "single-user minicomputer-class machine that would be specially microcoded to run Lisp", proposal only (p. 12). (2) MIT CONS (project begun 1974 by Greenblatt, with Knight, Holloway, Jarvis): built (p. 12–13). (3) MIT CADR: "some dozens of them were built" (p. 13). (4) LMI and Symbolics CADR clones (LM-2, LMI LAMBDA) and the Symbolics 3600: deployed commercially (pp. 13, 27). (5) Xerox Alto (1973), Dorado (design from 1976, prototype 1978, redesign 1979, built for use within Xerox and some sites), Dolphin (1100, commercially available late 1970s), Dandelion (1108, early 1980s): the "D-machines" (p. 14). (6) BBN Jericho (late 1970s), "remained internal to BBN" (p. 15). (7) Three Rivers PERQ, "a poorly performing microcoded machine", commercial (pp. 26, 28). (8) TI Explorer, "a microcoded machine that also ran the MIT software", commercial (p. 28) | pp. 12–15, 26–28 |
| Levels with message semantics | Hardware and microcode: not stated (the machines are described as microcoded to run Lisp, p. 12; no message mechanism is mentioned). Instruction set: not stated. Kernel: not stated (the 3600 operating system was programmed in Zetalisp, p. 26). Language: partly, for Zetalisp on Symbolics machines: Flavors, "a multiple inheritance, message-passing system", was added (p. 26) and the window system "was written using Flavors" (p. 13); other Lisp code uses function calls (inferred). Whether the machines started message-based at any level: not stated | pp. 12, 13, 26 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | Not stated (Flavors is named object-oriented and message-passing, but what receives messages and who may access its state is not described) | p. 26 |
| Message mechanism | Not stated beyond Flavors being "message-passing" with "multiple inheritance" | p. 26 |
| Non-message primitives | Not stated as such (the paper does not discuss message sends below the language). CONS design goals included "hardware support for type checking and garbage collection" (p. 12); Lisp-Machine Lisp added "Locatives, which provided a C-like ability to point into the middle of a structure" (p. 13) | pp. 12, 13 |
| Self-definition | CONS goal: "a largely Lisp-coded implementation (less reliance on assembly language or other low-level implementation language)" (p. 12). On the 3600, "the operating system, the editor, the compiler, the network server, the garbage collector, and the window system were all programmed in Zetalisp" (p. 26). Lower base: the machines were "specially microcoded to run Lisp" (Deutsch's vision, p. 12); the Dorado "was basically an emulation machine" interpreting byte codes, and Interlisp was ported to it "using the Interlisp virtual machine model" (p. 14). Whether running programs can inspect or change these levels, and what the base costs: not stated | pp. 12, 14, 26 |
| Interposition | Not stated | — |
| Operating system functions | n/a (I2) | — |
| Cost of message primitives | Not stated | — |
| Performance results | No measured values. Qualitative statements, measurement basis not stated: Symbolics 3600 "became the industry leader in Lisp machine performance for the next 5 years" (p. 13); the Alto "proved to be underpowered for the large Interlisp environment" (p. 14); "The Dorado running Interlisp was faster than a KL-10 running single-user Interlisp" (p. 14); Dolphin performance "better than that of the Alto, but bad enough that the machine was never truly successful as a Lisp engine" (p. 14); Dandelion "considerably faster than the Dolphin but still not as fast as the Dorado" (p. 14); "On Vax 780's, Le Lisp performed about as well as Symbolics 3600's" (p. 25); first 3600's without a garbage collector: ordinary programs "did not exhaust memory for several days and intensive ones could run for about 8 hours" (basis not stated); saving the image took "up to several hours" (basis not stated) (p. 27); the later incremental collector "proved to have relatively bad performance" (p. 27). Design figures for CONS: cost "less than $70,000 per machine" and "a factor of three better storage efficiency than the PDP-10 for compiled programs" (design figure, goals) (p. 12) | pp. 12–14, 25, 27 |
| Scaling | Not stated (single-user machines; no multi-processor measurement) | — |
| Attributed causes | All stated by the authors as third-party historians (participants in the Lisp community, not Lisp machine designers); none isolated by a measurement. (1) Dolphin: "taking a beating in the performance sweepstakes, primarily because it was a slow machine that ran the Interlisp virtual machine" (p. 24); implementation (inferred). (2) 3600 incremental collector: "relatively bad performance, possibly due to paging problems" (p. 27); implementation (inferred). (3) 3600 adoption helped because "the first 3600's did not have a garbage collector, which meant that the performance penalty of garbage collecting a large address space was not observed" (p. 27). (4) Alto underpowered "even with all the code density tricks" (p. 14). (5) VAX for Lisp: function calls "could not be accurately modeled with the VAX function-call instructions"; "Page tables occupied too large a fraction of memory, and paging overhead for large Lisp programs was a problem never fully solved on the VAX" (p. 11) | pp. 11, 14, 24, 27 |
| Fate and reasons | Lisp machine companies: "ran into difficulty in the late 1980's, perhaps because they didn't fully understand the consequences of this fact" [that "for most users the value lay ultimately in the software and not in its enabling hardware technology"]; "General-purpose hardware eventually became good enough to support Lisp once again" (p. 15). "As X3J13 progressed and the power of general purpose workstations increased—largely due to development of fast risc processors—stock hardware Lisp companies dominated, forcing most of the Lisp machine companies either out of business or out of their leadership position"; "customers were not willing to buy expensive 'dedicated' computers and then spend money maintaining them" (p. 35). When non-intrusive collectors appeared on stock hardware (Lucid, Franz, 1989), the belief "fostered" by Lisp machine companies that stock-hardware Lisps "could never have the performance—particularly for garbage collection" was "proven wrong", and "the Lisp machine companies suffered" (pp. 34–35). AI winter (from 1988): "AI companies started to have substantial financial difficulties, and so did the Lisp companies" (p. 30). Per machine: Alto "not widely accepted by users" for Interlisp (p. 14); Dorado "would have proved a very nice Lisp machine if it had been made widely available commercially" (p. 14); Dolphin "never truly successful as a Lisp engine" (p. 14); Jericho internal to BBN (p. 15); PERQ "never made much of a commercial impact outside the Pittsburgh area, probably because its performance and price-performance were relatively poor" (p. 28); Xerox "in the late 1980's got out of the Lisp business", its spinoff Envos "went out of business three years after it was founded" (p. 31); TI–LMI deal "seemed to have little or no effect on the business fortunes of either company, except to inject capital into LMI, prolonging its existence" (p. 28). Stated by the authors (third party to the machines) | pp. 14, 15, 28, 30, 31, 34–35 |
| Concurrency defects | n/a (I2) | — |
| What shapes programs | n/a (I2) | — |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Benefits argued: "Freed from the address-space constraints of previous architectures, all the Lisp machine companies produced greatly expanded Lisp implementations" (p. 15); with "greater speed and much greater address space" the MIT Lisp Machines let tools be written in Lisp (p. 6); CONS design goals (p. 12, see Performance results). Costs argued: "expensive 'dedicated' computers" (p. 35); Lisp machines "not as available and often were prohibitively expensive in Europe" (p. 25); general-purpose hardware with fast RISC processors caught up (pp. 15, 35); hardware GC support went unused early on: "users preferred to disable" the collector (p. 13). Common Lisp's portability goal was to "exclude features requiring microcode or hardware" (p. 23). Whether any of this applies to a message send as primitive: not addressed by the paper | pp. 6, 12, 13, 15, 23, 25, 35 |
| Model equivalence | n/a (I2) | — |
| Model mixing | n/a (I2) | — |
| Runtime limits | n/a (I2) | — |
| Many-core scaling | n/a (I2) | — |
| Adoption factors | Lisp machines (adopted, then declined): end-1970s lack of alternatives, "it appeared that the Vax was all there was" and Lisp machines "were the wave of the future" (p. 12); PDP-10 18-bit address space too small for AI programs, and special-purpose Lisp machines were "One response" (pp. 10–11); spread of their ideas "driven as much by the success and cachet of the Lisp machines as by the cachet of the ideas themselves" (p. 15); companies "competed primarily on the basis of hardware performance" since Symbolics, LMI and TI used software licensed from MIT (p. 26); Symbolics "most successful (as measured by number of installed machines at the end of the pre-Common-Lisp era)" (p. 27); TI Explorer "good price-performance" and "the high favor in which TI was held by the Department of Defense resulted in good sales" (p. 28); workstation performance on Lisp "not far off from the Lisp machines" by 1984 (p. 29); decline factors as in Fate and reasons (pp. 15, 30, 34–35). Software compatibility: Lisp-Machine Lisp "lived up to its stated goal of supporting MacLisp programs with only minimal porting effort" (p. 13) | pp. 10–13, 15, 26–29, 34–35 |
| Quality | Q1 yes; Q2 no; Q3 no; Q4 no; Q5 no; Q6 n/a; Q7 no; Q8 partly; Q9 yes (see table) | see Quality |
| Notes | See Notes | — |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| New: Lisp machine (special-purpose Lisp machine) | Deutsch's vision of "a single-user minicomputer-class machine that would be specially microcoded to run Lisp and support a Lisp development environment" | p. 12 |
| New: stock hardware | "commercially available, general-purpose, 'off-the-shelf' computers as opposed to computers specifically designed to support Lisp" | p. 23 |
| New: value lay in the software, not the hardware | "for most users the value lay ultimately in the software and not in its enabling hardware technology"; Lisp machine companies "perhaps" did not understand this | p. 15 |
| New: cachet | Adoption of Lisp machine ideas "driven as much by the success and cachet of the Lisp machines as by the cachet of the ideas themselves"; the "allure of cachet" behind industry interest in Lisp and AI | pp. 15, 29 |
| New: dedicated computers | Customers "not willing to buy expensive 'dedicated' computers and then spend money maintaining them" | p. 35 |
| New: general-purpose hardware good enough | "General-purpose hardware eventually became good enough to support Lisp once again"; workstation power increased "largely due to development of fast risc processors" | pp. 15, 35 |
| New: ephemeral garbage collection | Moon's collector for Lisp Machines that made continuous collection accepted, "subsequently adapted for use on stock hardware" | pp. 13, 27, 34 |
| New: CDR-coding | Compact representation of linear lists, one of two lasting ideas from Deutsch's Lisp machine proposal | p. 12 |
| New: emulation machine | The Dorado, "specifically designed to interpret byte codes produced by compilers ... basically an emulation machine" | p. 14 |
| New: Flavors | "a so-called non-hierarchical object-oriented language, a multiple inheritance, message-passing system", driven by the needs of the Lisp machine window system | p. 26 |
| New: AI winter | Term "first used in 1988 to describe the unfortunate commercial fate of AI"; it brought financial difficulties to Lisp companies | p. 30 |
| New: sufficiently smart compiler (SSC) | The argument, repeated in the Common Lisp Group, that a "sufficiently smart compiler" could solve a particular problem on stock hardware | p. 23 |

## Notes
- **Source read:** authors' manuscript "The Evolution of Lisp" from Richard Gabriel's site, https://www.dreamsongs.com/Files/Hopl2.pdf (77 pp., letter size, PDF created 2001-04-01; SHA-256 a3aedae8...2d3a), read 2026-10-07 and saved as `papers/P15.pdf`. It is not the publisher's typeset version (HOPL-II, pp. 231–270, per OpenAlex); pages cited are its printed numbers 1–77, and no fixed offset to the publisher's pages exists. It has unresolved citations printed as "[?]" (e.g. pp. 13, 25, 27).
- **Publisher's version not reached:** OpenAlex marks the ACM record gold open access (https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/155360.155373), but dl.acm.org returned HTTP 403 (bot check) for all three DOIs.
- **Longer version exists:** the same site has `HOPL2-Uncut.pdf` (109 pp., PDF created 2005), "The Evolution of Lisp" by the same authors. Its section 2.6 "Lisp Machines" (pp. 25–31 there) is much longer than in the version read: it opens with a technical discussion of stock hardware versus Lisp machines, naming "tagging, function calling, and garbage collection" as "the most frequently hardware-assisted operations" (uncut, p. 25). This version was only compared, not read; this record does not use it.
- **Criterion:** I2 holds on the full text. The paper is a historical account (p. 1) of architectures the authors describe as "specially microcoded to run Lisp" (p. 12) and "specifically designed to support Lisp" (p. 23), and it states reasons for their adoption and decline (pp. 15, 27, 28, 34–35). No exclusion criterion applies: not a survey (X9), conference paper of 40 pages (X5), in English (X6).
- The paper may also bear on SQ6/SQ19-style adoption questions under I4 (inferred); the SQ files were not inputs, so this is not checked.
- Gabriel and Steele were participants and, through Lucid, interested parties in the stock-hardware side of the story (pp. 21, 30–31); the reasons for the Lisp machines' decline are theirs, not their designers'.

9. I Introduction
   In 1981, Intel introduced the first object-based microproc-
essor, the iAPX 432 [Intel 8 1, Rattner 81, Organick 831. Like

   The concepts of object-based computing are deeply imbed-

+## Reference

+Steele, G. L., Jr., Gabriel, R. P. (1993). *The Evolution of Lisp*. HOPL-II (History of Programming Languages II), ACM, pp. 231–270. https://doi.org/10.1145/154766.155373 (other records: 10.1145/155360.155373; 10.1145/234286.1057818). Included under I2 (R0-017). Pages below are the printed page numbers (1–77) of the authors' manuscript saved as `papers/P15.pdf`, not the publisher's pages; see Notes.
+## Deepest pass

+2 (first pass of the whole paper: title, abstract, contents, introduction, section headings, section 5 scanned; second pass of every passage on Lisp machines and stock hardware: sections 2.5, 2.6, 2.9, 2.10.1–2.10.2, 2.11–2.12, pp. 10–35. Sections 3 and 4, on language features and Lisp as a language laboratory, were only searched for Lisp machine passages.)
+## First pass: the five Cs

+- **Category:** Historical account of a programming language (a HOPL paper), organised as "a series of slices through the subject matter" (p. 2): projects and people, technical themes, Lisp as a language laboratory, and why Lisp evolved as it did. It includes a history of the "ascension and decline of special purpose Lisp machines" (p. 1, abstract).

+- **Context:** Picks up "where McCarthy's paper in the first HOPL conference left off" (p. 1, abstract; p. 2). Sources are mostly the authors' own participation, mailing lists and manuals; the reference list includes Lisp machine papers and manuals (Deutsch 1973, Greenblatt 1974, Moon 1984, Weinreb and Moon 1978/1981) (pp. 12–13).

+- **Correctness:** The Lisp machine claims are narrative and qualitative, with no measurement reported; reasons are often hedged ("perhaps", "probably", "possibly") (pp. 15, 27, 28). The authors were participants: both in the Common Lisp Group (p. 21), and Gabriel a founder of Lucid, which became "the primary stock-hardware Lisp company" (pp. 30–31), i.e. a competitor of the Lisp machine companies (inferred). The manuscript read has unresolved citations shown as "[?]" (e.g. p. 13, p. 27).

+- **Contributions:** A chronology of Lisp dialects and implementations from Lisp 1.5 to the ANSI and ISO standards; the technical evolution of selected features (NIL and T, iteration, macros, numerical facilities, notable failures); Lisp as a language laboratory; "some reflections on the forces that have driven the evolution of Lisp" (p. 1, abstract).

+- **Clarity:** Clearly written and well organised; the authors warn the slice-by-slice organisation "inevitably leads to some redundancy" (p. 2). Lisp machine material is spread over several sections (2.5, 2.6, 2.9, 2.10, 2.11.2, 2.12).
+## Quality
+| Q | Answer | Why |
+| Q1 | yes | The abstract states in one place what the paper traces, examines and discusses (p. 1), and the introduction gives the section plan (p. 2). |

+| Q2 | no | No communication mechanism is described; Flavors is named "a multiple inheritance, message-passing system" (p. 26) but its format, naming, ordering and busy-receiver behaviour are not described. |

+| Q3 | no | The Lisp machines were built and sold (pp. 13, 26–28), but the paper's evidence is historical narrative; it reports no measurement taken from them (design or argument only, as far as the evidence goes). |

+| Q4 | no | No measured claim is made: comparisons name a baseline in words (Dorado "faster than a KL-10 running single-user Interlisp", p. 14; Le Lisp on Vax 780's "about as well as Symbolics 3600's", p. 25) but give no values, version or configuration. |
+| Q5 | no | Nothing is measured; no workload, hardware configuration or number of runs is reported. |
+| Q6 | n/a | The abstract and the conclusions (section 5) make no quantitative claim, so the question cannot apply. |

+| Q7 | no | Causes are only asserted, e.g. the Dolphin lost "primarily because it was a slow machine that ran the Interlisp virtual machine" (p. 24); the 3600 incremental collector's "relatively bad performance, possibly due to paging problems" (p. 27); none is isolated by a measurement. |

+| Q8 | partly | Limits are mentioned in passing: the organisation "inevitably leads to some redundancy" (p. 2); "we do not want to claim that the other companies did not have strong significance" (p. 27). No section on limitations or on the authors' own role. |

+| Q9 | yes | No author is listed as a designer or builder of the Lisp machines discussed (pp. 12–15, 26–28); but Gabriel co-founded Lucid, a stock-hardware Lisp company (p. 30), and both were in the Common Lisp Group (p. 21), so they were interested parties. |

(1) Dolphin: "taking a beating in the performance sweepstakes, primarily because it was a slow machine that ran the Interlisp virtual machine" (p. 24); implementation (inferred). (2) 3600 incremental collector: "relatively bad performance, possibly due to paging problems" (p. 27); implementation (inferred). (3) 3600 adoption helped because "the first 3600's did not have a garbage collector, which meant that the performance penalty of garbage collecting a large address space was not observed" (p. 27). (4) Alto underpowered "even with all the code density tricks" (p. 14). (5) VAX for Lisp: function calls "could not be accurately modeled with the VAX function-call instructions"; "Page tables occupied too large a fraction of memory, and paging overhead for large Lisp programs was a problem never fully solved on the VAX" (p. 11) | pp. 11, 14, 24, 27 |

  9.8 Discussion
  The Intel iAPX 432 is certainly one of the most sophisti-
  cated architectures in existence. By using the object-oriented
  approach throughout the development effort, the Intel 432
  designers have produced an extremely uniform and tightly-in-
  tegrated hardware/software system. This uniformity of hard-
  ware and software systems is due to the use of a consistent
  philosophy. Everything in the Intel 432 is an object. All objects
  have associated types that specify the operations that can be
  performed on those objects. Some objects have hardware-de-
  fined operations while others do not. However, from a lan-
  guage viewpoint, all objects are accessedin the same way.
  All objects, whether hardware-supported or not, are con-
  trolled by type manager modules. Programmers can freely add
  new types to the system by creating new type managers. The
  mechanisms of domain refinement and type definition object
  provide a way for type managersto exhibit privilege over their
  objects and the environments in which their procedures exe-
  cute. A type manager can restrict and later amplify privileges
  in ADS for its objects by using a privately held type control
  object. By permitting client accessto type management proce-
  dures through a refinement, an executing type management
  procedure can obtain accessto a richer environment than its
  caller.
  There are no special privileges in the Intel 432 system. The
  mechanisms used by programmer-defined type managers are

         I                   ABSTRACT
    The Smalltalk On A RISC lroject at U.C. Berkeley proved that
good performance executing a high-level language on a modified
RISC architecture was attainable. The system removed a layer of
interpretation, translating bytecodes to a register-based instruction
set. This paper describes the bytecode translator and how it was
affected by SOAR architectural features. The translator generates
code of reasonable density and speed. Because of bytecode seman-
tics, relatively few optimizations are possible, but hardware and
software mechanisms at runtime offset these limitations. Register
allocation with register windows is the major task of the compiler.
Several hardware features -could be easily performed by the com-
piler.

1. Introduction

     The goal of the Smailtalk On A RISC (SOAR) project at U.C. Berkeley was to
produce a high-performance execution engine for the Smalltalk-80 1 language [1]. The
heart of the effort is a Berkeley RISC processor extended to support Smalltalk [2]. The
processor was designed in conjunction with the runtime system [3], which together
have yielded substantial performance improvements over conventional Smalltalk-80
implementations. An extensive performance evaluation can be found in Ungar's disser-
tation [4]; SOAR runs Smalltalk roughly 2.5 times as fast as a Motorola 68010 with a
similar cycle time, which works out to be about the same speed as the Xerox Dorado
high-performance workstation. One reason for the SOAR system's speed is its compila-
tion of Smalltalk, It has been estimated that compiling Smalltalk to the SOAR
instruction set produces a factor of two speedup over conventional interpreted sys-
tems. This paper describes the SOAR compiler, presenting the mechanisms of compil-
ing Smalltalk to the special-purpose SOAR RISC instruction set.                            "

2. The Nature of the Compiler

     The Smalltalk-80 language is defined operationally in terms of a virtual machine
that executes stack-based instructions called bytecodes. The Smalltalk-80 program-
ming environment is a binary image that runs on the virtual machine. The problem
with the virtual machine is that it is inefficient if naively implemented.   It is com-
monly realized as a bytecode interpreter, which requires special hardware (such as that
possessed by the Dorado) to avoid interposing a layer of overhead between the virtual
machine and the native machine.

     An alternative is to compile bytecodes to native machine instructions, an
approach successfully taken by Deutsch and Schiffman [5]. The Deutsch and Schiffman
system dynamically translates procedures (called methods in Smalltalk) as needed,
keeping a cache of native-code methods and flushing the least-recently-used ones. The

    'Smaltaik-90 isa trademark of Xerox Corporation.

SOAR system takes this approach a step further and compiles all methods from
bytecodes into SOAR instructions - the canonical representation of a method in the
SOAR system is as SOAR instructions, not bytecodes. Where caching is done for space
efficiency, compiling everything simplifies and speeds up the system for a moderate
cost in space.

       We considered compiling      Smalitalk directly to SOAR,      avoiding bytecodes

entirely, but we did not take this path for three reasons. First, the virtual machine is
the semantic definition of the language. This implies that a correct bytecode compiler
is, along with correct system functions, a correct Smalltalk implementation. Second,

keeping bytecodes as an intermediate form permits mixed-mode debugging like that
found in LISP systems, where functions to be debugged are interpreted, and tested
functions that should run fast are compiled. Third, the standard virtual image is a
bytecode-based image; to produce a SOAR-based native image those bytecodes must
be translated to SOAR instructions. Rather than develop two separate compilers, one
for taking bytecodes to SOAR and another for compiling Smalltalk to SOAR, we
implemented one bytecode compiler with two implementations: a C version for image
conversion, and a Smalltalk version for use with the converted image. Debugging is
addressed in more detail in Lee's report [8], and image conversion in a recent paper
[3].

       The basic task of the compiler is to translate stack-oriented bytecodes into

RISC-style loads, stores, and other register-based instructions. It does this by assigning
Smalltalk variables and stack locations to registers and memory locations, and then
simulating at compile time the bytecode stack operations, converting them to SOAR
operations.      The simulated stack is used to remember value sources and operations;
when a value destination is encountered the code to load, compute, and store the value

is generated. If the Smaltalk variables A and B are assigned to registers, for example,
a push of A and a pop-and-store into B is translated into a register-to-register move;
the simulated stack is used to remember the source A until the destination B is
encountered.      The stack is simulated at compile time to avoid unnecessary computa-
tions at runtime.

      In this regard, the Smalltalk bytecodes perform the same function as any stack-
based intermediate language such as, for example, UCODE [7].                        Bytecodes are unlike
UCODE in that, as we will discuss later, they restrict the compiler writer, particularly
in implementing optimizations that would result in code motion or that require type
information to perform. For example, common subexpression elimination is exception-
ally difficult to do in Smalltalk.

      Given the restrictive semantics of the Smalltalk bytecodes and the simple archi-
tecture of SOAR, the compiler falls or stands on its success in mapping Smalltalk vari-
ables to registers and memory.


3. SOAR Register Windows

      One feature of the Berkeley RISC architectures is a register file of overlapping
register windows, each window corresponding to a procedure activation frame. The
windows are allocated on procedure call in a stack discipline, using the registers in the
window overlap to pass parameters. The advantage of register windows is fast pro-
cedure call and return, avoiding the saving and restoring of registers. Tests with
benchmarks indicate that SOAR Smalltalk would be 46% slower without them.2

      It is crucial that the size of these register windows be chosen wisely. If a method
requires more storage than can fit in a window, the extra values are spilled to
memory, slowing down the procedure call and the method's execution as well as
increasing its code size. If windows are too small, an excessive number of methods will
spill, degrading the performance of the whole system. On the other hand, if windows
are too large, registers will be wasted and fewer windows can be accommodated on the
processor chip.

      For SOAR, the goal was to have 90% to W% of all activation frames fit in
SOAR windows. Preliminary studies [9] indicated that a window size of 10 registers
with complete overlap was best. The SOAR windows are smaller than those of other
RISC designs such as RISC 11, which has 32, because Smalltalk methods are

      2 All results quoted in this paper are found in either Ungar's dissertation 141 or Bush's report 181, un-
les stated otherwise.
                                                                                           4


correspondingly    smaller   than   procedures   in   more   traditional   imperative-style
languages.

     An alternative would have been to use variable size windows at some expense in
hardware [10]. For SOAR, we concluded that variable size windows would not result
in significant enough improvement to offset the additional hardware complexity.

     The SOAR hardware divides each window into two identical sets of 8 registers, a
high set (15-8) and a low set (7-0). Each set contains 6 general purpose registers and 2
dedicated registers used for return addresses (15 and 7) and return values (14 and 6).

     The current method receives its parameters and stores its local variables in the
high register set. It sets up parameters for any methods that it calls in the low set.
Unlike other RISC designs, the SOAR architecture has no registers dedicated solely for
local use -- all are shared between two activation records. This allows the compiler
flexibility in register allocation -- registers can be used for arguments or local values
depending on what is appropriate. Temporaries that must persist through calls to
other methods ('retained' temporaries) are put in free high registers. 'Transitory' tem-
poraries (those whose life spans do not cross procedure calls, such as intermediate
results from compiler-generated expressions) can be put in the lows. Figure 1 presents
this categorization pictorially.

     Allocating variables and temporaries to registers is complicated by the fact that
it is possible to write a Smalltalk method whose variables and temporaries will not all
fit in a register window. When more registers are required than are available, we
resort to spilling. There are two rules used to determine what and when to spill to
memory. The first rule of assignment by category specifies that entire categories of
variables are spilled -- if not all of the arguments fit in the registers, for example, all
are spilled. The second rule of permanent assignment means that a variable cannot be
moved once it has been allocated a location -- if, for example, a local variable has been
put in a register, it will not later be spilled to make room for a temporary. Neither of
these rules result in minimal register usage or minimal memory traffic, but they are
reasonable and simple. Since a major goal of the SOAR architectural design was to
minimize spills at a reasonable cost, their infrequent occurrence justified an easily

       Spills can be implemented in one of two ways. First, space can be allocated from
a common spill pool, or a separate spill object can be allocated for each activation

frame that spills. The former has complications for garbage collection and processes,
and the latter eats up a register in each spilling frame. Both techniques have been
tried in SOAR; neither has shown itself to be clearly superior over the other.


4. How the SOAR Architecture Simplifies the Compiler

       Register windows and spills complicate the compiler; SOAR architectural support
for Smalltalk has in the main simplified it. An important architectural feature allows
the compiler to generate standard arithmetic and comparison instructions in spite of
the fact that the operations may be on non-integer objects.

       Since Smalltalk is polymorphic and variable types are not known at compile
time, it is never safe to generate integer instructions without runtime type checking.

The virtual machine requires a dynamic method lookup on each operator, including
'+'.    Implementing this lookup naively is very expensive. Studies have shown [II] that
in fact most arithmetic operations in Smalltalk involve only integers. SOAR takes
advantage of this fact by assuming all simple arithmetic operations (plus, minus, com-
parisons, etc.) will be performed only on integers. The compiler thus treats all such
operations as if they were on integers, and generates integer code.                   If, say, an add
instruction is initiated on two objects, and one or both of them turn out to be non-
integers, the hardware will trap and transfer to a handler that will look up the correct

method for the intended operation.            When the execution of the looked-up method is
complete, the trap handler returns to the instruction immediately following the one
that caused the trap.

       It would not be difficult for the compiler to generate code to test explicitly for
integer tags, but it would slow down system performance by an estimated 26% and


       'The Smalltalk and the C versions of the compiler differ in this regard: the C version effectively
makes two passes over each method. However, speed was not as critical for the C version as for the
Smalltalk version.

                                                                                                                                   7


               would increase image size by 15%.

                       The tag mechanism is also used to provide hardware assist for garbage collection,
               thus further simplifying the task of code generation. SOAR uses a generation scaveng-
               ing scheme, dividing memory into regions of old and new objects, and uses generation
               tags on pointers to detect when pointers to new objects are stored into old ones. The
               tag check is performed in the hardware, and a trap handler records the necessary
               information if a trap is taken. Benchmark results indicate that tagged stores are so
               rare that the compiler could in fact generate explicit tests and only slow the system
               about 1% and expand the image 2%.

                       The compiler also takes advantage of hardware that maps registers to memory
               addresses, and allows what we call a pointer to register. Since a Smalltalk program
               can access any object in memory, and activation records are just another kind of
               object, it is necessary to handle references to them. Remember that activation records
               exist as on-chip register windows. The pointer to register feature permits the compiler
               to ignore complications that would otherwise be caused by overt references to activa-
               tion records. Once again, however, it turns out that checking for pointers to activa-
               tion records is not as severe a problem as it was initially feared to be. The instances
               requiring such a check do not occur often, and Ungar concluded that the feature could
               be removed with only a 3% performance penalty.

               5. How Bytecode Compilation Simplifies the Compiler

                       Both language and pragmatic considerations limited the optimizations we could
               perform.

               next concatenate two strings. In the latter case it is not true that 'A+B' equals 'B+A'.
               Furthermore, which method is invoked is, by definition, a function of the leftmost
               operand ('A' in our example). Together these facts preclude almost all expression
               evaluation optimization.

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Design description of a planned machine (the J-Machine and its node, the Message-Driven Processor, MDP), written at the "advanced design stage", with design figures and no evaluation section (pp. 1, 13).
- **Context:** Message-passing multicomputers (Caltech Cosmic Cube, Intel iPSC, N-CUBE, Ametek), shared-address machines (BBN Butterfly, IBM RP3), single-chip nodes (InMOS transputer, Caltech MOSAIC) (p. 3); concurrent models it aims to support: actors, dataflow, communicating processes (pp. 1–2); the authors' own earlier MDP and network papers [5–10, 12–15] (pp. 3, 6, 14).
- **Correctness:** The premise is that "A fast network is of little use if very large overheads are required to initiate and receive messages at the processing nodes" (p. 7) and that the difficulty "is not developing the mechanisms conceptually. It is implementing them efficiently" (p. 5). Both are argued, not measured; the only comparison is delivery plus dispatch "< 3µs on the J-Machine as opposed to 5ms on an iPSC" (p. 3).
- **Contributions:** A message-driven node: a SEND instruction, automatic hardware buffering into two priority queues, and a dispatch mechanism that creates a task per arriving message in one clock cycle, with "no receive instruction" (pp. 7–9); tags for futures and c-futures (p. 12); ENTER/XLATE translation instructions exposing a set-associative cache to support a global virtual address space (pp. 12–13); a 3-D mesh network of up to 65,536 nodes (pp. 2, 5).
- **Clarity:** Short and clear, with a worked end-to-end example (Sum message, Figure 1, pp. 4–5) and assembly fragments (Figures 4, 6; pp. 8, 10). The scan is legible; the OCR text layer has errors in units (µs), checked against the page images.

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Design description of a planned machine (the J-Machine and its node, the Message-Driven Processor, MDP), written at the "advanced design stage", with design figures and no evaluation section (pp. 1, 13).
- **Context:** Message-passing multicomputers (Caltech Cosmic Cube, Intel iPSC, N-CUBE, Ametek), shared-address machines (BBN Butterfly, IBM RP3), single-chip nodes (InMOS transputer, Caltech MOSAIC) (p. 3); concurrent models it aims to support: actors, dataflow, communicating processes (pp. 1–2); the authors' own earlier MDP and network papers [5–10, 12–15] (pp. 3, 6, 14).
- **Correctness:** The premise is that "A fast network is of little use if very large overheads are required to initiate and receive messages at the processing nodes" (p. 7) and that the difficulty "is not developing the mechanisms conceptually. It is implementing them efficiently" (p. 5). Both are argued, not measured; the only comparison is delivery plus dispatch "< 3µs on the J-Machine as opposed to 5ms on an iPSC" (p. 3).
- **Contributions:** A message-driven node: a SEND instruction, automatic hardware buffering into two priority queues, and a dispatch mechanism that creates a task per arriving message in one clock cycle, with "no receive instruction" (pp. 7–9); tags for futures and c-futures (p. 12); ENTER/XLATE translation instructions exposing a set-associative cache to support a global virtual address space (pp. 12–13); a 3-D mesh network of up to 65,536 nodes (pp. 2, 5).
- **Clarity:** Short and clear, with a worked end-to-end example (Sum message, Figure 1, pp. 4–5) and assembly fragments (Figures 4, 6; pp. 8, 10). The scan is legible; the OCR text layer has errors in units (µs), checked against the page images.

| Q2 | partly | Three of the four are given: message format (EXECUTE <priority> <opcode> <arg>…, p. 191); naming (physical opcode address, global object identifiers, pp. 189, 191–192); busy receiver (buffered until idle or lower priority, p. 191; queue-overflow trap, p. 192). Ordering and delivery guarantees are not stated. |
| Q3 | partly | The evidence is from "instruction-level and a register-transfer (RT) level simulators" (p. 195). The chip is a prototype still to be built ("will have", p. 193). |
| Q4 | partly | The order-of-magnitude claim names baseline machines (Cosmic Cube, iPSC, S-NET at "about 300µs", p. 190) but gives no version or configuration. Table 1 has no baseline (p. 195). |
| Q5 | partly | The simulators and the expected 100 ns clock are given (p. 195). There are no workloads beyond "a number of simple operations", no reason for choosing them, and no run counts (p. 195). |
| Q6 | partly | "Less than ten clock cycles per message" and the order-of-magnitude reduction are backed by Table 1 and p. 190. "Access … 2^28 words … in less than 10µs" and "an order of magnitude more concurrency" (stated as a conjecture) have no supporting data (pp. 195–196). |
| Q7 | no | The causes are only asserted, e.g. "The MDP achieves much of its performance by using a message-driven control mechanism" (p. 195). No breakdown or ablation is given. |
| Q8 | partly | One objection (memory "unbalanced" for a 4 MIP processor) is answered in passing (p. 196), and benchmarks are deferred to "the near future" (p. 195). There is no limitations section. |
| Q9 | no | All authors propose and design the architecture ("We propose…", p. 189). That all are designers is inferred from the first-person authorship. |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: message-driven processor | A processing node whose "controller is driven by the incoming message stream". Each arrival schedules a code sequence. | pp. 189, 191 |
| new: direct execution of messages | Overhead is reduced "by directly executing messages rather than interpreting them with sequences of instructions". "no instructions are required to receive or buffer the message". | pp. 189, 191 |
| new: single primitive message (EXECUTE) | Only EXECUTE <priority> <opcode> <arg>… is hard-wired. Richer messages are ROM macrocode, and the paper says they run "almost as efficiently" as hard-wired ones. | p. 191 |
| new: message unit / instruction unit split | The MU receives, buffers and vectors. The IU "simply executes instructions". | pp. 189, 192, 195 |
| new: memory-based architecture for fast context switches | Instructions read or write on-chip memory in one cycle. With four general registers, a context saves or restores in under 10 cycles. | pp. 189, 191, 196 |
| new: priority register sets | Two register sets, one per priority level, so a low-priority message is preempted "without saving state". | pp. 189, 191 |
| new: associative (set-associative) memory | The same on-chip memory is accessed by address or by content. It is used to translate object IDs to node and address, and class+selector to a method address (a method cache). | pp. 189, 193 |
| new: global name space / object identifiers | Global object IDs are translated at run time. Code is kept as one distributed copy. Local and non-local objects are handled uniformly through tags and traps. | pp. 189, 194, 196 |
| new: futures via tags | A reply target is tagged "context future". Use before the reply suspends the context. | pp. 190, 194–195 |
| new: fine-grain concurrency (grain size) | The natural grain is "about 20 instruction times". The MDP aims at about 10 instructions, against several hundred on existing machines. | pp. 190, 195 |
| new: congestion as governor (no send queue) | With no send queue, network congestion blocks producing objects. | p. 191 |

## Notes
- **Source and version:** ACM Digital Library publisher PDF of the ISCA '87 paper (© 1987 ACM, pp. 189–196), not the 1998 reprint (10.1145/285930.285993). dl.acm.org returned HTTP 403 to direct download, so the identical PDF was taken from the Internet Archive snapshot of https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/30350.30372 (timestamp 20240413161934) and saved as `papers/P69.pdf`. It is a scan with an OCR text layer. Table 1 (p. 195) was checked on the rendered page image.
- **Criterion:** screening's I1 is confirmed: the message-transmit instruction (I1(a), p. 192) and hardware message buffering and dispatch (I1(b), pp. 191–192). No exclusion criterion applies. It is not X3: the message mechanism is in the processor itself, not only in the network interface (pp. 189, 191). It is not X4: the node is for general concurrent programs and is described as an emulator for "other programming models" (p. 196). I2 is not met, because this is a design proposal, not a retrospective or evaluation of an existing architecture.
- **Relation to P12:** this paper is the 1987 architecture proposal of the MDP. From this paper alone, the design read here (single EXECUTE message, two priority levels, 4K-word memory-based node, expected 100 ns clock; pp. 189–191, 195) is a design stage with simulated results only. Whether the results overlap P12's (X8) is for the gate. This record was written from P69 alone.
- The comparison figure of "about 300µs" for Cosmic Cube, iPSC and S-NET (p. 190) carries no citation or measurement setup in the text.

    When a call occurs, the processor reads the context link
field to find the AD for the next context object to use. The
length of this object is compared with the length fields stored
in the called instruction object. If the instruction object re-
quires a context object larger than the preallocated size, a fault
will occur. The operating system can then allocate a context of
the needed size. Or, if the context link is null, indicating that
the preallocated contexts have been consumed, a fault will
allow the operating system to perform additional allocations.
Otherwise, the hardware quickly constructs the new context
object from the linked segment.

9.4.5 Parameter Passing
   Parameter passing on the Intel 432 is associated with the
preallocation of contexts and is handled by software. In addi-
tion to the default context object size, associated with each
process is a default data part size and access part size of a
parametersegmento be passed between contexts on procedure
calls. However, instead of allocating a separateparameter seg-
ment, an area of the data part and accesspart of each context
object is reserved for parameter passing. When the operating
system constructs the linked list of contexts, it places in the
context messagefield of each context, an AD for a refinementof
the previous context object. This refinement provides address-
ability to the parameter data and accessfields as if they were a
single contiguous segment.
    Figure 9-9 illustrates how a procedure accessesparameters
passed by its caller. The calling procedure places its data and
accessparameters in the predefmed parameter fields of its con-
text object. The operating system had previously created a re-
finement object descriptor for these parameter spaces and
placed an AD for the refinement in the next context object.
When the call occurs, the called context can accessits parame-
ters through its context messageAD.

object-based programming. As previously described, the Intel
432 provides a set of basic system object types. Each of the
system object types is controlled by a type manager that is
implemented partially in hardware-through a set of type-spe-
cific instructions-and partially in operating system software.                         173

In addition, the dynamic/system bit (bit 0) of the TCO must
indicate that the TCO is for a system object. TCOs for the
creation of specific system object types are constructed by the
operating system and given to the operating system type man-
agers for those types. The type manager for a system object is
privileged only in its possession of the TCO for its type.
    Possessionof a TCO for a specific type also allows the type
manager to execute an AMPLIFY RIGHTS instruction for objects
of its type. In this way, the type manager can return restricted
ADS to its clients. These restricted ADS cannot be used to
accessthe objects to which they refer. When a client returns an
AD to a type manager as a parameter, however, the type man-
ager can use its TCO to amplify the rights in the AD. Given an
AD for an object and an AD for a TCO with matching type,
the MPLIFY RIGHTS instruction ORs the rights bits specified in
the TCO with the rights in the object AD, creating an AD with
additional privileges. If the TCO and AD types do not match,
the AMPLIFY RIGHTS instruction will cause a fault.


9.5.3 Programmer-Defined Types
   To build a private type management system, a programmer
obtains a type definition object (TDO) from the operating sys-
tem. A TDO has no processor-defined fields, although its ac-
cess part will typically be used to hold ADS for the domains
that implement the type manager. The basic function of the
TDO is to be the representative “type” for its objects. That is,
while the type of a system object is specified by an 8-bit system
object type field, the type of a dynamic object is specified by an
AD for a TDO. All objects created by a specific type manager
have an image of the AD for the type manager’s TDO stored in
their object table object descriptor (shown as TDO-AD in Fig-
ure 9-3).
   Once a type manager has obtained a TDO, it then obtains a
TCO from the operating system for its type. This TCO will be
for a dynamic object, as specified in its system type field and in
the dynamic/system field. A TCO for a dynamic object con-
tains an additional field-a single AD in its accesspart. This is
the AD for the defining TDO. When the type manager exe-
cutes a CREATE TYPED OBJECT instruction to allocate a Se@lXnt
for the object’s representation, it specifies its TCO and the size
of the segment to allocate. The hardware copies the TDO ac-
cessdescriptor from the TCO into the object descriptor for the                         177

  object type manager, protects its objects using restriction and
  amplification. When a client requests the creation of a new
  object, the type manager creates the object using the CREATE

  specifies this AD as a parameter, the type manager amplifies
  rights in the AD to regain accessto the object’s representation.
  Once again, the key to amplification is the possession of a
  TCO. The type manager executes an AMPLIFY RIGHTS instruc-

  the TCO and the object descriptor for the object both contain

9.6 Storage     Resources                                             9.6 Storage Resources

   Previous sections have described the creation of storage seg-
ments through the CREATE OBJECT and CREATE TYPED OBJECT
instructions; however, they have not described the mechanism
by which primary memory is allocated. The abstraction of pri-
mary storage is encapsulated in Intel 432 storage resourceobjects.
A storage resource object (SRO) is a system object from which
memory is allocated. Every memory allocation instruction
specifies, either explicitly or by default, an SRO from which its
primary memory is taken.
    Figure 9-13 illustrates the structure of an SRO and its asso-
ciated objects. The representation of an SRO consists princi-
pally of the AD for a physical storage object that describes a pool
of available primary memory, and an AD for an object table.
Each storage specifier in the physical storage object contains
the primary memory address and size of a single contiguous
block of free system memory. Initially, each physical storage -
object has one storage specifier for a single large block. As
storage is dynamically allocated and deallocated from an SRO,
its memory becomes fragmented and new storage specifiers
must be created to address the discontiguous pieces.

  9.8 Discussion
  The Intel iAPX 432 is certainly one of the most sophisti-
  cated architectures in existence. By using the object-oriented
  approach throughout the development effort, the Intel 432
  designers have produced an extremely uniform and tightly-in-
  tegrated hardware/software system. This uniformity of hard-
  ware and software systems is due to the use of a consistent
  philosophy. Everything in the Intel 432 is an object. All objects
  have associated types that specify the operations that can be
  performed on those objects. Some objects have hardware-de-
  fined operations while others do not. However, from a lan-
  guage viewpoint, all objects are accessedin the same way.
  All objects, whether hardware-supported or not, are con-
  trolled by type manager modules. Programmers can freely add
  new types to the system by creating new type managers. The
  mechanisms of domain refinement and type definition object
  provide a way for type managersto exhibit privilege over their
  objects and the environments in which their procedures exe-
  cute. A type manager can restrict and later amplify privileges
  in ADS for its objects by using a privately held type control
  object. By permitting client accessto type management proce-
  dures through a refinement, an executing type management
  procedure can obtain accessto a richer environment than its
  caller.

  mechanisms used by programmer-defined type managers are

             Compiling Smalltalk-80 to a RISC


         I                   ABSTRACT
    The Smalltalk On A RISC lroject at U.C. Berkeley proved that
good performance executing a high-level language on a modified
RISC architecture was attainable. The system removed a layer of
interpretation, translating bytecodes to a register-based instruction
set. This paper describes the bytecode translator and how it was
affected by SOAR architectural features. The translator generates
code of reasonable density and speed. Because of bytecode seman-
tics, relatively few optimizations are possible, but hardware and
software mechanisms at runtime offset these limitations. Register
allocation with register windows is the major task of the compiler.
Several hardware features -could be easily performed by the com-
piler.

                          Compiling Smalltalk-80 to a RISC


1. Introduction

     The goal of the Smailtalk On A RISC (SOAR) project at U.C. Berkeley was to
produce a high-performance execution engine for the Smalltalk-80 1 language [1]. The
heart of the effort is a Berkeley RISC processor extended to support Smalltalk [2]. The
processor was designed in conjunction with the runtime system [3], which together
have yielded substantial performance improvements over conventional Smalltalk-80
implementations. An extensive performance evaluation can be found in Ungar's disser-
tation [4]; SOAR runs Smalltalk roughly 2.5 times as fast as a Motorola 68010 with a
similar cycle time, which works out to be about the same speed as the Xerox Dorado
high-performance workstation. One reason for the SOAR system's speed is its compila-
tion of Smalltalk, It has been estimated that compiling Smalltalk to the SOAR
instruction set produces a factor of two speedup over conventional interpreted sys-
tems. This paper describes the SOAR compiler, presenting the mechanisms of compil-
ing Smalltalk to the special-purpose SOAR RISC instruction set.                            "

2. The Nature of the Compiler

     The Smalltalk-80 language is defined operationally in terms of a virtual machine
that executes stack-based instructions called bytecodes. The Smalltalk-80 program-
ming environment is a binary image that runs on the virtual machine. The problem
with the virtual machine is that it is inefficient if naively implemented.   It is com-
monly realized as a bytecode interpreter, which requires special hardware (such as that
possessed by the Dorado) to avoid interposing a layer of overhead between the virtual
machine and the native machine.

     An alternative is to compile bytecodes to native machine instructions, an
approach successfully taken by Deutsch and Schiffman [5]. The Deutsch and Schiffman
system dynamically translates procedures (called methods in Smalltalk) as needed,
keeping a cache of native-code methods and flushing the least-recently-used ones. The

    'Smaltaik-90 isa trademark of Xerox Corporation.


                                                                                          S'S


                              %r
                                                                                          2


SOAR system takes this approach a step further and compiles all methods from
bytecodes into SOAR instructions - the canonical representation of a method in the
SOAR system is as SOAR instructions, not bytecodes. Where caching is done for space
efficiency, compiling everything simplifies and speeds up the system for a moderate
cost in space.

       We considered compiling      Smalitalk directly to SOAR,      avoiding bytecodes

entirely, but we did not take this path for three reasons. First, the virtual machine is
the semantic definition of the language. This implies that a correct bytecode compiler
is, along with correct system functions, a correct Smalltalk implementation. Second,

keeping bytecodes as an intermediate form permits mixed-mode debugging like that
found in LISP systems, where functions to be debugged are interpreted, and tested
functions that should run fast are compiled. Third, the standard virtual image is a
bytecode-based image; to produce a SOAR-based native image those bytecodes must
be translated to SOAR instructions. Rather than develop two separate compilers, one
for taking bytecodes to SOAR and another for compiling Smalltalk to SOAR, we
implemented one bytecode compiler with two implementations: a C version for image
conversion, and a Smalltalk version for use with the converted image. Debugging is
addressed in more detail in Lee's report [8], and image conversion in a recent paper
[3].

       The basic task of the compiler is to translate stack-oriented bytecodes into

RISC-style loads, stores, and other register-based instructions. It does this by assigning
Smalltalk variables and stack locations to registers and memory locations, and then
simulating at compile time the bytecode stack operations, converting them to SOAR
operations.      The simulated stack is used to remember value sources and operations;
when a value destination is encountered the code to load, compute, and store the value

is generated. If the Smaltalk variables A and B are assigned to registers, for example,
a push of A and a pop-and-store into B is translated into a register-to-register move;
the simulated stack is used to remember the source A until the destination B is
encountered.      The stack is simulated at compile time to avoid unnecessary computa-
tions at runtime.




                     VXV P'                   No, 0     ~      ~      -      vC
                                                                                                               3


      In this regard, the Smalltalk bytecodes perform the same function as any stack-
based intermediate language such as, for example, UCODE [7].                        Bytecodes are unlike
UCODE in that, as we will discuss later, they restrict the compiler writer, particularly
in implementing optimizations that would result in code motion or that require type
information to perform. For example, common subexpression elimination is exception-
ally difficult to do in Smalltalk.

      Given the restrictive semantics of the Smalltalk bytecodes and the simple archi-
tecture of SOAR, the compiler falls or stands on its success in mapping Smalltalk vari-
ables to registers and memory.


3. SOAR Register Windows

      One feature of the Berkeley RISC architectures is a register file of overlapping
register windows, each window corresponding to a procedure activation frame. The
windows are allocated on procedure call in a stack discipline, using the registers in the
window overlap to pass parameters. The advantage of register windows is fast pro-
cedure call and return, avoiding the saving and restoring of registers. Tests with
benchmarks indicate that SOAR Smalltalk would be 46% slower without them.2

      It is crucial that the size of these register windows be chosen wisely. If a method
requires more storage than can fit in a window, the extra values are spilled to
memory, slowing down the procedure call and the method's execution as well as
increasing its code size. If windows are too small, an excessive number of methods will
spill, degrading the performance of the whole system. On the other hand, if windows
are too large, registers will be wasted and fewer windows can be accommodated on the
processor chip.

      For SOAR, the goal was to have 90% to W% of all activation frames fit in
SOAR windows. Preliminary studies [9] indicated that a window size of 10 registers
with complete overlap was best. The SOAR windows are smaller than those of other
RISC designs such as RISC 11, which has 32, because Smalltalk methods are

      2 All results quoted in this paper are found in either Ungar's dissertation 141 or Bush's report 181, un-
les stated otherwise.
                                                                                           4


correspondingly    smaller   than   procedures   in   more   traditional   imperative-style
languages.

     An alternative would have been to use variable size windows at some expense in
hardware [10]. For SOAR, we concluded that variable size windows would not result
in significant enough improvement to offset the additional hardware complexity.

     The SOAR hardware divides each window into two identical sets of 8 registers, a
high set (15-8) and a low set (7-0). Each set contains 6 general purpose registers and 2
dedicated registers used for return addresses (15 and 7) and return values (14 and 6).

     The current method receives its parameters and stores its local variables in the
high register set. It sets up parameters for any methods that it calls in the low set.
