lines: +id: P48
+row: 3a
+by: reader
+status: proposed
+inputs: [papers/P48.pdf, sls/1-protocol/quality.md, sls/1-protocol/extraction-form.md, sls/1-protocol/criteria.md, sls/1-protocol/changes/2026-10-06-reading-pilot.md]
+## Reference

+Kevin Elphinstone, Gernot Heiser (2013). *From L3 to seL4: What Have We Learnt in 20 Years of L4 Microkernels?* Proceedings of the 24th ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP '13), Farmington, PA, USA, pp. 133–150. https://doi.org/10.1145/2517349.2522720. P48, round-file row R0-065, included at screening under I1.

+Version: the proceedings version (ACM copyright block and DOI on p.133), downloaded from sigops.org (`https://www.sigops.org/s/conferences/sosp/2013/papers/p133-elphinstone.pdf`) and saved as `papers/P48.pdf`. Its 18 PDF pages carry the printed proceedings page numbers 133–150, so the offset is 132 (PDF page 1 = p.133). All pages cited below are the printed ones. The body runs pp.133–147 and the references pp.147–150.
+## Deepest pass
+## First pass: the five Cs

+- **Category:** A retrospective by two of the system's designers. It reviews 20 years of design and implementation decisions across the L4 microkernel family, from L3 to seL4, and reports which were "Retained", "Replaced", "Abandoned", "Added" or remain "Unresolved" (pp.133, 136–147). It reports a few measurements (Table 1, p.135; pp.137, 140, 146), but it is not an evaluation paper.

+- **Context:** Liedtke's L4 papers [Liedtke 1993a, 1995] and the "microkernel minimality principle" (p.136); the early-1990s IPC cost problem [Condict et al. 1994; Chen and Bershad 1993] (p.133); EROS and capabilities (pp.135, 138); seL4 verification [Klein et al. 2009] and WCET analysis [Blackham et al. 2011] (p.135); the multikernel [Baumann et al. 2009] (pp.133, 143).

+- **Correctness:** The main assumption is that IPC latency counted in cycles can be compared across very different processors. The authors hedge this themselves: "as far as comparisons across vastly different ISAs and micro architectures have any validity" (p.147). Most "lessons" are argued from the authors' own experience rather than measured. The few numbers are partly taken from cited work (Warton 2005, Nourai 2005, Liedtke 1993a; pp.138, 144).

+- **Contributions:** (1) A history and family tree of L4 kernels (Fig. 1, p.134; pp.133–135). (2) One-way IPC cost across eleven kernel and processor pairs from 1993 to 2013 (Table 1, p.135) and kernel sizes (Table 2, p.136). (3) A verdict on each original L4 design principle and implementation trick (Sections 3–4, pp.136–146). (4) The conclusion that "the most general principles behind L4, minimality (including running device drivers at user level) and a strong focus on performance, still remain relevant" (p.147).
+- **Clarity:** Clearly written. Each subsection ends with a boxed verdict (e.g. "Abandoned: Long IPC.", p.138). The measurement method behind Table 1 is not described.
+## Quality
+| Q | Answer | Why |

+| Q1 | yes | The abstract states the aim in one place: "we examine the lessons learnt in those 20 years about microkernel design and implementation" (p.133), and the introduction repeats it (p.133). |

+| Q2 | partly | Three of the four items are described: message format (in-register and virtual message registers, long messages; p.137), naming of the receiver (thread IDs, then port-like endpoints; p.138), and the busy receiver (rendezvous blocking, timeouts, then poll/block flags; pp.136, 138–139). Delivery and ordering guarantees are not stated. |
+| Q3 | yes | The systems are running kernels, several deployed commercially (pp.134–135); Table 1 reports one-way IPC on real processors (p.135). |

+| Q4 | partly | Some claims name a baseline: in-register transfer vs passing via the kernel stack on ARM11 and Cortex A9 (p.137), and Warton's event kernel vs the Pistachio process kernel (p.144). Others do not: Table 1 has no baseline (p.135), and "fastest IPC we had measured on any other kernel on the same hardware" does not name the kernel (p.146). |

+| Q5 | partly | Table 1 gives the processor and clock rate for each kernel (p.135), and the workload is one-way IPC. No measurement procedure, number of runs or reason for the choice of workload is reported. |

+| Q6 | yes | The quantitative conclusions ("IPC latency, has remained essentially unchanged (in terms of clock cycles)" and "the code size has essentially remained constant", p.147) are reported in Table 1 (p.135) and Table 2 (p.136). The abstract makes no numeric claim. |

+| Q7 | partly | Some attributed effects are measured: the benefit of in-register transfer shrinks from ARM11 to Cortex A9 (p.137), and the mapping database takes 25–50% of kernel memory (p.140). The causes of seL4's 188-cycle IPC are only asserted ("partially a result of ...", p.146). |

+| Q8 | partly | There is no limitations section. Hedges appear in passing (p.147 comparability caveat; "we make no strong representations here", p.143), and the paper lists items as "Unresolved" (p.143). |

+| Q9 | no | Both authors are designers of seL4, the main system examined: "we instead opted for a from-scratch implementation for our capability-based seL4 kernel" (p.135); "We base our examination ... on seL4, which we know well" (p.135). |
+## Extracted fields
+| Field | Value | Page |

+| Reference | Elphinstone, Heiser (2013), SOSP '13, pp.133–150; P48; included under I1 at screening (I1(c) confirmed below; possible I4, see Notes). Proceedings version from sigops.org, printed pages = publisher pages, offset 132. | p.133 |

+| Paper type | Retrospective ("we examine the development of L4 over the last 20 years", p.133). Also design (seL4's design decisions, e.g. kernel memory model, pp.141–142) and implementation (pp.143–146). Partly evaluation (Table 1, p.135). | pp.133, 135, 141–146 |

+| System | **L3**: Liedtke, "in the early 1980s on i386 platforms"; "commercially deployed in a few thousand installations (mainly schools and legal practices)"; deployed commercially (p.133–134). **Original L4**: Liedtke (GMD), V2 ABI from 1995, "completely in assembler on i486-based PCs", ported to Pentium; running kernel (p.134). **L4/MIPS, L4/Alpha**: TU Dresden and UNSW, 1997 (Table 1); open source; Alpha was "the first multiprocessor version of L4"; running kernel (pp.134–135). **Version X**: Liedtke at IBM Watson (p.134). **Fiasco / Fiasco.OC**: TU Dresden, C++; "estimated shipments up to 100,000"; deployed commercially (pp.134–135). **Hazelnut**: Karlsruhe, C, 2002 (Table 1); running kernel (p.134). **L4Ka::Pistachio**: Karlsruhe, V4 ABI, C++, after 2001; ported by UNSW/NICTA; running kernel (p.134). **L4-embedded / OKL4 microkernel**: NICTA, then Open Kernel Labs; adopted by Qualcomm for modem firmware; deployed commercially, "in the billions" (pp.134–135 fn.2). **PikeOS**: Sysgo, commercial V2 clone, certified for avionics; deployed commercially (p.135). **NOVA**: Dresden, 2010 (p.135). **OKL4 Microvisor**: OK Labs, 2010 (p.135). **seL4**: NICTA, 2013 (Table 1); formally verified, with WCET analysis; running kernel (pp.133, 135). Itanium and SPARC versions "were never completed" (p.134 fn.1). | pp.133–135 |

+| Levels with message semantics | **Hardware, microcode, instruction set:** no (inferred). The kernels run on conventional processors (i486, Pentium, MIPS, Alpha, ARM, x86; Table 1, p.135), and the paper describes no hardware message mechanism. **Kernel, within a core:** partly. "User code obtains a system service by communicating with servers via an inter-process communication (IPC) mechanism, typically message passing" (p.133). Interrupts are modelled "as IPC messages, which the kernel sends to the driver" (p.139). Original L4 page mappings "were established through IPC" (p.140). Other paths exist: seL4 kernel objects are used by invoking "object-specific methods" through a capability (p.141), and the paper does not say whether this is IPC; shared memory (p.137); notifications (p.136). **Kernel, between cores:** not stated. The multicore section covers kernel locking (big kernel lock, multikernel, clustered multikernel) but not how threads on different cores communicate (p.143). **Runtime, language:** not stated. **Started message-based, then added other paths:** yes. "The original L4 supported synchronous (rendezvous-style) IPC as the only communication, synchronisation, and signalling mechanism" (p.136). Later kernels added asynchronous notifications (L4-embedded, seL4 AEPs), counting semaphores (NOVA) and virtual IRQs (Fiasco.OC, OKL4) (pp.136–137). Long IPC was removed in favour of shared buffers (pp.137–138). | pp.133, 135–141, 143 |

+| Receiving unit and state ownership | **Receiving unit:** In original L4, threads: "Original L4 had threads as the targets of IPC operations" (p.138). In seL4 and Fiasco.OC, port-like endpoints: "the root of the queue of pending senders or receivers is a now a separate kernel object, instead of being part of the recipient's thread control block" (p.138). An asynchronous endpoint "can be bound to a specific thread" (p.137). Interrupts are delivered to user-level driver processes (p.139). **State ownership:** A process is "essentially a page table and a number of associated threads" (p.140). Its memory can be shared with others: a process could map or grant its pages to another process via IPC (original L4, p.140); "Shared buffers ... are generally preferred for bulk data transfer" (p.137); Linux "effectively shares memory with its applications" (p.138). Kernel objects are not directly readable: "user-visible kernel objects do not mean that someone with authority over a kernel object can directly read or write it. The capability provides the right to invoke (a subset of) object-specific methods" (p.141). Userland can load or store only memory in a Frame mapped in its address space (p.142). A block of virtual IPC message registers is shared between the kernel and user level (p.143). | pp.137–143 |

+| Message mechanism | **Synchronous:** original L4 IPC is rendezvous-style, and "avoids buffering in the kernel" (p.136). Send and receive are combined in one system call: client `call` ("a send followed by an atomic switch to a receive phase") and server `reply-and-wait` (pp.138, 144). **Asynchronous:** seL4 AEPs, where "sending is non-blocking and asynchronous to the receiver, who has a choice of blocking or polling". Each AEP is a single-word notification field into which a send ORs a bit mask (pp.136–137). OKL4 is "fully-asynchronous" (virtual IRQs) (pp.137, 139). **Naming:** original L4 used globally unique thread IDs with version numbers (pp.138, 144). seL4 and Fiasco.OC use endpoints with "capability-mediated access control" (pp.138–139). The kernel delivered "the sender's unforgeable ID to the receiver" in original L4 (p.139). **Format:** in-register "short" messages; virtual message registers (16–64, configurable) mapped partly to physical registers and partly to a pinned per-thread memory area; "long" messages of buffers and strings, later abandoned (p.137). **Buffering:** endpoints "do not provide any buffering" (p.138). **Busy receiver:** the sender blocks (rendezvous). Original L4 had 4 timeouts per IPC; L4-embedded and seL4 replaced them by one poll-or-block flag per phase (pp.138–139). **Ordering and delivery guarantees:** not stated, beyond endpoint wait queues (p.145) and that inside a clan "the kernel guarantees message integrity" (p.139). **Dispatch:** not stated. **Scheduling on IPC:** direct process switch, where the receiver runs on the sender's time slice; in seL4 this happens only where it conforms with priorities (p.145). | pp.136–139, 144–145 |

+| Non-message primitives | (1) **Shared memory** at user level, used for bulk data instead of long IPC. Reasons: long IPC caused "significant kernel complexity" (nested page faults), was "rarely used", and "violates the minimality principle"; for seL4, nested exceptions introduce concurrency that hinders verification (pp.137–138). (2) **Kernel–user shared memory** for virtual message registers. Reasons: portability and lower cost for moderate-size messages (pp.137, 143). (3) **In-kernel scheduler with a fixed policy** ("usually hard-priority round-robin"). Reason: "no-one has come up with a truly general in-kernel scheduler or a workable mechanism which would delegate all scheduling policy to user-level without imposing high overhead" (pp.136, 142–143). (4) **In-kernel timer driver and interrupt-controller driver.** Reasons: the timer is used "for preempting user processes at the end of their time slice", and the interrupt controller driver "is required to safely distribute interrupts to user-level processes" (p.139). (5) **Capability invocation of kernel objects** (methods such as `revoke()` on Untyped; retype) (pp.141–142); whether this is a message is not stated. (6) **Counting semaphores** (NOVA) and **virtual IRQs** (OKL4, Fiasco.OC), with no reason stated beyond the drawbacks of synchronous-only IPC (pp.136–137). (7) **OKL4 channels**, an asynchronous bulk-transfer mechanism, "retained for compatibility" for a >50-thread application "where a separate communication page per pair of communicating threads was too costly" (p.138). (8) **Interrupts disabled in the kernel, with preemption points.** Reasons: simpler implementation, better average case, and seL4 verification (p.145). (9) **Big kernel lock / RCU** on multicore. Reasons: verification for the lock; scalability for RCU (p.143). (10) **User access to a timer**, which replaced timeouts for timed sleeps (p.139). (11) **IOMMUs** for safe pass-through device access by user-level drivers (p.139). | pp.136–145 |

+| Self-definition | OS services are implemented in user-mode servers, and the kernel "provides a set of general mechanisms" (p.133). Device drivers are user-level processes, except the timer and interrupt-controller drivers (p.139). The kernel itself is written in a lower language outside the message model: assembler (original L4), C/C++ (later kernels), and C for seL4 because "the requirements of verifications forced the choice of C" (pp.134, 146–147). seL4's C is "mostly a 'blind' manual translation from Haskell" (p.136 fn.4). Sizes run from 6.4 to 37.6 kSLOC; seL4 is 10.2 kSLOC and "compiles into about 9 k ARM instructions" (Table 2 and fn.4, p.136). In seL4, "most (architecture-agnostic) resource-management code [is] moved to userland" (p.146). Whether a running program can inspect or change the kernel level: not stated. The paper does say that "the formal verification of seL4 creates a powerful disincentive to changing the kernel" (p.143). Remaining base and its cost: the in-kernel scheduler is "the last major holdout of policy in the kernel. This probably represents the largest limitation of generality of L4 kernels" (p.147). | pp.133, 136, 139, 143, 146–147 |

+| Interposition | **Yes, in original L4, by clans and chiefs:** "messages crossing a clan boundary, whether outgoing or incoming, are redirected to the clan's chief, who can thus control the flow of messages". Level: kernel. Cost: "only added two cycles per IPC operation" where communication is direct (Liedtke's claim), but "each such re-direction adds two messages to a (logically) single round-trip IPC, a significant overhead". The mechanism was abandoned (p.139). A more general "IPC redirection [Jaeger et al., 1999]" was tried and "failed to gain traction" (p.139). **Current kernels:** "capability-mediated access control to endpoints" (p.139); whether this lets a third component be placed between sender and receiver without changing either is not stated. **Other:** user-level page-fault handlers (pagers) (pp.137, 140); IOMMUs for user-level drivers (p.139); para-virtualized Linux on L4 "with only a few percent overhead" (p.133); NOVA and the OKL4 Microvisor are aimed at virtualization (p.135). | pp.133, 135, 137, 139–140 |

+| Operating system functions | **Protection:** original L4 used unforgeable sender IDs and clans and chiefs (p.139); all modern L4 kernels use capability-based access control (pp.135, 140). Central component: the kernel, yes (inferred). **Scheduling:** "All versions of L4 have achieved this multiplexing through a fixed-policy scheduler (pluggable in Fiasco.OC)" (p.142). Central: yes, the in-kernel scheduler. On early x86 multiprocessors, "per-processor scheduling queues (and minimal sharing of kernel data across cores)" were used, but for embedded multicores "a global scheduler makes more sense" (p.143). Decentralised version: "All past attempts to export scheduling policy to user level have failed, generally due to intolerable overheads, or were incomplete or domain-specific" (p.143). **Resource allocation (memory):** original L4 used the primordial address space σ0 (central) and recursive mappings (p.140), and task IDs "handed out first-come, first-served" (p.140). seL4 uses user-level control via Untyped memory: "Retyping is the only way to create objects in seL4. Hence, by limiting access to Untyped memory, a system can control resource allocation" (p.142). Per-process kernel heaps are used in NOVA, Fiasco and OKL4 (p.141). **Resource allocation (devices):** user-level drivers, with interrupts delivered as IPC (p.139). **Naming:** original L4 used global thread IDs, which "introduced covert channels" (p.138); later kernels use endpoints named by capabilities (p.138). **Failure handling:** IPC timeouts were "of little use as a DOS defence"; "Traditional watchdog timers represent a better approach to detecting unresponsive IPC interactions (e.g. resulting from deadlocks)" (p.138). **Multicore coordination:** "either a big kernel lock or a multikernel approach". seL4 explores a "clustered multikernel", meaning a big lock across cores that share an L2 cache plus a restricted multikernel with "no memory migration ... between kernels". +## Concepts
+| Concept | What the paper says | Page |

+| Microkernel minimality principle (new) | "A concept is tolerated inside the µ-kernel only if moving it outside the kernel, i.e. permitting competing implementations, would prevent the implementation of the system's required functionality" [Liedtke 1995]; "Retained" as the key design principle. | p.136 |

+| Synchronous (rendezvous-style) IPC (new) | The original L4's "only communication, synchronisation, and signalling mechanism"; avoids kernel buffering; "Replaced" by synchronous IPC augmented with, or replaced by, asynchronous notification. | pp.136–137 |

+| Asynchronous endpoint / notification (new) | A single-word notification field; a send ORs a bit mask into it, and the receiver blocks or polls; "similar to multiple binary semaphores allocated within a single word". | pp.136–137 |
+| Virtual message registers (new) | A configurable set of 16–64 message registers, some physical and the rest in a pinned per-thread memory area. | p.137 |
+| Long IPC (new) | Multi-buffer messages copied by the kernel through a temporary mapping window; "Abandoned" because of complexity and verification, with shared buffers used instead. | pp.137–138 |
+| IPC endpoint (port-like) (new) | A kernel object that holds the queue of pending senders or receivers and is the message destination instead of a thread ID; no buffering. | p.138 |
+| Clans and chiefs (new) | Kernel redirection of messages that cross a clan boundary to the clan's chief; supports confinement; "Abandoned". | p.139 |
+| User-level device drivers / interrupts as IPC (new) | Drivers are user processes, and interrupts are "IPC messages, which the kernel sends to the driver"; "Retained". | p.139 |
+| Recursive page mappings / mapping database (new) | Authority over frames comes from existing mappings, established through IPC (map, grant, unmap); needs a mapping database. | pp.140–141 |

+| Untyped memory and retype (seL4 kernel memory model) (new) | All kernel memory is subject to capabilities; "Retyping is the only way to create objects in seL4"; capability derivation tree; called "seL4's main contribution to OS design". | pp.141–142 |
+| Event-based (single-stack) kernel (new) | One kernel stack with continuations instead of one stack per thread; "Replaced: Process kernel by event kernel in seL4, OKL4 and NOVA". | p.144 |

+| Lazy scheduling / Benno scheduling (new) | Lazy: blocked threads are left in the ready queue. Benno: the ready queue holds all runnable threads except the running one, which gives a bounded WCET. | pp.144–145 |
+| Direct process switch (new) | On IPC the kernel switches straight to the partner thread on the caller's time slice; "a form of time-slice donation". | p.145 |
+| Clustered multikernel (new) | A big-lock kernel across cores sharing an L2 cache, combined with a restricted multikernel (no memory migration between kernels). | p.143 |
+| IPC fast path (new) | Hand-optimised common-case IPC code, once in assembler and in seL4 in C; it achieves 188 cycles on ARM11. | p.146 |

+- **Source read:** full text, proceedings version (printed pp.133–150), from `https://www.sigops.org/s/conferences/sosp/2013/papers/p133-elphinstone.pdf`, saved as `papers/P48.pdf`. The ACM DL PDF returned HTTP 403. All of the body (pp.133–147) was read, including Tables 1–3 and Figure 1, plus the start of the reference list. The cited works (Warton 2005, Nourai 2005, Liedtke 1993a/1995, Blackham and Heiser 2012) were not checked. Deepest pass: 2 (every section, table and figure read; no reconstruction or checking of the cited measurements).

+- **Criterion:** I1(c) is confirmed. The paper names IPC and message passing as the means by which user code obtains kernel-level system services: "User code obtains a system service by communicating with servers via an inter-process communication (IPC) mechanism, typically message passing" (p.133). The family consists of microkernels (pp.133–135). No exclusion criterion appears to apply: X2 and X3 do not apply because the message mechanism is the kernel's (p.133), and X9 does not apply because the paper is a retrospective with its own measurements and reasons (pp.135, 146). **Possible additional criterion, I4:** the paper gives reasons for using non-message mechanisms inside a message-based system, which may answer an SQ on model mixing (SQ11 per the form's *Serves* column). I could not check this, because the SQ files were not among my inputs. The evidence: shared buffers "are generally preferred for bulk data transfer" over long IPC (p.137); asynchronous notifications were added because synchronous-only IPC "forces a multi-threaded design onto otherwise simple systems" (p.136); NOVA added counting semaphores (p.137); OKL4 channels (p.138). The multicore discussion (p.143) may also bear on SQ13/SQ14. If I4 is added, *Model mixing* should be filled from these pages.

+- **Abstract:** in the PDF text layer, the abstract ("The L4 microkernel has undergone 20 years of use and evolution ...") sits in the right column of p.133. Its only claim is: "We demonstrate that while much has changed, the fundamental principles of minimality and high IPC performance remain the main drivers of design and implementation decisions" (p.133).

+- **Table 1 provenance:** the paper does not say whether the authors measured all eleven rows themselves or took them from the original publications. It thanks "Adrian Danis for some last-minute seL4 optimisations and measurements" (p.147), which suggests the 2013 seL4 rows are the authors' own (inferred).
+- **seL4 kernel object types (Table 3, p.142):** TCB, CNode, Synchronous Endpoint, Asynchronous Endpoint, Page Directory, Page Table, Frame, Untyped Memory.

+- **Overlap:** P48 summarises results from other L4 papers (Liedtke 1993a; Härtig et al. 1997; Klein et al. 2009). If any of those are included, X8 does not apply automatically, because P48 adds its own retrospective reasons. This is noted for the gate.

+## First pass: the five Cs
+- **Category:** Design and implementation description of a research prototype many-core processor chip, with silicon measurements (power, maximum frequency, two NAS benchmarks) (pp. 173, 179–180).

+- **Context:** Follows Intel's 80-tile TeraFLOPS network-on-chip [1] (pp. 173, 175); message-passing protocol "inspired by software coherency models such as SHMEM [9], MPI and openMP [10]" (p. 176); the programmer's view is in Mattson et al. [11] (p. 176).

+- **Correctness:** The motivating claim, that "the computational value gained through additional cores will at some point be exceeded by the protocol overhead needed to maintain cache coherency among the cores" (p. 173), is asserted without measurement or citation. The measured results (silicon, Fmax, power, NAS LU/BT speedup) support the claims about power and frequency range. The paper does not compare against a coherent design.

+- **Contributions:** A 48-core, 24-tile 6×4 2D-mesh chip with no hardware cache coherency; per-tile 16 KB Message Passing Buffer (MPB, "on-die shared memory"); a new cache-line memory type (MPMT) and a new instruction (INVDMB) for software-managed coherency; a 4-stage virtual cut-through router; 4 DDR3 controllers; 8 voltage and 28 frequency islands for DVFS (pp. 173–178).

+- **Clarity:** Clearly organised circuits paper; the message-passing protocol is given in one short section (pp. 176–177) and much of its semantics (naming, synchronisation, busy receivers) is left to the cited programmer's-view paper [11]. Fig. 7(b) and Fig. 11 are not labelled as measured or simulated in their captions.

+- **Source read:** full text, publisher's typeset version (IEEE JSSC vol. 46, no. 1, pp. 173–183), ResearchGate upload by Michael Konow (1 June 2014) with a cover sheet, obtained from the mirror https://search.iczhiku.com/paper/WjR2NH8uksdALAbZ.pdf and saved as `papers/P21.pdf` (12 PDF pages). Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar report the paper as closed access; the ResearchGate direct link returned 403; a Semantic Scholar PDF link found by search (pdfs.semanticscholar.org/a768/...) is an unrelated slide deck. Figures were read from rendered page images.

+- **Criterion (for gate 3c):** I1 holds only in a qualified way. The paper names "message passing" throughout (title, p. 173) and adds hardware for it, the MPB, MPMT and INVDMB (pp. 174, 176–177), which fits I1(b) "a hardware or microcode mechanism". But the paper itself calls the protocol "a novel message passing based software protocol used to maintain data consistency in shared memory" (p. 173), and data moves by loads and stores into "on-die shared memory" (p. 174); there is no send instruction (p. 174). X2 does not apply as worded, because the instruction set and hardware do have message-specific mechanisms (MPB, MPMT, INVDMB, pp. 174, 177). The paper also plausibly meets I4 for the many-core scaling SQs served by the *Many-core scaling* field (SQ13, SQ14) and for *Model equivalence* (SQ10), since it builds message passing on non-coherent shared memory and argues against hardware coherency at scale (pp. 173, 176) (inferred; I did not read the SQ files). Verdict change, if any, is yours.

+- **Hardware messages beyond core-to-core:** voltage change commands are messages to the VRC, a mesh agent "addressable by all cores" (p. 178); every on-die agent communicates by packets (p. 176). This is relevant to SQ1 at the hardware level even though the core-to-core path is shared-memory based.

+- **Scope of results:** NAS benchmarks were run only up to 32 (LU) and 36 (BT) cores, not 48, at 533 MHz (p. 179); the paper says the benchmarks "were successfully ported to the processor architecture with minimal effort" (p. 179) without stating what the port involved.

+- **Small inconsistencies:** the abstract gives nominal 1.1 V for 1 GHz cores / 2 GHz mesh (p. 173), while the 125 W typical point is at 1.14 V (pp. 180–181); core Fmax starts at 300 MHz at 730 mV (p. 179) while the conclusion and Fig. 14 give 0.7 V and 125 MHz as an operating point (pp. 180–181). The ResearchGate cover gives February 2011; the journal header gives January 2011 (p. 173).

+- The programmer's model (synchronisation, receiver naming, what happens when a receiver is not ready) is deferred to Mattson et al. [11], "The Intel 48-core single-chip cloud computer (SCC) processor: Programmer's view" (p. 181); candidate for snowballing.

+## First pass: the five Cs

+- **Category:** Design, implementation and microbenchmark evaluation of a capability-based microkernel with a single-level persistent store (EROS) on a commodity processor, the Pentium (p. 170–171, 180).

+- **Context:** The belief that "the desirable features of transparent persistence and capability-based protection are widely believed to have prohibitive performance", which the paper says "is largely justified by experience" with the i432, Mach and the AS/400 (p. 170–171). It builds on GNOSIS/KeyKOS (TymShare) as "a clean-room reimplementation of the GNOSIS architecture in C++" (p. 170), on L3/L4 IPC design (p. 181–182) and on the authors' earlier IPC and state-caching papers [44], [45] (p. 171, 173, 176).

+- **Correctness:** Assumes that lmbench-inspired microbenchmarks with "semantically similar" EROS operations are a fair comparison with Linux 2.2.5 (p. 180); the paper itself states that "the microbenchmarks currently available for EROS do not support general conclusions about application performance" (p. 171) and that "A full validation of our performance claim requires application-level benchmarks" (p. 183). The claim that microbenchmarks "approximately predict real system performance" rests on KeyKOS experience [5, 16], not on EROS measurements (p. 183).

+- **Contributions:** (1) The EROS kernel architecture: a few primitive capability types (numbers, nodes, pages, processes, entry and resume capabilities) and capability invocation as the only system call (p. 172–174); (2) software caching of nodes and pages into machine-specific forms (process table as a cache, page tables as a read-only cache, producer and product chains) (p. 175–178); (3) user-level storage allocation (space bank), virtual copy and process construction (p. 179–180); (4) microbenchmarks showing EROS "performs favorably on 6 out of 7 benchmarks" against Linux on the same machine (p. 182).

+- **Clarity:** Well structured and readable. Figure 11 uses the large-to-small context switch (1.19 µs) as the EROS value, while the text gives 1.60 µs for the large-space case, which is slower than Linux's 1.26 µs (p. 181); the "6 out of 7" count (p. 182) depends on that choice (my observation; the paper does not discuss it).

# Agent contract

What every agent in `.claude/agents/` does, whatever its role. The agent's own file adds only its role.

## You receive
From the step skill that dispatched you:
- **Row:** the flow row you run (e.g. `3a`), defined in `ai/flow-sls.md` or `ai/flow-dsrm.md`.
- **Inputs:** the exact files you read. Paths are relative to `research/` unless they start with `ai/` or `artifact/`.
- **Outputs:** the exact files you write.

## You do
1. Read the row in its flow file, then every input file. Read nothing else from `research/`; your view of the research is the inputs.
2. For each output, copy its template from `ai/template/` (the table in `ai/template/README.md` maps output to template) and fill every `{placeholder}`.
3. Set the frontmatter: `id`, `row`, `by:` your agent name, `status: proposed`, `inputs:` the files you read.
4. Write only the output files. Every other file, and every `status`, belongs to me.

## Your output is done when
- Every output file exists and has every section of its template.
- No `{placeholder}` or `[ ]` is left. A field you cannot fill says why, in one line.
- Every claim about a paper carries its P ID and page, or the reference and page for papers not yet in the review.
- Every fact comes from a file or source you actually read in this run. A fact you cannot trace to one is left out and named in your report.

## You return
A short report to the skill:
- Each file written, with one line on what it holds.
- Open issues: fields you could not fill, sources you could not reach, decisions you found that are mine to make.
- Each decision that is mine as a choice: two to four concrete options, the exact edit each one makes to which file, and the one you recommend. The gate asks me with these (`ai/gate.md`).

# P29

## Reference
Paul M. Hansen, Mark A. Linton, Robert N. Mayo, Marguerite Murphy, David A. Patterson (1982). *A Performance Evaluation of the Intel iAPX 432*. ACM SIGARCH Computer Architecture News 10(4), 17–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/641542.641545. P29, included under I2 (row R0-033). Pages below are the page numbers printed on `papers/P29.pdf` (pp. 17–26), which match the publisher's page range (Crossref: 17–26). PDF page n = printed page n + 16. Version: a scanned photocopy of the published issue (see Notes).

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Third-party measurement study (benchmark evaluation) of one processor against three contemporaries; a short report of 7 pages of text and tables plus 2 figure pages (pp. 17–26).
- **Context:** Intel's own claims for the 432 [Intel 81] and its project goals [Mazor 81] (p. 17); benchmark programs from EDN [Grappel and Hemmenway 81], Byte [Gilbreath 81], Baskett's puzzle and Wichmann's Ackermann study (p. 18); procedure-call frequency studies [Clark and Levy 82], [Ditzel and McLellan 82], [McDaniel 82] (p. 18).
- **Correctness:** The premise is that an object-oriented architecture with "software-transparent multiprocessing and fault tolerance" may cost performance, posed as "An interesting question is how much performance is degraded" (p. 17). The authors hedge that "a high-level language system consists of the compiler and the machine, so we are not measuring just the architecture and hardware implementation" (p. 17). Four programs only, limited by "The time allotted to our visit at Intel" (p. 18). Several 1983 figures are forecasts, not measurements (p. 22).
- **Contributions:** Execution time and code size of four integer and character programs on the iAPX 432 (Ada, release 2 hardware and release 3 simulator) against the 8086, 68000 and VAX-11/780 (Pascal, C) (pp. 20–22). Headline: "A single 4 MHz, release 2 432 is currently about 1/20th of a VAX-11/780" (p. 23).
- **Clarity:** Clear and short; every machine configuration (clock, wait states, compiler version, who ran it) is listed (pp. 18–19). Weak points: the Table 2(a) header labels the search column "484" (p. 21); how the 432 release 2 times were normalised to 8 MHz in Table 3 is not explained (p. 22); the y-axis of Figure 2 is not evenly spaced (p. 26).

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The abstract states the aim: "an experiment to test the 432 as a high-level language uniprocessor" (p. 17). |
| Q2 | no | The paper describes no communication mechanism of the 432; it excludes "object-oriented programming, ... multiple processes, and multiple processors" from the study (p. 17). |
| Q3 | yes | Table 1 is "measured on real hardware", a release 2 432 system at Intel (pp. 19–20). The release 3 timings come from a simulator (p. 19), and the 1983 figures are forecasts (p. 22). |
| Q4 | partly | The measured results name their baselines (VAX-11/780 VMS Pascal, 8086, 68000 with clock, wait states and compiler; pp. 19–21). The 1983 claim ("1/5th the speed of Pascal programs on the 1983 VAX", p. 23) uses a hypothetical baseline. |
| Q5 | partly | Programs and the reason for each are given (p. 18) and the hardware configurations (pp. 18–19). The number of runs is not stated. |
| Q6 | partly | "about 1/20th of a VAX-11/780" matches Table 1(b) (.05–.07; p. 20). "1/5th" in 1983 rests on Figure 2 forecasts (p. 26). "5 processors may perform as well as a VAX" has no table or figure behind it (p. 23). The abstract has no quantitative claim. |
| Q7 | partly | The cost of parameter and global access is isolated by running modified programs (* rows, Table 1, p. 20). The code-size causes (no immediates, 16-bit addresses; p. 21) are only asserted. |
| Q8 | partly | Limits are mentioned in passing: compiler and machine measured together (p. 17), only four programs (p. 18), "we can not compare completely equal systems" (p. 23). There is no dedicated section. |
| Q9 | yes | All five authors are at UC Berkeley (p. 17), and none is named as a 432 designer. Intel's Konrad Lai ran the 32-bit release 2 and all release 3 runs (p. 19). |

## Extracted fields
| Field | Value | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | See Reference above. I2: the authors refer to "the object-oriented architecture" of the 432 and test it "as a high-level language uniprocessor", and they report measured performance (Tables 1–3). | pp. 17, 20–22 |
| Paper type | evaluation (third-party benchmark measurement, with forecasts) | pp. 17, 22–23 |
| System | Intel iAPX 432: a "32-bit VLSI microprocessor" announced by Intel in 1981, from a project "that started in 1975". Built by Intel. | p. 17 |
| System | Status: silicon. A release 2 system "running with a 4 MHz clock and 12 wait states", "a half-speed prototype of an 8 MHz system"; the experiments are called "432/670" experiments. Release 3 was planned to ship in December, and its timings "were obtained from a simulator" (simulated). 432/800 systems (release 3, 4 wait states) and 10 MHz chips were planned for the first quarter of 1983. | pp. 19, 22 |
| Levels with message semantics | not stated for every level. The paper does not describe messages, ports or any send operation. It quotes Intel that the 432 supports "an object-oriented programming methodology" and "true software-transparent, multiprocessor operation", but describes no mechanism behind either. | p. 17 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | not stated | — |
| Message mechanism | not stated. The only call mechanism measured is the Ada procedure call, through Ackermann's function (no message semantics are claimed for it). | p. 18 |
| Non-message primitives | not stated. The paper notes only that the 432 systems "support virtual memory and provide error correcting memory", without saying how. | p. 19 |
| Self-definition | not stated. The paper quotes Intel that the 432 "is designed to be programmed entirely in high-level languages". | p. 17 |
| Interposition | not stated | — |
| Operating system functions | n/a (I2) | — |
| Cost of message primitives | not stated. Nearest proxy: Ackermann(3,6), "more than 170,000 procedure calls", "useful in measuring the cost of a procedure call", takes 260,000 ms on the 432 (4 MHz, release 2, Ada). That is at most about 1.5 ms per call including the work of the function (inferred). The 432 time for acker(3,6) was itself extrapolated from acker(1,2) by the VAX ratio. | pp. 18–20 |
| Performance results | Execution time, ms (measured), 432 4 MHz release 2, Ada 16-bit, unmodified. search 35; sieve 3200; puzzle 350,000; acker 260,000. Baseline VAX-11/780 VMS Pascal 32-bit: 1.4; 259; 11,530; 9850. Ratio to VMS Pascal: .04; .08; .03; .04; average .05±.02. | p. 20 |
| Performance results | 432 Ada programs modified to avoid expensive parameter and global access (*, measured): 16-bit search 14.2, puzzle 165,000; 32-bit search 16.1, puzzle 180,000 (ms). Ratio to VMS Pascal: average .07±.02 for both word sizes. | pp. 18, 20 |
| Performance results | Other machines (measured, ratio to VMS Pascal, average±sd): VAX C 1.3±.4; VAX UNIX Pascal 1.1±.2; 68000 8 MHz C .6±.4; 68000 8 MHz Pascal 16-bit .5±.2, 32-bit .4±.2; 68000 16 MHz Pascal 16-bit 1.8±1.0, 32-bit 1.6±.9; 8086 5 MHz Pascal .4±.3. | p. 20 |
| Performance results | Code size, bytes of object code and constants, excluding libraries and OS (measured from compiler output). 432 release 3 Ada 16-bit: search 612, sieve 180, puzzle 2443, acker 144. Baseline VMS Pascal: 636, 411, 2904, 340. Ratio .6±.2. 68000 Pascal 16-bit .5±.2; VAX C .5±.2; 8086 Pascal .9±.1. | pp. 19, 21 |

These rel. 2 values are exactly half of the 4 MHz times (inferred); the method is not stated. 432 rel. 3 Ada (simulated): 4.4; 978; 45,700; 47,800. | pp. 19, 22 |

A 0-wait-state 432 is "expected to be about 25% faster" (no data). | p. 22 |
| Performance results | Figure 1, average performance relative to the 4-wait-state 68000 at 8 MHz (read off): 432 rel. 2 ≈ 0.28; 432 rel. 2 modified ≈ 0.44; 432 rel. 3 ≈ 0.77; 8086 0 ws ≈ 1.47; 68000 0 ws ≈ 2.0. | p. 25 |
| Performance results | Figure 2, relative to the VAX-11/780 (read off; the axis spacing is uneven). Measured: 432 4 MHz R2 and R2* below 0.1. Predicted: 432 10 MHz R3 4 ws ≈ 0.3; 8086 5 MHz ≈ 0.4 measured and 8 MHz ≈ 0.65 predicted; 68000 8 MHz 4 ws ≈ 0.5 measured, 0 ws ≈ 0.9 predicted, 16 MHz ≈ 1.8 measured; VAX 1.0 measured, ≈ 1.35 predicted. | p. 26 |
| Performance results | Conclusion: "A single 4 MHz, release 2 432 is currently about 1/20th of a VAX-11/780, and we expect Ada programs on the 1983 version to run about 1/5th the speed of Pascal programs on the 1983 VAX." The 1983 baselines are forecasts: DEC Pascal "1.2 to 1.4 times faster", 68000 systems "1.5 to 3 times faster", the 8086 "at least 3 times faster" (analytical). | pp. 22–23 |
| Scaling | Not measured; uniprocessor only ("We limited ourselves to studying uniprocessor performance"). Hedged estimate: "For some applications a 432 system consisting of 5 processors may perform as well as a VAX-11/780. We need multiprocessing benchmarks that could assess such systems." | pp. 17, 23 |
| Attributed causes | "Accessing parameters and global variables is very expensive inside a procedure in release 2 of the 432 and will be much less expensive in release 3. This overhead can be avoided by either changing the compiler or modifying the program source". Third party. Due to the implementation (release 2 and its compiler). Isolated: the modified (*) programs measure it (search 35 → 14.2 ms, puzzle 350,000 → 165,000 ms at 16 bits). | pp. 18, 20 |

| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: high-level language uniprocessor | The 432 is tested "as a high-level language uniprocessor" for integer and character programs. | pp. 17, 23 |
| new: high-level language system = compiler + machine | "a high-level language system consists of the compiler and the machine, so we are not measuring just the architecture and hardware implementation". | p. 17 |
| new: object-oriented architecture with software-transparent multiprocessing and fault tolerance | The 432 features whose performance cost the study asks about; Intel claims it is "the first commercial system to support an object-oriented programming methodology". | p. 17 |
| new: wait states | "the time, measured in clock ticks, that a processor is idle while waiting for memory". Relative performance of different architectures cannot be predicted from clock rate and wait states. | pp. 18–19 |
| new: normalized performance | Times scaled to 8 MHz, 16-bit, at 4 or 0 wait states to compare the machines. | p. 22 |
| new: time and space cost of the 432 approach | What the authors say they evaluate, instead of speculating on a software version of the 432's functions on conventional machines. | p. 23 |

## Notes
- **Source and version:** Internet Archive item `PerformanceEvaluationOfTheIntelAPX432` (uploaded 2019, scanned 2013 with a ScanSnap; the archive also offers an OCR text file). It is a 10-page photocopy whose printed page numbers 17–26 match the SIGARCH CAN 10(4) page range on Crossref. Page 17 carries a "THIS MATERIAL MAY BE PROTECTED BY COPYRIGHT LAW (TITLE 17 U.S. CODE)" stamp, so it is likely a library copy of the published issue (inferred). The paper is dated "May 17, 1982" (p. 17). The ACM full text (dl.acm.org) was blocked by a Cloudflare challenge, and Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar list no open copy. Saved as `papers/P29.pdf` (the image scan). Table values were read from the page images, not the OCR text, which garbles digits (8 → B).
- **Uploader's claim, not the paper's:** the Internet Archive description calls this "the paper that sank it" and says the 432 "quickly disappeared". This is not stated in the paper and is not used in any field above.
- **Criterion:** consistent with screening (I2; pp. 17, 20). The paper does not meet I1 on its own text: it never uses message, send, port, IPC or method invocation (checked over the full text). Whatever message mechanism the 432 has is outside this paper.
- **Scope:** uniprocessor, integer and character programs only. Object-oriented programming, floating point, multiple processes and multiple processors were excluded (p. 17), so none of the 432's object or inter-process mechanisms were measured.

- **Paper errors:** the Table 2(a) column header reads "484" where the other tables say "search" (p. 21).

# P102

## Reference
David Wentzlaff, Anant Agarwal (2009). *Factored Operating Systems (fos): The Case for a Scalable Operating System for Multicores*. ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 43(2), pp. 76–85. https://doi.org/10.1145/1531793.1531805

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** A position and design paper with motivating measurements. It argues that SMP operating systems cannot scale to "1000+ core systems" (p. 2), measures two Linux scaling problems (p. 3–4), and describes the design of a new message-passing OS (fos) whose prototype is "under active development" (p. 2, p. 8). fos itself is not evaluated.
- **Context:** Microkernels (Mach, L3, L4; p. 2, p. 8), scalable shared-memory kernels (Tornado/K42, Hive, Disco/Cellular Disco, Corey; p. 9), distributed OSes (Amoeba, Sprite, Clouds; p. 9) and distributed Internet services (DNS, BitTorrent, Chord, AFS, GFS; p. 9–10). The authors' own Raw and Tilera on-chip networks are cited for message costs (p. 8).
- **Correctness:** The Linux measurements are on real hardware (p. 3), and the cache study runs in a QEMU-based simulator (p. 4). The case for fos rests on argument, for example "We believe that the shared nothing, message passing only, approach will encourage OS developers to think very carefully about exactly what data is being shared, which will lead to more scalability" (p. 5). The paper names its own open questions in Section 3.4 (p. 8).
- **Contributions:** (1) A measurement showing that the Linux 2.6.24.7 physical page allocator "does not scale beyond 8 cores under heavy load" (p. 2, Fig. 1 p. 3). (2) A simulated measurement of OS/application cache interference on Apache2 (p. 4). (3) Three recommendations: avoid hardware locks, separate OS from application cores, and avoid global cache-coherent shared memory (p. 5). (4) The fos design: a microkernel with mailbox messaging, OS services split into fleets of servers bound to cores, a name server, and space multiplexing instead of time multiplexing (p. 5–7).
- **Clarity:** Well structured and readable. The figure labels in the author PDF use an odd font encoding (the text cannot be extracted), but the rendered figures are legible. The message format is not described.

| Q5 | partly | Workloads and hardware or simulator configurations are given (p. 3, p. 4), and the allocator workload is partly justified (p. 4). The number of runs is not reported. |

| Q7 | partly | Lock contention is isolated by an oprofile breakdown by function (Fig. 1, p. 3). Interference misses are isolated by simulating separate OS-only and application-only caches (p. 4). ## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| factored operating system (fos) (new) | An OS "factored into function specific services", each "distributed into spatially distributed servers" that "collaborate and communicate only via message passing" | p. 5 |
| space multiplexing replaces time multiplexing (new) | "Scheduling becomes a layout problem not a time multiplexing problem"; the OS "runs on distinct cores from applications" | p. 5 |
| fleet (new) | The set of servers of one type that together provide one OS function, e.g. physical memory allocation, file system, scheduling | p. 6 |
| fos client (new) | "The code executing on a single core under the fos-microkernel"; applications and OS servers "act as peers" | p. 6 |
| receive mailbox (new) | A named, protected endpoint owned by a client, with a large buffer in the receiver's address space; a send to a full mailbox returns an error | p. 6, 8 |
| message proxy library / translation library (new) | Turns a traditional system call into a message to an OS-layer server and unpacks the reply | p. 6 |
| microkernel to OS layer delegation (new) | The microkernel delegates naming and privilege to OS-layer fleets, caches their answers, and avoids cycles by knowing the delegates' locations and granting static privileges ("privilege fixed point") | p. 7 |
| stateless, transaction-oriented server with continuations (new) | A server processes each transaction to completion without preemption, stores a continuation for long-latency operations, and needs no local locking | p. 7 |
| notional lock / lock server (new) | A lock held by a server and acquired by message; "the cost of software-based lock management may dwarf the performance wins of removing traditional locks" | p. 8 |
| OS-application and OS-OS locality aliasing (new) | OS and application working sets competing for implicitly shared caches and TLBs on one core, including "anti-locality cache collisions" | p. 4 |
| best-effort OS interfaces (new) | Interfaces that return information "which may be slightly out of date" for higher performance, with an accurate but slower alternative | p. 2 |

## Notes
- **Source and version:** author preprint PDF, downloaded on 2026-10-07 from https://www.princeton.edu/~wentzlaf/documents/Wentzlaff.2009.OSR.fos.pdf and saved as `papers/P102.pdf` (11 pages, created 2009-03-02, marked "To appear in ACM SIGOPS Operating System Review ... April 2009", p. 1). The ACM PDF returned 403, and Unpaywall lists no open-access copy. The publisher page range 76–85 is from Crossref. Read in full, figures included (second pass).
- **Criterion:** the full text meets I1(c) as screened. The OS layer's servers "communicate only via the messaging interface provided by the microkernel layer" (p. 6), the paper uses the terms "message passing", "send" and "mailbox" (p. 5–6), and fos runs without an underlying conventional kernel (p. 5). No exclusion applies. X2 does not: messaging is the kernel's own mechanism, not a library on a conventional kernel. X3 does not: the target is a single multicore chip (p. 9). X5 does not: a 10-page journal article. The paper may also answer SQ13/SQ14 under I4 (inferred), through its Linux scaling measurements and its named limits of cache-coherent shared memory (p. 3, p. 5). That would not change the include verdict.
- **For SQ10 (model equivalence, I4 field):** fos messages may be carried on shared memory: "The fos-microkernels transport the message to the destination via on-chip networks or shared memory" (p. 6). The cost of doing so is not reported.
- **For SQ11 (model mixing):** "Within an application, communication can be achieved via shared memory communication or messaging", and fos keeps shared memory for applications "if the underlying hardware supports it" (p. 6).
- **For SQ7/SQ8 (defects, what shapes programs):** the paper argues, without counts, that "Adding locks into an operating system is time consuming and error prone" and that locks "can introduce circular dependencies and hence cause deadlocks" (p. 3). It also argues that "global shared memory easily allows the introduction of data races which can be difficult to detect at test time" (p. 5). It expects that "the shared nothing, message passing only, approach will encourage OS developers to think very carefully about exactly what data is being shared" (p. 5). It says "the message passing nature of fos discourages this usage model [lock managers] by making programming in this manner difficult" (p. 7). All of these are argument, not measurement.
- **Open questions the authors name:** whether shared OS structures (virtual memory, buffer cache) "can be accessed with good performance" (p. 8); whether all multi-sequence operations can be written without local locks: "it is not certain that all cases can be handled" (p. 8); whether "a hardware solution or the software solution explored by fos proves more scalable" (p. 8).

I wrote the P21 record from the full text, read to pass 2. It meets I1 only in a qualified way: there is no message-send instruction, and the paper calls its protocol a software layer over shared memory. Whether to keep I1 is your call at gate 3c.

**Files written**
- `/home/garro/dev/faculty/Thesis/research/sls/3-reading/P21.md` (`status: proposed`): five Cs, Q1–Q9, every field in the new form, 7 new concepts and notes, all with printed page numbers.
- `/home/garro/dev/faculty/Thesis/research/papers/P21.pdf`: the publisher's typeset version, 12 PDF pages.

**Source and version read**
- Full text, publisher's typeset version: IEEE JSSC vol. 46, no. 1, January 2011, pp. 173–183. It is Michael Konow's ResearchGate upload (1 June 2014) with a one-page ResearchGate cover sheet in front.
- I got it from a mirror, `https://search.iczhiku.com/paper/WjR2NH8uksdALAbZ.pdf`. Its TLS certificate has expired, so the download skipped the certificate check (`curl -k`).
- Page offset: PDF page = printed page − 171.
- Sources that failed: Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar list it as closed access; the ResearchGate link returned 403; a Semantic Scholar PDF found by search turned out to be an unrelated slide deck.
- I read the figures from rendered page images. Two figures don't say whether their values are measured or simulated: Fig. 7(b), message latency through the on-die buffer vs main memory, and Fig. 11, the NAS benchmark speedups. The record notes this.

**Deepest pass:** 2.

**Criterion (decision at gate 3c)**
- **For I1(b):** "message passing" is named throughout, and the chip adds hardware for it (p. 174, pp. 176–177):
  - a 16 KB Message Passing Buffer (MPB) per tile;
  - a Message Passing Memory Type (MPMT) cache-line bit;
  - a new INVDMB instruction that invalidates those lines.
- **Against:** the paper itself calls the protocol "a novel message passing based software protocol used to maintain data consistency in shared memory" (p. 173). Cores move data by loads and stores into "on-die shared memory" (p. 174), and there is no send instruction.
- **X2:** does not apply as worded, because the hardware has mechanisms made for message passing (pp. 174, 177).
- **Possible I4 (my inference; the SQ files were not among my inputs):**
  - many-core scaling (SQ13 and SQ14, by the form's field mapping): 48 cores with no hardware coherency, NAS speedup "effectively linear" (pp. 173, 179);
  - model equivalence (SQ10): message passing built on non-coherent shared memory, with an argument against hardware coherency at scale (pp. 173, 176).

Options:
- **A (recommended):** keep I1 and add I4. Edit the verdict line for R0-023 in the round file to "I1, I4" and the *Reference* line in P21.md to "I1, I4". Then fill *Model equivalence* in P21.md instead of leaving it `n/a (I1)`.
- **B:** keep I1 only. No edits.
- **C:** recast as I4 only, treating the message passing as software over shared memory. Edit the R0-023 verdict to I4. In P21.md, the I1-only fields (*Levels with message semantics*, *Receiving unit*, *Message mechanism*, *Non-message primitives*, *Cost of message primitives*) become `n/a (I4)`.

**Open issues**
- **Not stated in the paper:** synchronous vs asynchronous messages, message ordering, what happens when the receiver is busy, dispatch, interposition, protection, scheduling, and what happened to the chip later. The paper leaves the programmer's model to its ref. [11], Mattson et al. 2010, "The Intel 48-core single-chip cloud computer (SCC) processor: Programmer's view" (p. 181). That paper is a snowballing candidate.
- **Limits of the results:** the NAS runs go only to 32 cores (LU) and 36 cores (BT), never 48, and have no outside baseline (p. 179). All values in *Scaling* and the Fig. 7(b) latencies are marked `(read off)`.
- **Small inconsistencies, recorded in Notes:**
  - nominal 1.1 V in the abstract vs 1.14 V at the 125 W point (pp. 173, 180);
  - January 2011 in the journal header vs February 2011 on the ResearchGate cover;
  - the screening reference line gives 2010, but the issue year is 2011 (published online 9 November 2010).

I wrote the P21 record from the full text, read to pass 2. It meets I1 only in a qualified way: there is no message-send instruction, and the paper calls its protocol a software layer over shared memory. Whether to keep I1 is your call at gate 3c.

**Files written**
- `/home/garro/dev/faculty/Thesis/research/sls/3-reading/P21.md` (`status: proposed`): five Cs, Q1–Q9, every field in the new form, 7 new concepts and notes, all with printed page numbers.
- `/home/garro/dev/faculty/Thesis/research/papers/P21.pdf`: the publisher's typeset version, 12 PDF pages.

**Source and version read**
- Full text, publisher's typeset version: IEEE JSSC vol. 46, no. 1, January 2011, pp. 173–183. It is Michael Konow's ResearchGate upload (1 June 2014) with a one-page ResearchGate cover sheet in front.
- I got it from a mirror, `https://search.iczhiku.com/paper/WjR2NH8uksdALAbZ.pdf`. Its TLS certificate has expired, so the download skipped the certificate check (`curl -k`).
- Page offset: PDF page = printed page − 171.
- Sources that failed: Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar list it as closed access; the ResearchGate link returned 403; a Semantic Scholar PDF found by search turned out to be an unrelated slide deck.
- I read the figures from rendered page images. Two figures don't say whether their values are measured or simulated: Fig. 7(b), message latency through the on-die buffer vs main memory, and Fig. 11, the NAS benchmark speedups. The record notes this.

**Deepest pass:** 2.

**Criterion (decision at gate 3c)**
- **For I1(b):** "message passing" is named throughout, and the chip adds hardware for it (p. 174, pp. 176–177):
  - a 16 KB Message Passing Buffer (MPB) per tile;
  - a Message Passing Memory Type (MPMT) cache-line bit;
  - a new INVDMB instruction that invalidates those lines.
- **Against:** the paper itself calls the protocol "a novel message passing based software protocol used to maintain data consistency in shared memory" (p. 173). Cores move data by loads and stores into "on-die shared memory" (p. 174), and there is no send instruction.
- **X2:** does not apply as worded, because the hardware has mechanisms made for message passing (pp. 174, 177).
- **Possible I4 (my inference; the SQ files were not among my inputs):**
  - many-core scaling (SQ13 and SQ14, by the form's field mapping): 48 cores with no hardware coherency, NAS speedup "effectively linear" (pp. 173, 179);
  - model equivalence (SQ10): message passing built on non-coherent shared memory, with an argument against hardware coherency at scale (pp. 173, 176).

Options:
- **A (recommended):** keep I1 and add I4. Edit the verdict line for R0-023 in the round file to "I1, I4" and the *Reference* line in P21.md to "I1, I4". Then fill *Model equivalence* in P21.md instead of leaving it `n/a (I1)`.
- **B:** keep I1 only. No edits.
- **C:** recast as I4 only, treating the message passing as software over shared memory. Edit the R0-023 verdict to I4. In P21.md, the I1-only fields (*Levels with message semantics*, *Receiving unit*, *Message mechanism*, *Non-message primitives*, *Cost of message primitives*) become `n/a (I4)`.

**Open issues**
- **Not stated in the paper:** synchronous vs asynchronous messages, message ordering, what happens when the receiver is busy, dispatch, interposition, protection, scheduling, and what happened to the chip later. The paper leaves the programmer's model to its ref. [11], Mattson et al. 2010, "The Intel 48-core single-chip cloud computer (SCC) processor: Programmer's view" (p. 181). That paper is a snowballing candidate.
- **Limits of the results:** the NAS runs go only to 32 cores (LU) and 36 cores (BT), never 48, and have no outside baseline (p. 179). All values in *Scaling* and the Fig. 7(b) latencies are marked `(read off)`.
- **Small inconsistencies, recorded in Notes:**
  - nominal 1.1 V in the abstract vs 1.14 V at the 125 W point (pp. 173, 180);
  - January 2011 in the journal header vs February 2011 on the ResearchGate cover;
  - the screening reference line gives 2010, but the issue year is 2011 (published online 9 November 2010).

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** A tutorial description of one commercial processor architecture designed by others. The abstract says "these are covered in a tutorial fashion" (abstract). It is not an evaluation, as far as the abstract shows.

The material is "related to earlier developments in computer architecture" (abstract). - **Correctness:** Cannot be judged from the abstract. It makes no performance claim and reports no evidence (abstract).
- **Contributions:** An explanation of the 432's "sophisticated segmentation structure and the design of its instruction set", which the abstract says is where "the novelty of the new processor lies chiefly" (abstract).

    - a Message Passing Memory Type (MPMT) cache-line bit;
    - a new INVDMB instruction that invalidates those lines.
  - **Against:** the paper itself calls the protocol "a novel message passing based software protocol used to maintain data consistency in shared memory" (p. 173). Cores move data by loads and stores into "on-die shared memory" (p. 174), and there is no send instruction.
  - **X2:** does not apply as worded, because the hardware has mechanisms made for message passing (pp. 174, 177).
  - **Possible I4 (my inference; the SQ files were not among my inputs):**

######## PDF PAGE 1
C O V E R

F E A T U R E

Can We Make
Operating Systems
Reliable and Secure?
Andrew S. Tanenbaum, Jorrit N. Herder, and Herbert Bos
Vrije Universiteit, Amsterdam

Microkernels—long discarded as unacceptable because of their lower performance
compared with monolithic kernels—might be making a comeback in operating systems
due to their potentially higher reliability, which many researchers now regard as more
important than performance.

W

hen was the last time your TV set crashed
or implored you to download some emergency software update from the Web? After
all, unless it is an ancient set, it is just a computer with a CPU, a big monitor, some analog electronics for decoding radio signals, a couple of
peculiar I/O devices—a remote control, a built-in VCR
or DVD drive—and a boatload of software in ROM.
This rhetorical question points out a nasty little secret
that we in the computer industry do not like to discuss:
Why are TV sets, DVD recorders, MP3 players, cell
phones, and other software-laden electronic devices reliable and secure but computers are not? Of course there
are many “reasons”—computers are flexible, users can
change the software, the IT industry is immature, and
so on—but as we move to an era in which the vast
majority of computer users are nontechnical people,
increasingly these seem like lame excuses to them.
What consumers expect from a computer is what they
expect from a TV set: You buy it, you plug it in, and it
works perfectly for the next 10 years. As IT professionals, we need to take up this challenge and make computers as reliable and secure as TV sets.
The worst offender when it comes to reliability and
security is the operating system. Although application
programs contain many flaws, if the operating system
were bug free, bugs in application programs could do
only limited damage, so we will focus here on operating systems.

However, before getting into the details, a few words
about the relationship between reliability and security
are in order. Problems with each of these domains often
have the same root cause: bugs in the software. A buffer
overrun error can cause a system crash (reliability problem), but it can also allow a cleverly written virus or
worm to take over the computer (security problem).
Although we focus primarily on reliability, improving
reliability can also improve security.

WHY ARE SYSTEMS UNRELIABLE?
Current operating systems have two characteristics
that make them unreliable and insecure: They are huge
and they have very poor fault isolation. The Linux kernel has more than 2.5 million lines of code; the Windows
XP kernel is more than twice as large.

This contract declares that the channel accepts three messages, Request, Reply, and Error, the first with a positive
integer as parameter, the second with any integer as parameter, and the third with no parameters. When used for a
channel to a server, the Request messages go from the client
to the server and the other two messages go the other way.
A state machine specifies the protocol for the channel.
In the Start state, the client sends the Request message,
putting the channel into the Pending state. The server
can either respond with a Reply message or an Error message. The Reply message transitions the channel back to
the Start state, where communication can continue. The
Error message transitions the channel to the Stopped
state, ending communication on the channel.

The heap
If all data, such as file blocks read from disk, had to
go over channels, the system would be very slow, so an
exception is made to the basic rule that each process’s
data is completely private and internal to itself.
Singularity supports a shared object heap, but at each
instant every object on the heap belongs to a single
process. However, ownership of an object can be passed
over a channel.
As an example of how the heap works, consider I/O.
When a disk driver reads in a block, it puts the block on
the heap. Later, the system passes the handle for the
block to the user requesting the data, maintaining the
single-owner principle but allowing data to move from
disk to user with zero copies.

The file system
Singularity maintains a single hierarchical name space
for all services. A root name server handles the top of
the tree, but other name servers can be mounted on its
nodes. In particular, the file system, which is just a
process, is mounted on /fs, so a name like /fs/users/
linda/foo could be a user’s file. Files are implemented as
B-trees, with the block numbers as the keys. When a user
process asks for a file, the file system commands the disk
driver to put the requested blocks on the heap.
Ownership is then passed as described.

ach of the four different attempts to improve operating system reliability focuses on preventing buggy
device drivers from crashing the system.
In the Nooks approach, each driver is individually
hand wrapped in a software jacket to carefully control
its interactions with the rest of the operating system, but
it leaves all the drivers in the kernel. The paravirtual
machine approach takes this one step further and moves
the drivers to one or more machines distinct from the
main one, taking away even more power from the drivers. Both of these approaches are intended to improve
the reliability of existing (legacy) operating systems.
In contrast, two other approaches replace legacy operating systems with more reliable and secure ones. The
multiserver approach runs each driver and operating system component in a separate user process and allows
them to communicate using the microkernel’s IPC mechanism. Finally, Singularity, the most radical approach,
uses a type-safe language, a single address space, and formal contracts to carefully limit what each module can do.
Three of the four research projects—L4-based paravirtualization, Minix 3, and Singularity—use microkernels.
It is not yet known which, if any, of these approaches will
be widely adopted in the long run. Nevertheless, it is interesting to note that microkernels—long discarded as unacceptable because of their lower performance compared
with monolithic kernels—might be making a comeback
due to their potentially higher reliability, which many people now regard as more important than performance. The
wheel of reincarnation has turned. ■
