## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: generic operation / sending a message | "performing a generic operation is called sending a message"; "This message passing is how generic operations are performed" | p. 283 |
| new: method | "a function that handles a specific kind of message to a specific kind of object" | p. 284 |
| new: flavor | "in its simplest form, is a definition of an abstract type"; defined by defflavor, methods by defmethod | p. 286 |
| new: instance ("active object") | dtp-instance: "an instance of a flavor, i.e. an 'active object'"; a structure whose header points to an "instance descriptor" holding the method table | pp. 173, 309 |
| new: combined method | automatically generated function that "calls the appropriate methods in the right order", incorporating wrappers | p. 309 |
| new: select-method | an a-list of symbols and functions; the first argument is looked up to find the function to call; may have a default handler | p. 144 |
| new: entity | a closure-like primitive datatype "assumed to be a message-receiving object" | p. 311 |
| new: message-receiving stream | "A stream is a message-receiving object"; first argument names the operation | p. 338 |
| new: subprimitive | functions "normally hand-coded in microcode" that "take the place of machine language in other systems" and "cannot do full checking" | p. 172 |
| new: invisible pointer / forwarding | pointer that "does not represent a Lisp object", followed automatically on memory read and write | p. 174 |
| new: encapsulation | addition made by trace or advise around a function spec's basic definition, kept when the basic definition is redefined | p. 153 |
| new: communication through shared Lisp objects | processes share one address space and communicate "in arbitrary ways through shared Lisp objects" instead of "special restricted mechanisms for inter-process communication" | p. 429 |
| new: sequence break | "a kind of interrupt" that resumes the scheduler | p. 429 |
| new: generic instructions | "the machine is designed so that all instructions can be generic; that is, they determine the types of their operands at run time" | p. 484 |

## Notes
- **Source and version read:** the 4th edition (July 1981) of the manual, scanned PDF from Bitsavers (`https://bitsavers.trailing-edge.com/pdf/mit/cadr/chinual_4thEd_Jul81.pdf`), saved as `papers/P73.pdf`. The page images have no text layer; they were read as images. The DOI target is a one-page notice in ACM SIGART Bulletin no. 78 (Crossref: p. 10–10); its PDF at dl.acm.org was not reachable (Cloudflare challenge), so only its Crossref/OpenAlex abstract was read. The notice gives "471-page"; the scan has 532 numbered body pages plus ix front-matter pages, so the notice may describe a different printing (inferred, not checked). The edition is matched to the notice by date (manual July 1981, notice October 1981) and authors; that it is the edition announced is inferred.
- **Criterion:** the full text supports I1(b) at the microcode level: when an instance is called with a message keyword, "The microcode binds self to the object, binds the instance variables ... and calls a dtp-select-method" (p. 309), and the term "message" is used throughout (pp. 283–285). Against this, the manual says "no new features are added to Lisp for message sending; we simply define a convention on the way objects take arguments" (p. 285), and inter-process communication is through shared Lisp objects (p. 429). X2 does not apply as far as read (no conventional host kernel; dispatch is in microcode, p. 309). X5: the manual is a "system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer" (MIT AI Lab, title page; that MIT built the hardware is from the notice abstract); the DOI record itself, a one-page notice, would fall under X5 (2 pages or fewer). Which record P73 points to is for gate 3c.
- **Not read:** chapters on areas (15), compiler (16), mixing flavors and method combination in detail (20.7–20.12), packages (23), installing microcode (24.8.5), stack groups (12), errors (26). They may bear on Self-definition, Operating system functions and Interposition.

"date": "1982-05-17", "description": "In the late 1970s, Intel corporation invested a huge amount of resources in a \"revolutionary\" new microprocessor architecture, the Intel iAPX 432. It was designed to transparently support multiprocessor operation and direct execution of object-oriented languages. It was intended to be the 32-bit future for Intel's microprocessor business.

This is the paper that sank it. Informally circulated, it demonstrates, with a simple set of routine benchmarks, that the 432 was hopelessly slow compared to other readily available computer architectures of the era. Even Intel's own 8086 (by then a few years old) was several times faster.

The 432 quickly disappeared from Intel's CPU line up, and they focused their efforts on evolving the 'x86 line of processors over the next half century.

# P49

## Reference
Tanenbaum, A. S., Herder, J. N., Bos, H. (2006). *Can We Make Operating Systems Reliable and Secure?*. IEEE Computer 39(5) (May 2006), pp. 44–51, cover feature. https://doi.org/10.1109/mc.2006.156. P49, round-file row R0-067; screened include under I1. The full text meets I1(c) (see Notes). Version read: publisher layout ("Published by the IEEE Computer Society", "0018-9162/06/$20.00 © 2006 IEEE", p. 44), 8 PDF pages, taken from https://minix3.org/docs/jorrit-herder/computer-may06.pdf and saved as `papers/P49.pdf`. Pages cited are the printed ones: printed page = PDF page + 43 (PDF page 1 = p. 44, PDF page 8 = p. 51). The volume number 39(5) is not printed on the pages (inferred from "May 2006").

## Deepest pass
2 (whole text read, every section, figure caption and reference; the authors' claims were not checked against the cited design papers, so not a third pass)

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** A magazine argument comparing "four different approaches that researchers are using to make future operating systems more reliable and secure, proceeding from the least radical to the most radical solution" (p. 45): Nooks, paravirtual machines on L4, multiserver operating systems (Minix 3), and language-based protection (Singularity). It is a position or analytical argument with a design description of the authors' own Minix 3 (pp. 47–49), not a primary research paper.
- **Context:** Operating systems are "huge" and have "very poor fault isolation" (p. 45); bug density figures from cited studies [1, 2, 3] are used to estimate kernel bug counts (p. 44). Builds on Nooks [4, 5], L4 and L4Linux [7, 8, 9], Minix 3 [10], Singularity (no citation given) and the Burroughs B5000 (p. 49).
- **Correctness:** The bug estimates assume bug count scales with lines of code, at "a conservative estimate of six bugs per 1,000 lines" taken from other code bases (pp. 44, 48); this is an assumption, not a measurement of these kernels. Performance claims for Minix 3 are given in one paragraph without baseline version or run counts (p. 49); the paravirtualization overhead "about 3 to 8 percent" is attributed to "performance measurements" with no citation or setup (p. 47).
- **Contributions:** (1) a side-by-side description of four approaches to OS reliability (pp. 45–50); (2) the observation that three of the four "use microkernels" and that microkernels "might be making a comeback due to their potentially higher reliability" (p. 50); (3) a description of Minix 3's message-passing IPC, its integration of interrupts with message passing, and its reincarnation server (pp. 47–49).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well organised by approach; written for a general audience, so mechanisms are described only at the level of principle.

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | Stated in one place: "Here we address four different approaches ... proceeding from the least radical to the most radical solution" (p. 45). |
| Q2 | partly | For Minix 3: "fixed-length messages", "rendezvous principle", direct copy when "both the sender and the receiver are ready", undeliverable events "marked pending a bitmap" (p. 48); how receivers are named is not described beyond "allowed destinations" (p. 48). Singularity channels get message typing and protocol (pp. 49–50) but no buffering or busy-receiver behaviour. |
| Q3 | yes | The authors' own figures come from Minix 3, a kernel that runs real programs and "can build itself" (p. 49); figures for Nooks and L4 are reported from others' work (pp. 46–47). |
| Q4 | partly | Minix 3's loss is measured against "in-kernel drivers" with no named system or version (p. 49); the 6-second build and the 3–8 percent paravirtualization overhead name no baseline (pp. 47, 49). |
| Q5 | partly | The build gives workload ("112 compilations and 11 links") and hardware ("2.2-GHz Athlon"), but no run count and no reason for the workload (p. 49); the "less than 10 percent" figure has no setup at all (p. 49). |
| Q6 | n/a | Cannot apply: the standfirst (abstract) and the conclusion make no quantitative claim, only that microkernels have "lower performance" and "potentially higher reliability" (pp. 44, 50). |
| Q7 | partly | The user-mode driver overhead is isolated by comparing against in-kernel drivers (p. 49); other causes ("eliminates kernel traps and context switches", p. 49; reliability from kernel size and static data structures, p. 48) are only asserted. |
| Q8 | partly | A dedicated "Limitations" subsection exists only for Nooks (p. 46); Minix 3's limits are mentioned in passing ("currently only servers that do not maintain much internal state can be restarted", p. 48; restarting "will not remove the bug", p. 48); no threats to validity for the article's own claims. |
| Q9 | partly | Herder is the first author of the cited Minix 3 design paper [10] (p. 51), and Minix 3 is the only system the article itself measures (p. 49); no author is listed as a designer of Nooks, L4 or Singularity. Whether Tanenbaum and Bos built Minix 3 is not stated in the paper (inferred likely). |

## Extracted fields
| Field | Value | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | Tanenbaum, Herder, Bos (2006), *Can We Make Operating Systems Reliable and Secure?*, IEEE Computer, May 2006, pp. 44–51; P49; I1 (I1(c), see Notes). Publisher layout; printed page = PDF page + 43 | 44, 51 |
| Paper type | Position or analytical argument (comparison of four approaches, conclusion that microkernels "might be making a comeback"); design (description of Minix 3) | 45, 47–49, 50 |
| System | (1) Nooks, on Linux, by "the Nooks team" [4, 5]; status: running (inferred from "experiments show", p. 46). (2) L4 microkernel built "in the 1990s" by "a research group at the University of Karlsruhe", with L4Linux and driver virtual machines [7, 8, 9]; running kernel (inferred). (3) Minix 3, multiserver OS, builders not named in the text (design paper by Herder et al. [10]); running kernel, "available for free download under the Berkeley license", for the Pentium. (4) Singularity, by "Microsoft Research", year not stated; status not stated. (5) Burroughs B5000, mentioned as historical precedent only | 46, 47, 49 |
| Levels with message semantics | Kernel, Minix 3: partly. Between OS processes, messages are the only stated path: servers and drivers "cannot directly call each other's functions or share data structures. Instead, Minix 3 performs IPC by passing fixed-length messages"; user library calls "do their work by sending messages to servers"; interrupts are turned into messages ("the kernel turns it into a normal message"). Other paths: "kernel calls" from drivers and servers (whether these are messages is not stated), and "The clock driver shares the microkernel's address space". Kernel, Singularity: partly. "all process-to-process communication uses these channels" and user processes "obtain system services by sending strongly typed messages to the microkernel", but a "shared object heap" is an exception and the microkernel "handles thread synchronization with mutexes". Language (Sing#): partly, "augmented with message passing primitives" and "fully supports channels in the language". Instruction set and hardware: not stated (Pentium with MMU, x86). Between cores versus within a core: not stated; the paper does not discuss multiprocessors. Started message-based and later added non-message paths: for Singularity the heap is presented as a design exception made because channels alone "would be very slow"; no history of later additions is stated | 47, 48, 49, 50 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | Minix 3: process (driver, server or user process), each "in its own private address space, protected by the memory management unit (MMU) hardware"; others reach its memory only through "kernel calls (which the kernel inspects for validity)"; the clock driver shares the kernel's address space. Singularity: process, "a closed entity" with its own code, data, runtime and garbage collector; all processes in "a single virtual address space"; isolation by the compiler ("will not allow a process to touch another process's data"); objects on the shared heap belong to "a single process" at each instant, and "ownership of an object can be passed over a channel" | 47, 48, 49, 50 |
| Message mechanism | Minix 3: synchronous "rendezvous principle: When both the sender and the receiver are ready, the system copies the message directly from the sender to the receiver"; "fixed-length messages"; "does not require message queuing or buffering"; "an asynchronous event notification mechanism is available. Events that cannot be delivered are marked pending a bitmap in the process table"; interrupt handlers set a bit in the driver's "pending interrupts" bitmap "and then continue without blocking"; naming: per-process "allowed destinations" (how destinations are named is not stated); user processes "can use only the rendezvous principle and can send to only the Posix servers"; dispatch: not stated. Singularity: "strongly typed messages" over "point-to-point bidirectional channels"; a channel contract declares message types and a state machine for the protocol (example contract C1); synchrony, buffering and busy-receiver behaviour not stated | 48, 49, 50 |
| Non-message primitives | Minix 3: "kernel calls" for privileged operations such as "reading a selected portion of a specific user's address space or writing to authorized I/O ports" (reason: drivers in user mode "cannot execute privileged instructions or read or write the computer's I/O ports"); clock driver sharing the microkernel's address space (no reason given); interrupts, handled by the microkernel and converted to notifications; MMU protection. Singularity: "shared object heap" (reason: "If all data, such as file blocks read from disk, had to go over channels, the system would be very slow"); "mutexes" for thread synchronization in the microkernel (no reason given); MMU used "only to map pages"; trusted hardware abstraction layer hiding "I/O ports, interrupt request lines, direct memory access channels, and timers" | 47, 48, 49, 50 |
| Self-definition | Singularity: "written almost entirely in Sing#", but "a small portion is written in C#, C++, or assembler and must be trusted since it cannot be verified", namely "the hardware abstraction layer and the garbage collector" (cost of that base: it cannot be verified). Running inspection or change: the design "forbids dynamic process extensions" and "does not permit loadable modules"; components carry metadata used by "External verifiers" before execution. Minix 3: implementation language not stated; no reflection stated | 49, 50 |
| Interposition | Nooks: yes between kernel and driver: "the call actually goes to a wrapper that checks the parameters for validity and manages the call"; goal "as few changes as possible to existing drivers and the kernel" (so not strictly "without changing either"); stubs generated automatically, bodies handwritten, "455 wrappers"; isolation via "the virtual memory page map"; shadow drivers log driver–kernel communication; cost not stated. Paravirtual machines: drivers "do not have to be modified" but the Linux kernel is (about 3,000 plus 5,000 lines); overhead "about 3 to 8 percent". Minix 3: the kernel's per-process bitmaps can block sends (for example "sending messages to the audio driver"), which is filtering, not interposition of a third component (inferred); placing a component between Minix 3 processes: not stated | 45, 46, 47, 48 |
| Operating system functions | Minix 3. Protection: MMU address spaces plus "bitmaps and ranges within the kernel's process table" controlling permitted kernel calls, IPC capabilities and I/O ports; central component yes (the kernel's process table). Scheduling: the microkernel "performs process scheduling"; central yes. Resource allocation: "the process manager, which handles process and memory management"; device access through kernel calls; central yes (single process manager, inferred from the text). Naming: "the data store, a simple name server that the other servers use"; central yes. Failure handling: the "reincarnation server, which is the parent process of all the other servers and all the drivers", restarts failed drivers and servers; central yes. ## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** A magazine argument comparing "four different approaches that researchers are using to make future operating systems more reliable and secure, proceeding from the least radical to the most radical solution" (p. 45): Nooks, paravirtual machines on L4, multiserver operating systems (Minix 3), and language-based protection (Singularity). It is a position or analytical argument with a design description of the authors' own Minix 3 (pp. 47–49), not a primary research paper.
- **Context:** Operating systems are "huge" and have "very poor fault isolation" (p. 45); bug density figures from cited studies [1, 2, 3] are used to estimate kernel bug counts (p. 44). Builds on Nooks [4, 5], L4 and L4Linux [7, 8, 9], Minix 3 [10], Singularity (no citation given) and the Burroughs B5000 (p. 49).
- **Correctness:** The bug estimates assume bug count scales with lines of code, at "a conservative estimate of six bugs per 1,000 lines" taken from other code bases (pp. 44, 48); this is an assumption, not a measurement of these kernels. Performance claims for Minix 3 are given in one paragraph without baseline version or run counts (p. 49); the paravirtualization overhead "about 3 to 8 percent" is attributed to "performance measurements" with no citation or setup (p. 47).
- **Contributions:** (1) a side-by-side description of four approaches to OS reliability (pp. 45–50); (2) the observation that three of the four "use microkernels" and that microkernels "might be making a comeback due to their potentially higher reliability" (p. 50); (3) a description of Minix 3's message-passing IPC, its integration of interrupts with message passing, and its reincarnation server (pp. 47–49).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well organised by approach; written for a general audience, so mechanisms are described only at the level of principle.

| new: fault isolation | Current OSes have "very poor fault isolation"; "Every single one of the millions of lines of kernel code can overwrite key data structures that an unrelated component uses" | 44, 45 |
| new: lightweight protection domain (sandboxing) | Nooks wraps each driver "in a layer of protective software to form a lightweight protection domain, a technique sometimes called sandboxing" | 45 |
| new: interposition (wrappers) | Nooks section titled "Interposition": kernel–driver calls go to "a wrapper that checks the parameters for validity and manages the call" | 45–46 |
| new: shadow driver | Logs communication between a driver and the kernel and replays it to a restarted driver | 46 |
| new: paravirtualization | Modifying the OS so it does "not do anything that cannot be virtualized"; drivers run in separate Linux virtual machines on L4 | 46–47 |
| new: multiserver operating system | "only a tiny microkernel runs in kernel mode with the rest of the operating system running as a collection of fully isolated user-mode server and driver processes" | 47 |
| new: rendezvous message passing | Minix 3 IPC: "fixed-length messages using the rendezvous principle", copied directly when both sides are ready, with no queuing or buffering in the kernel | 48 |
| new: interrupts integrated with message passing | "Minix 3 elegantly integrates interrupts with the message passing system": handlers set a pending bit, "the kernel turns it into a normal message" | 48 |
| new: IPC capabilities | Per-process restriction of "available IPC primitives, allowed destinations, and user event notifications" through bitmaps in the kernel's process table | 48 |
| new: reincarnation server (self-healing) | Parent of all servers and drivers; kills and restarts one that crashes or "fails to respond to the periodic pings" | 48 |
| new: language-based protection | Protection by type-safe language and compiler instead of MMU, as in the Burroughs B5000 and Singularity | 49 |
| new: channel contract | Sing# channels with "formal typing and protocol specifications": declared messages and a state machine for the protocol | 49–50 |
| new: single-owner shared heap | "at each instant every object on the heap belongs to a single process. However, ownership of an object can be passed over a channel", allowing zero-copy I/O | 50 |
| new: wheel of reincarnation | Microkernels, discarded for performance, "might be making a comeback" for reliability: "The wheel of reincarnation has turned" | 50 |

- **Possible I4 relevance (for the gate):** the paper argues that software size and driver error rates make OSes unreliable (pp. 44–45, citing [1, 2, 3]) and that fault isolation rather than bug removal is the remedy (p. 45); this may bear on the SQs served by *What shapes programs* (SQ8), but I did not read the SQ files, so this is not a criterion claim. - **Singularity facts are third-party:** the authors are not Singularity's designers and give no citation for it (pp. 49–50, reference list p. 51); its design claims should be traced to Singularity's own papers before synthesis.

the FAT32 file system. All of the components of the application are
multithreaded, and each process also has message-passing channels
to stdin and stdout. The SMTP server processes incoming SMTP
commands; when a mail message is sent through the server, it is
sent to the storage service. The storage service sends the email to
the antivirus service to be scanned. If the antivirus service finds
the email is clean, than the storage service writes the email into an
appropriate mailbox. The antivirus process is CPU and memory
bound, since it checks messages against an in-memory database of
virus signatures. The SMTP server is I/O-bound to the network,
and the storage service is I/O-bound to disk. Therefore, the antivirus service expresses a negative affinity with the mailstore, so
that it has a maximum number of CPU cycles available to it, and
is not interrupted by hardware interrupts either from the disk or
the network. On the other hand, the mail service expresses a positive affinity with the file system, and the SMTP service expresses
no preference with regards to the networking stack. Thus, while
many components are involved in the mail server application, there
are few affinity values that must be expressed to maximize performance. The mail server benchmark results are covered in detail in
Section 4.5.2.

4.

EVALUATION
Our evaluation sets out to answer the following questions:
• Does Helios make it easier to use programmable devices?
• Can offloading with satellite kernels improve performance?
• Does kernel isolation improve performance on NUMA architectures?
• Does Helios benefit applications executing on NUMA architectures?

4.1 Methodology
We evaluated Helios on two different platforms. The first platform is an Intel Core2 Duo processor running at 2.66 GHz with 2
GB of RAM. The programmable device is a hardware RAID development board based on Intel XScale IOP348 processor running
at 1.2GHz with 256 MB of RAM, and featuring an onboard Intel Gb Ethernet adapter. The development board is attached to the
host by an 8-lane PCI Express interface. The second platform is a
dual dual-core (2 chips, 2 cores per chip) motherboard where each
core is a 2 GHz Opteron processor. Each chip runs within its own
NUMA domain, and each NUMA domain has 1 GB of RAM, for a
total of 2 GB. The machine runs with an Intel Gb PCI Ethernet card
and a 200 GB hard drive. When we run networking experiments,
machines are connected with a gigabit Ethernet switch. Performance was measured by using the total number of CPU cycles that
elapsed during an experiment; the cycle-count was then converted
into standard units of time.
When we run experiments evaluating the benefits of satellite kernels on NUMA architectures we run in two configurations. First, a
configuration that uses a non-NUMA aware version of Helios with
BIOS interleaved-memory turned on, which interleaves memory on
4 KB page boundaries. This version runs a single satellite kernel
across all processors. Second, a NUMA-aware version of Helios
(no interleaved memory) that runs the coordinator kernel in NUMA
domain 0, and a satellite kernel in NUMA domain 1. Each kernel
executes on the two processors native to its NUMA domain. We
measured the raw memory latency of each type of memory and
found that L2 cache misses to remote memory were 38% slower
than local memory, and accesses to interleaved memory were on
average 19% slower than accesses to local memory.

4.2 Using Affinity to set Placement Policies
To see how well satellite kernels, remote channels, affinity and
our 2-stage compilation strategy worked, we took a number of applications originally written for Singularity (i.e., with no thought
towards offloading to another architecture) and added affinity values to each application’s manifest. Once we arranged for our build
system to compile to both ISAs, all of our examples ran without
modification except for one: our TCP testing harness used floating
point code to calculate throughput numbers. Our programmable device does not have a floating point unit, and we had not yet added
floating point emulation code to the kernel. As a stop-gap measure
we changed the way floating-point code was calculated. Later, we
added floating-point emulation code to the satellite kernel to ensure
other applications could run unmodified.
We had the same networking chip set on both the programmable
device and on a non-programmable networking card. The networking driver for this chip, which was written for Singularity, worked
without modification once compiled to ARM byte-code. Further,
our networking stack, which supports TCP, IP, UDP, DHCP, and
ARP protocols, worked without modification on the programmable
device by adding a positive affinity value between it and the networking driver.

4.3 Message-passing Microbenchmark
Our next benchmark measured the cost of remote (RMP) and local (LMP) message passing on the two platforms that support satellite kernels. We ran SingBench, which was originally designed to
benchmark the performance of Singularity message passing, using
local message passing and remote message passing both to a satellite kernel on a NUMA domain and a satellite kernel on the XScale
I/O card. The benchmark forks a child process and then it measures
the time to send and receive a message of a certain size.
The results are presented in Figure 5. The x-axis shows the
amount of data sent one-way during the test, and the y-axis shows
the time in microseconds to send and receive a single message.
Since no copies are made during LMP, the time is constant as the
size of the message grows. RMP on NUMA grows with the size of
the message, while RMP on XScale is bound mainly by the time
to program the ADMA controller. Therefore, once messages are
greater than 32 KB in size, message passing over the PCI-E bus is
more efficient than message passing between two NUMA domains.

4.4.1 Netstack Subsystem Offload
We were interested to see whether we could improve the performance of an application by offloading a dependent operating
system component onto the XScale I/O card. We took an existing Singularity service that decompresses PNG images and made
it available via a TCP/IP connection. We then ran two versions of
it, one where everything ran on a single x86 CPU, and one where
the NIC driver and networking stack (ARP, DHCP, IP, TCP) were
offloaded onto the XScale programmable device.
We then ran the PNG decompression service and connected 8
clients (chosen by the number required to saturate the x86 CPU)
over the network and then sent PNGs of varying sizes as fast as
possible to be decompressed. The results are shown in Figure 6.
The first column shows the size of the PNG sent over the network.
Larger PNGs took longer to decompress, and therefore slowed down
overall performance. The second and third columns show the average uploads per second processed by the PNG decompression
service when the netstack and NIC driver ran on the x86 CPU, and
when they were offloaded to the XScale I/O card. In general, the
benefits of offloading tracked the amount of CPU freed up by offloading the networking stack and NIC driver, which can be seen in
the average speedup in the fourth column. Finally, the fifth column
shows the reduction in interrupts to the x86 processor when the netstack and NIC driver were offloaded. The reduction occurred because the XScale CPU absorbed all of the interrupts generated by
the NIC. Since the x86 processor took fewer interrupts, the PNG
decompression service operated more efficiently and therefore its
performance improved.

number of driver threads to increase the load on the system. We
also added code to synchronize the filesystem at configurable inter-

We used affinity to quickly change and test four different policies
for offloading portions of the storage subsystem. We incrementally
offloaded the IDE driver, then the file system, then the PostMark
driver process. We used the same IDE controller (Silicon Image
3114) attached to the XScale I/O card and the PC host, and the
same physical disk drive in all experiments. The results are shown

Our first set of runs, shown under the column C1, demonstrated
that offloading the IDE driver to the XScale I/O card improved performance by 70%. Upon further investigation, we discovered that
the PCI card overloaded a configuration register (initially used to
define the cacheline size of the CPU) to define a low-water mark
that determined when the card should fill its hardware queue with
operations destined for the disk. Since the cacheline size was used
for the water mark, which differed between each architecture, the
low-water mark was set too high and was not set uniformly. After
reconfiguring the card, the performance of executing all processes
on the x86 was roughly 2x faster than offloading the IDE driver to
the XScale I/O card.
Our experience with configuring the PCI card was not unusual;
in heterogeneous systems, small configuration changes often lead
to large performance changes, and these performance changes may
require changing the placement of processes. Using affinity simplifies performance tuning by allowing us to quickly cycle through
different placement policies.

We are certain that the scheduler could be optimized to remove
these serialization bottlenecks and improve single-kernel performance. Yet there would undoubtedly be other bottlenecks as the
number of cores grows. Helios provides a simple mechanism around
scaling problems: by growing the number of kernels, lock contention is decreased.

4.5 Benefits of Performance Isolation
4.5.1 Scheduling Microbenchmark
Our next benchmark tested the utility of kernel isolation on our
two-node NUMA machine. Many operating systems have had much
work put into them to eliminate locking bottlenecks as the number
of cores increases. We hypothesized that executing satellite kernels
would be a simple way to scale around locking serialization problems. We ran a Singularity scheduling stress-test, which measures
the time it takes 16 threads to call threadyield one million times.
Helios uses the Singularity MinScheduler, which is a round-robin
scheduler without priorities. The MinScheduler favors threads that
have recently become unblocked and tries to avoid or minimize
reading the clock, resetting the timer, and holding the dispatcher
lock. The scheduler also does simple load-balancing by assigning
work to idle processors through an IPI interrupt. The scheduler has
known scaling problems, mainly because a single lock protects the
dispatching mechanism.
The results of the scheduling benchmark can be seen in Figure 9.
The version labeled “No satellite kernel” ran all 16 threads on a version of Helios that is not NUMA-aware. The right hand bar graph
shows a NUMA-aware version of Helios that runs two kernels. The
version with two kernels scales around the serialization bottleneck
and must run only 8 threads per kernel; it is 68% faster than the
single-kernel version of Helios. The greater than 2x improvement
in performance over a single kernel is caused by the load-balancing
algorithm, which issues expensive IPI interrupts and harms performance as the number of cores grows.

We were interested to see how Helios could improve performance of a more involved benchmark on a NUMA machine. We
therefore ran a mail server benchmark and measured application
throughput. The application, which is describe in Section 3.7.4, is
composed of an SMTP server, an antivirus scanner, and a storage
service. Since Singularity had no antivirus agent, we wrote our own
and used the virus definitions for the popular ClamAV antivirus application. We attempted to make the antivirus agent as efficient
as possible, but it is the bottleneck in the system since the SMTP
server waits for emails to be scanned and written to disk before
confirming an email’s receipt. We hypothesized that the antivirus
scanner, which is memory and CPU bound, would benefit from kernel isolation. Its negative affinity with the storage service causes it
to run in isolation when two satellite kernels are present.
We randomly selected 1,000 emails from the Enron email corpus [19] and had a single client send the emails as fast as possible. The results are in Figure 10. The left hand graph shows the
emails-per-second processed by the email server (which includes
a blocking scan to the virus scanner). Using satellite kernels improves throughput by 39%. Since satellite kernels isolate remote
vs local memory, every application component benefits from faster
memory accesses on L2 cache misses. Further, satellite kernels ensure that processes always use local memory when accessing kernel
code and data structures.
The right hand graph of Figure 10 shows the instructions-percycle (IPC) of the anti-virus scanner. We captured this metric using the performance counters available on AMD processors. The
graph shows that the antivirus scanner improves its IPC by 20%
when running on a satellite kernel. By running on its own kernel,
other applications never have the opportunity to pollute the antivirus scanner’s L1 or L2 cache, improving its cache-hit rate and

RELATED WORK

To the best of our knowledge, Helios is the first operating system
to provide a seamless, single image operating system abstraction
across heterogeneous programmable devices.
Helios treats programmable devices as part of a “distributed system in the small,” and is inspired by distributed operating systems
such as LOCUS [33], Emerald [16, 31], and Quicksilver [27].
Helios is derived from the Singularity operating system [13] and
extends Singularity’s message-passing interface [6] to work transparently between different satellite kernels. A pre-cursor to this
approach is found in the Mach microkernel [1], which provided an
IPC abstraction that worked identically for processes within a single system, and for processes on remote systems over a local or
wide area network.
Programmable devices and runtimes. Programmable devices
have a long history in computer systems, and many prior operating systems have found ways to offload work to them. The IBM
709 [14] used channel processors to remove the burden of I/O
from the main CPU and to allow I/O transfers to complete asynchronously. Subsequent systems such as the IBM System/360 and
System/370 [15] and Control Data CDC6600 [32] continued this
trend with increased numbers of channel processors. However,
the range of operations supported by channel processors appears
to have been limited to basic data transfer and signaling. The Bus
Master DMA devices found on commodity PCs today are the logical descendants of channel processors.

Auspex Systems [12], which designed network file servers, ran a
UNIX kernel on one CPU and dedicated other CPUs to the network
driver, the storage system, and the file system. The offloaded processes were linked against a compact runtime that supported memory allocation, message passing, timers, and interrupt servicing.
The process offloading avoided the costs associated with UNIX for
time critical components.
Keeton et al. [18] proposed intelligent disks, adding relatively
powerful embedded processors to disks together with additional
memory to improve the performance of database applications. The
Active Disk project [26] has validated this approach empirically,
and the Smart Disk project [5] has validated this approach theoretically for a range of database workloads.
Network adapters have also been a focus of offloading. SPINE
was a custom runtime for programmable network adapters built by
Fiuczynscki et al. [9, 8]. The SPINE runtime provided a type safe
programming environment for code on the network adapter and
included abortable per packet computation to guarantee forward
progress and to prevent interference with real-time packet processing tasks, such as network video playback.
More recently, the AsyMOS [23] and Piglet [24] systems dedicated a processor in an SMP system to act as a programmable
channel processor. The channel processor ran a lightweight device
kernel with a virtual clock packet scheduler to provide quality-ofservice guarantees for network applications. McAuley and Neugebauer [20] leverage virtual machine processor features to create virtual channel processors. The virtual channel processors are used to
sandbox I/O system faults and they run I/O tasks on either the CPU,
or an I/O processor, depending on which performs better.
Helios benefits from this large body of prior work that demonstrates the benefits of using programmable devices to offload work.
Helios builds on this work by focusing on a generalized approach
for developing, deploying and tuning applications for heterogeneous systems.
Helios uses satellite kernels to export general OS abstractions to
programmable devices. An alternative approach is to instead create
specialized runtime systems. The Hydra framework developed by
Weinsberg et al. [34] provides a programming model and deployment algorithm for offloading components onto programmable peripherals, including network adapters. Hydra assumes components
are able to communicate through a common mechanism, and provides a modular runtime. Unlike Helios and SPINE, the runtime
environment does not provide safety guarantees.
Heterogeneous architectures. The Hera-JVM [21] manages
heterogeneity by hiding it behind a virtual machine. This additional
layer of abstraction allows developers to exploit heterogeneous resources through code annotation or runtime monitoring, and it allows threads to migrate between general purpose processors and
powerful floating point units that are part of the Cell architecture.
This approach is closely related to Emerald [31], which allows objects and threads to migrate between machines of different architec-

 === PAGE 13
tures over a local area network. Helios takes a different approach
by making the differences in heterogeneous architectures explicit
and by compiling multiple versions of a process for each available
architecture.
Multi-kernel systems. Other operating systems have been built
around the premise of running multiple kernels within a single machine, but prior efforts have focused on a homogeneous CPU architecture. Hive [4] exported a single instance of the IRIX operating
system while dividing work and resource management among different NUMA domains to improve fault tolerance. Each NUMA
domain ran its own copy of the IRIX kernel. Hive could migrate
threads between NUMA domains, and would share memory between domains to give threads the illusion of executing on a single
kernel. Hive shared I/O devices by running distributed applications,
such as NFS, in different NUMA domains. Alternatively, Cellular
Disco [11] ran multiple kernels within a single machine by running multiple virtual machines across NUMA domains to create a
virtual cluster. Chakraborty [3] explored dividing cores between
OS and applications functionality, and reserving certain cores for
specific system calls. Finally, the Corey [2] operating system optimized multi-core execution by exposing APIs to applications to
avoid unnecessary sharing of kernel state.
In general, there has been much research into improving the performance of NUMA architectures. For example, the Tornado operating system [10] and K42 [30] decompose OS services into objects
to try and improve resource locality. In contrast, Helios uses satellite kernels to ensure that resource requests are always local to an
application.
More recently, the Barrelfish [28] operating system strives to
improve performance by using a mix of online monitoring and
statically defined application resources requirements to make good
placement decisions for applications. Helios and Barrelfish are
complimentary efforts at managing heterogeneity. Barrelfish focuses on gaining a fine-grained understanding of application requirements when running applications, while the focus of Helios is
to export a single-kernel image across heterogenous coprocessors
to make it easy for applications to take advantage of new hardware
platforms.

6.

CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

Helios is an operating system designed for heterogeneous programming environments. Helios uses satellite kernels to simplify
program development, and it provides affinity as a way to better reason about deploying and performance tuning applications
for unknown hardware topologies. We demonstrated that applications are easily offloaded to programmable devices, and we demonstrated that affinity helps to quickly tune application performance.
In the future, we see three main areas of focus. First, although
we have found satellite kernels and affinity to be useful tools, their
deployment has been limited to only one programmable device.
Further, Helios has not yet been ported to the most promising programmable device: a GPU. We currently lack a compiler to create DirectX textures from CIL, and graphics cards do not provide
timers or interrupt controllers, which are required to run a satellite
kernel. In the future, we want to port Helios to the Intel Larrabee
graphics card and measure the benefits provided by satellite kernels
to applications targeted at GPUs.
Second, while we found workloads that benefit from the strong
kernel isolation provided by Helios, the inability of processes to
span NUMA domains limits the scalability of large, multi-threaded
processes. In the future, we want to allow processes to span NUMA
domains (should they require it) by moving CPUs and memory between satellite kernels.

Third, Helios is an experimental operating system with a limited
number of applications. In the future, we want to determine how to
create satellite kernels from a commodity operating system such as
Windows, which supports a much larger API. A commodity operating system provides a much larger set of applications with which
we can experiment.
Ultimately, the hardware on programmable devices has outpaced
the development of software frameworks to manage them. Helios
provides a general framework for developing, deploying, and tuning applications destined for programmable devices of varying architectures and performance characteristics.

I've written the P49 record from the full published text, and the full text confirms the screening verdict, include under I1(c). The X criteria didn't decide the paper early, so I read it to the end.

**Files written**
- `/home/garro/dev/faculty/Thesis/research/sls/3-reading/P49.md`: the record, `status: proposed`. Every field and quality answer cites a printed page.
- `/home/garro/dev/faculty/Thesis/research/papers/P49.pdf`: the publisher's layout of IEEE Computer, May 2006, pp. 44–51, 8 PDF pages. Printed page = PDF page + 43. sha256 7067f9a2…41b2e9.

**Source and version:** the publisher's layout, downloaded from https://minix3.org/docs/jorrit-herder/computer-may06.pdf. It carries "Published by the IEEE Computer Society" and "0018-9162/06/$20.00 © 2006 IEEE" on p. 44. Unpaywall lists the DOI as closed access. A 7-page author manuscript is at https://www.cs.vu.nl/~ast/Publications/Papers/computer-2006a.pdf; I only looked at its first page and did not use it.

**Deepest pass:** 2. I read every section, caption and reference, but did not check the claims against the cited design papers.

**Criterion:**
- **I1(c), as screening proposed.** In Minix 3 the microkernel "implements interprocess communication" (p. 47), and servers and drivers "cannot directly call each other's functions or share data structures. Instead, Minix 3 performs IPC by passing fixed-length messages" (p. 48). Singularity's processes talk to each other and to the microkernel by "strongly typed messages" over channels (p. 49).
- **X9 does not apply.** The body reads partly as an overview of four approaches (p. 45), but the title and standfirst don't call it a survey. It also reports its own Minix 3 measurements (p. 49) and gives a reason microkernels were abandoned (p. 47).

**Open issues**
1. **Possible X8 overlap.** The Minix 3 design also appears in Herder et al., "Modular System Programming in MINIX 3", ;login: 2006 (ref. 10, p. 51). I did not check whether that paper is in the review, because the round file was not one of my inputs. If it gets in later, X8 needs checking.
2. **Possible I4.** The paper argues from bug density and driver error rates (pp. 44–45) and mentions the Burroughs B5000's protection by compiler (p. 49). That might serve SQ8 or SQ9, but I did not read the SQ files, so I only note it. Those fields are `n/a (I1)` in the record.
   - **Option A (recommended):** keep I1 only. No edit.
   - **Option B:** add I4 to the R0-067 verdict in `research/sls/2-search/R0.md`, and have the record's *What shapes programs* and *Hardware–language trade-off* fields filled from pp. 44–45 and 49.
3. **Q6 is `n/a`.** The standfirst and conclusion make no numeric claims, so I treated the question as not applicable. The alternative is a vacuous "yes".
   - **Option A (recommended):** keep `n/a`. No edit.
   - **Option B:** change the Q6 row in the record to `yes`.
4. **Q9 is `partly`.** Herder is first author of the cited Minix 3 design paper. The paper does not say whether Tanenbaum or Bos built Minix 3; I marked that as inferred.
5. **Two kinds of claims are only as good as the paper's own wording.**
   - The Singularity claims are third-party, and the paper gives no citation for them. They should be traced to Singularity's own papers before synthesis.
   - Every performance figure lacks a named baseline version or a run count. I marked the Minix 3 figures as "measured (inferred)".

  - **I4 may also apply,** through the hardware–language trade-off, which the extraction form maps to SQ9: "Several features supported by the SOAR hardware could easily be performed by the compiler at marginal increased time and space costs" (p. 10).

  **Open issues**

       - (b) If [4] or [8] gets included, apply X8 at that point and add a line to P261.md *Notes* naming the kept paper.
       - (c) Add [4] and [8] to snowballing now.
     - I recommend (b), plus (c) for Ungar's dissertation, since it is the primary SOAR evaluation.

     - Options:
       - (a) Keep I2.
       - (b) Record the verdict as I2 + I4.
       - (c) Reclassify as I4 only. The I2-only fields (Levels, Receiving unit, Message mechanism and the others) would then become n/a, keeping the SQ9 field.
     - I recommend (b).

  4. **Q9 is "no":** all four authors appear in the cited SOAR design and build papers ([2], [3], [4], [8]; p. 11).

The text was extracted page by page with `pdftotext`; quotes below join words split by line-end hyphenation (e.g. "oneway" to "one-way"). All pages are the printed ones. No other source was needed: every claim cites P48 itself.

---
id: P261
row: 3a
by: reader
status: proposed
inputs: [papers/P261.pdf, sls/1-protocol/quality.md, sls/1-protocol/extraction-form.md, sls/1-protocol/criteria.md, sls/1-protocol/changes/2026-10-06-reading-pilot.md]
---
# P261

## Reference
William R. Bush, A. Dain Samples, David Ungar, Paul N. Hilfinger (1987). *Compiling Smalltalk-80 to a RISC*. Technical report, Division of Computer Science, University of California at Berkeley ("Productivity Engineering in the UNIX Environment", DARPA contract N00039-84-C-0089), distributed by DTIC as ADA179330 (DTIC date 06 Aug 87). https://openalex.org/W7208241813. Version read: the DTIC microfiche scan of the technical report (Internet Archive copy of www.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a179330.pdf, snapshot 2018-07-27, saved as `papers/P261.pdf`, 18 PDF pages). PDF pp. 1–5 are DTIC and contract front matter, PDF p. 6 holds the abstract (no printed number), and the paper body is printed pp. 1–11 = PDF pp. 7–17 (PDF page = printed page + 6; printed numbers are not visible on pp. 5 and 11, inferred from sequence). Pages cited below are printed pages; the abstract is cited as `abstract (PDF p. 6)`. The ASPLOS-II version named in the reference line was not read and its page range is not verified. Criteria: screened I2; full text appears to meet I2 (p. 1, pp. 3–10) and possibly I4 through the hardware–language trade-off (p. 10), see Notes.

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Implementation paper on a compiler for a language-specialised processor, with a measurement section and estimates of what each hardware feature is worth (pp. 1–10).
- **Context:** Part of the Smalltalk On A RISC (SOAR) project at Berkeley; builds on the SOAR architecture paper [2], the SOAR runtime paper [3], Ungar's dissertation [4] and Bush's report [8]; compares with Deutsch and Schiffman's dynamic translator [5] and with the Xerox Dorado (pp. 1–2, 9).
- **Correctness:** The compiler's own measurements (compile time, code expansion, register use) are reported with workload and machine (pp. 8–10). Most figures about SOAR hardware are taken from other reports: "All results quoted in this paper are found in either Ungar's dissertation [4] or Bush's report [8], unless stated otherwise" (p. 3, footnote 2), and several are called estimates (pp. 1, 6, 8).
- **Contributions:** Describes the bytecode-to-SOAR translator (simulated stack, register allocation in overlapping windows, spill rules) (pp. 2–6); shows how SOAR's tags, traps and pointer-to-register simplify it (pp. 6–7); reports compile time, code expansion and register-window use over the whole Smalltalk-80 image (pp. 8–10); concludes that "Several features supported by the SOAR hardware could easily be performed by the compiler at marginal increased time and space costs" (p. 10).
- **Clarity:** Short and clearly written; the scan is legible though the OCR text layer has errors (numbers were checked against the page images).

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | "This paper describes the SOAR compiler, presenting the mechanisms of compiling Smalltalk to the special-purpose SOAR RISC instruction set" (p. 1); same in the abstract (PDF p. 6). |
| Q2 | partly | Describes how a send is compiled: receiver and return address in dedicated registers, arguments in the overlapping low registers (p. 4, Figure 1 p. 5), receiver named by the leftmost operand (p. 7), dispatch by an in-line cache of the last method (p. 8). Delivery/ordering guarantees and the busy-receiver case are not stated. |
| Q3 | partly | The compiler is a working artefact run on the whole Smalltalk-80 image on a Dorado (p. 8); whether the SOAR performance figures come from silicon or a simulator is not stated in this paper (they are cited from [4] and [8], p. 3). |

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Implementation and evaluation report (a master's thesis issued as a technical report). It covers a language (Concurrent Smalltalk, CST), its compiler (Optimist II) and an operating system (Cosmos) for the Message-Driven Processor (MDP) and J-Machine. Measurements were taken on a simulator (pp. 1, 4, 101).
- **Context:** The J-Machine and MDP of Dally's group [14, 16] (p. 2). JOSS, Totty's earlier kernel, is the source of the BRAT and the object-migration protocol (p. 5). The first Optimist compiler [21] (p. 22). Related work: Smalltalk-80 and optimised Smalltalk (TS), Yokote and Tokoro's CONCURRENTSMALLTALK, and the actor languages Cantor and Acore (pp. 10–13).
- **Correctness:** Premise: "the routing time for a message sent from one end of even a large J-Machine to another is on the order of several microseconds. Operating system overhead on processing and dispatching that message of more than a few microseconds is not acceptable" (p. 2). Instruction counts are given as "rough estimates" (p. 102). They are cross-checked against runs on 4- and 16-node simulated J-Machines in MDPSim (pp. 108–109). The network-saturation limit is a first-order analytical model (p. 110).
- **Contributions:** Listed on p. 4: a redesign of CST; Optimist II (compiler and interpreter); Cosmos; CST runtime libraries; changes to MDPSim; "Modifications to the MDP architecture that make it more suitable for Concurrent Smalltalk." Measured results: a grain size of about 60 instructions, about 100–120 instructions per function call, and about 2 (internal memory) or about 4 (external DRAM) cycles per instruction (pp. 114, 127–128).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well structured, with message-format figures and per-routine instruction-count tables (Figs. 4-10 to 4-21, Tables 7-1 to 7-6). The scan is image-only, with no text layer. Appendix E (the compiler listing) was removed for space (p. 184).

# P15

## Reference
Steele, G. L., Jr., Gabriel, R. P. (1993). *The Evolution of Lisp*. HOPL-II (History of Programming Languages II), ACM, pp. 231–270. https://doi.org/10.1145/154766.155373 (other records: 10.1145/155360.155373; 10.1145/234286.1057818). Included under I2 (R0-017). Pages below are the printed page numbers (1–77) of the authors' manuscript saved as `papers/P15.pdf`, not the publisher's pages; see Notes.

## Deepest pass
2 (first pass of the whole paper: title, abstract, contents, introduction, section headings, section 5 scanned; second pass of every passage on Lisp machines and stock hardware: sections 2.5, 2.6, 2.9, 2.10.1–2.10.2, 2.11–2.12, pp. 10–35. Sections 3 and 4, on language features and Lisp as a language laboratory, were only searched for Lisp machine passages.)

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Historical account of a programming language (a HOPL paper), organised as "a series of slices through the subject matter" (p. 2): projects and people, technical themes, Lisp as a language laboratory, and why Lisp evolved as it did. It includes a history of the "ascension and decline of special purpose Lisp machines" (p. 1, abstract).
- **Context:** Picks up "where McCarthy's paper in the first HOPL conference left off" (p. 1, abstract; p. 2). Sources are mostly the authors' own participation, mailing lists and manuals; the reference list includes Lisp machine papers and manuals (Deutsch 1973, Greenblatt 1974, Moon 1984, Weinreb and Moon 1978/1981) (pp. 12–13).
- **Correctness:** The Lisp machine claims are narrative and qualitative, with no measurement reported; reasons are often hedged ("perhaps", "probably", "possibly") (pp. 15, 27, 28). The authors were participants: both in the Common Lisp Group (p. 21), and Gabriel a founder of Lucid, which became "the primary stock-hardware Lisp company" (pp. 30–31), i.e. a competitor of the Lisp machine companies (inferred). The manuscript read has unresolved citations shown as "[?]" (e.g. p. 13, p. 27).
- **Contributions:** A chronology of Lisp dialects and implementations from Lisp 1.5 to the ANSI and ISO standards; the technical evolution of selected features (NIL and T, iteration, macros, numerical facilities, notable failures); Lisp as a language laboratory; "some reflections on the forces that have driven the evolution of Lisp" (p. 1, abstract).
- **Clarity:** Clearly written and well organised; the authors warn the slice-by-slice organisation "inevitably leads to some redundancy" (p. 2). Lisp machine material is spread over several sections (2.5, 2.6, 2.9, 2.10, 2.11.2, 2.12).

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The abstract states in one place what the paper traces, examines and discusses (p. 1), and the introduction gives the section plan (p. 2). |
| Q2 | no | No communication mechanism is described; Flavors is named "a multiple inheritance, message-passing system" (p. 26) but its format, naming, ordering and busy-receiver behaviour are not described. |
| Q3 | no | The Lisp machines were built and sold (pp. 13, 26–28), but the paper's evidence is historical narrative; it reports no measurement taken from them (design or argument only, as far as the evidence goes). |
| Q4 | no | No measured claim is made: comparisons name a baseline in words (Dorado "faster than a KL-10 running single-user Interlisp", p. 14; Le Lisp on Vax 780's "about as well as Symbolics 3600's", p. 25) but give no values, version or configuration. |
| Q5 | no | Nothing is measured; no workload, hardware configuration or number of runs is reported. |
| Q6 | n/a | The abstract and the conclusions (section 5) make no quantitative claim, so the question cannot apply. |
| Q7 | no | Causes are only asserted, e.g. the Dolphin lost "primarily because it was a slow machine that ran the Interlisp virtual machine" (p. 24); the 3600 incremental collector's "relatively bad performance, possibly due to paging problems" (p. 27); none is isolated by a measurement. |
| Q8 | partly | Limits are mentioned in passing: the organisation "inevitably leads to some redundancy" (p. 2); "we do not want to claim that the other companies did not have strong significance" (p. 27). No section on limitations or on the authors' own role. |
| Q9 | yes | No author is listed as a designer or builder of the Lisp machines discussed (pp. 12–15, 26–28); but Gabriel co-founded Lucid, a stock-hardware Lisp company (p. 30), and both were in the Common Lisp Group (p. 21), so they were interested parties. |

# P45

## Reference
Edmund B. Nightingale, Orion Hodson, Ross McIlroy, Chris Hawblitzel, Galen Hunt (2009). *Helios: heterogeneous multiprocessing with satellite kernels*. Proceedings of the ACM SIGOPS 22nd Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP '09), Big Sky, Montana, pp. 221–234. https://doi.org/10.1145/1629575.1629597

## Deepest pass
3

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** design, implementation and evaluation of an operating system (a multikernel built from microkernels), measured on running hardware (p. 1–2, 9).
- **Context:** builds on Singularity and its channel message passing ("We built Helios by modifying the Singularity [13] operating system", p. 2; Fähndrich et al. [6], p. 3, 5). Places itself after Mach's network-transparent IPC (p. 12), after offload work on channel processors, Auspex, SPINE, AsyMOS and Piglet (p. 12), and next to the multikernels Hive, Cellular Disco and Corey and to Barrelfish ("complimentary efforts at managing heterogeneity", p. 12–13).
- **Correctness:** the main assumptions are stated. Programmable devices are assumed to provide "a timer, an interrupt controller, and the ability to catch an exception (i.e., trap)" (p. 2). The memory and PCI "network" between kernels is assumed "very robust compared to traditional LAN or WAN networks", so "traditional distributed systems protocols (e.g., TCP) are not required" (p. 3). Software isolation through type safety is assumed sufficient to protect processes that all run in ring 0 (p. 4, 6). The assumptions look plausible for the two platforms tested. The evaluation uses one XScale card and one two-domain NUMA machine (p. 9, 13).
- **Contributions:** satellite kernels that "export a single, uniform set of OS abstractions across CPUs of disparate architectures" (p. 1); remote message passing that "extends a standard microkernel message-passing abstraction to a satellite kernel infrastructure" (p. 1); affinity, a placement hint expressed on message-passing channels (p. 1–3); two-phase compilation from CIL (p. 2, 4). Results reported: "up to a 28% performance improvement by offloading tasks to the XScale I/O card" and "a 39% improvement in performance by automatically splitting the application among multiple NUMA domains" (p. 1).
- **Clarity:** clearly written, with explicit design goals (p. 2). Some numbers in the text do not match the figures (see Notes).

(6) **Porting effort**, lines of code and manifest changed (Fig. 4): TCP test harness 5 LOC changed; all others 0 LOC; 0–3 manifest lines (p. 9). | p. 9, 10, 11, 12 |
| Scaling | One machine with 2 NUMA domains × 2 cores = 4 cores (p. 9). **Scheduler microbenchmark**, 16 threads each calling threadyield 1 million times. One kernel across both domains (non-NUMA-aware, interleaved memory) about 24 s vs two kernels (8 threads each) about 7.6 s (read off); text: "68% faster", with a "greater than 2x improvement". Mean of 5, 90% CI (p. 11, Fig. 9). **Mail server**, 1 vs 2 kernels on the same 4 cores: +39% throughput (measured, p. 11). No result at any other core or kernel count. On kernel count: point-to-point connections "worked well for a small number of satellite kernels, but if in the future machines have a very large number of programmable devices or NUMA domains, an alternative network topology may be required" (p. 3). | p. 3, 9, 11 |
| Attributed causes | All are stated by the designers. (a) Fig. 5 shapes: "Since no copies are made during LMP, the time is constant"; "RMP on XScale is bound mainly by the time to program the ADMA controller" (p. 9). Inherent to the design (copy vs no copy) and to the implementation (ADMA); not isolated by a breakdown. (b) memcpy cost: "direct memory accesses across the PCI-E bus stall the initiating CPU" (p. 7). Implementation; measured (50% of CPU time). (c) Netstack offload: "the benefits of offloading tracked the amount of CPU freed up"; fewer interrupts because "the XScale CPU absorbed all of the interrupts generated by the NIC" (p. 10). Partly isolated: context-switch reduction is measured, CPU freed is not shown. (d) PostMark C1 70% gain: the card used the cacheline-size register as a low-water mark, so "the low-water mark was set too high and was not set uniformly" (p. 10). Implementation (device configuration); isolated by the reconfigured C2 run. (e) Scheduler: two kernels "scale around the serialization bottleneck", the single dispatcher lock. The >2x "is caused by the load-balancing algorithm, which issues expensive IPI interrupts and harms performance as the number of cores grows" (p. 11). Implementation, per the authors: "We are certain that the scheduler could be optimized to remove these serialization bottlenecks", though "there would undoubtedly be other bottlenecks as the number of cores grows" (p. 11). Not isolated. (f) Mail server: "every application component benefits from faster memory accesses on L2 cache misses", and processes "always use local memory when accessing kernel code and data structures" (p. 11). Not isolated. (g) Antivirus IPC: "other applications never have the opportunity to pollute the antivirus scanner's L1 or L2 cache" (p. 11). IPC measured; the cache-hit rate is not measured. (h) Fig. 11 only 10%: "domain 0 is already executing many other processes (including the networking stack and the indexer)" (p. 12). Not isolated. | p. 7, 9, 10, 11, 12 |
| Fate and reasons | Research prototype: "Helios is an experimental operating system with a limited number of applications" (p. 13). Future work stated: port to a GPU, i.e. Intel Larrabee, because current graphics cards "do not provide timers or interrupt controllers" and there is no CIL-to-DirectX compiler; let processes span NUMA domains; build satellite kernels from "a commodity operating system such as Windows" for a larger application base (p. 13). Later fate: not stated (2009 paper). | p. 13 |
| Concurrency defects | n/a (I1) | — |
| What shapes programs | n/a (I1) | — |
| Hardware–language trade-off | n/a (I1) | — |
| Model equivalence | n/a (I1) | — |
| Model mixing | n/a (I1) | — |
| Runtime limits | n/a (I1) | — |
| Many-core scaling | Cores: 4 (2 NUMA domains × 2 Opteron cores) plus, on the other platform, a 2-core host and one XScale card (p. 9). Shared memory or coherence: NUMA domains "are cache coherent with other NUMA domains", but Helios treats "NUMA as a shared-nothing multiprocessor", one kernel per domain (p. 1, 5); programmable devices "are not cache coherent" with the host (p. 5). Communication between kernels: remote message passing over shared FIFOs and memcpy (NUMA) or ADMA over PCI Express (XScale) (p. 3, 7). Within a kernel: shared memory and a single dispatcher lock (p. 4, 11). Result: see *Scaling*. Limits named: single-kernel lock contention ("by growing the number of kernels, lock contention is decreased", p. 11); IPIs as cores grow (p. 11); remote memory latency (p. 5, 9); all-to-all point-to-point topology for many kernels (p. 3); processes confined to one domain (p. 5, 13). | p. 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 |
| Adoption factors | n/a (I1) | — |
| Quality | See *Quality* table above. | p. 1–13 |
| Notes | See *Notes* below. | — |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: satellite kernel | A microkernel, "composed of a scheduler, a memory manager, a namespace manager, and code to coordinate communication between other kernels", run on each programmable device and each NUMA domain, exporting the same OS abstractions. | p. 1–2 |
| new: coordinator kernel | "The first satellite kernel to boot", which discovers devices, launches the other kernels and manages the namespace. | p. 2, 4, 6 |
| new: remote message passing (RMP) vs local message passing (LMP) | Both implemented "beneath the same inter-process communication abstraction". LMP is zero-copy within a kernel; RMP marshals and copies once between kernels' exchange heaps. | p. 3, 6–7 |
| new: shadow endpoint | Per remote channel, endpoints B0 and A0 shadow the remote endpoint's state, so the original channel interface is preserved. | p. 6 |
| new: affinity (positive, negative, self-reference, platform) | An integer on a message-passing channel in the process manifest. Positive: "prefers local message passing"; negative: "non-interference"; self-reference: copies run on different kernels; platform: preference for a kind of kernel. Hints used only at process start. | p. 3, 7–8 |
| new: centralised namespace | "The namespace is the only component of Helios that relies on centralized control." | p. 6 |
| new: NUMA as a shared-nothing multiprocessor | Each NUMA domain runs its own kernel and manages its own resources; processes may not span domains. | p. 1, 5 |
| new: software isolation (from Singularity) | Processes isolated by type and memory safety, all in one address space at ring 0, so no MMU is required. | p. 4, 6 |
| new: channel contract and exchange heap (from Singularity) | A Sing# contract defines a state machine of legal messages on a channel; message data lives in an exchange heap whose ownership is checked at compile time. | p. 5 |
| new: two-phase compilation | Ship CIL; compile to each available ISA after install. | p. 2, 4 |

## Notes
- **Source:** full text, the authors' camera-ready copy at https://www.sigops.org/s/conferences/sosp/2009/papers/nightingale-sosp09.pdf (PDF from `helios.dvi`, 5 Aug 2009, 14 pages), saved as `papers/P45.pdf`. The Microsoft Research copies returned HTTP 403. There are no printed page numbers, so pages are PDF pages; publisher pages 221–234 (Crossref), offset +220. All 14 pages read, figures inspected as images (third pass).
- **Criterion:** the full text confirms I1(c). "all other operating system services, including device drivers, execute as processes and use message passing for communication" (p. 3), and the kernels coordinate through remote message passing (p. 2). This is a kernel, not a library on a conventional kernel, so X2 does not apply. It runs on one machine, so X3 does not apply. No criterion change.
- **Text and figure mismatches** (reported, not resolved):
  - p. 9 says "once messages are greater than 32 KB in size, message passing over the PCI-E bus is more efficient than message passing between two NUMA domains". In Fig. 5 (p. 10) the RMP NUMA curve passes above RMP XScale between 4 KB and 8 KB (read off).
  - Fig. 11 (p. 12) goes from 20.7 s to 17.7 s, about 14.5% less time (computed). The text says "improved by only 10%".
  - Fig. 10 bars read off as about 60 and about 79 emails/s (about +32%). The text says 39%. The bar reading is imprecise.
- **Percentages:** "68% faster" (p. 11) and "28% faster" (p. 11) match a reduction in run time (about 24 to 7.6 s; about 248 to 178 s, read off), not a throughput ratio.
- **For SQ1 and SQ2:** the paper keeps system calls on purpose because "Local message-passing is slower than a system call" (p. 2). Remote messages between kernels are built on shared memory and DMA (p. 7). Message passing is exclusive between processes, not inside the kernel or inside a process.
- **Other related systems** cited, not yet in the review: Singularity [13], Fähndrich et al. EuroSys '06 [6], Hive [4], Barrelfish [28], Mach [1], Corey [2], K42 [30], Tornado [10] (p. 12–13). Possible snowballing leads.

# Agent contract

What every agent in `.claude/agents/` does, whatever its role. The agent's own file adds only its role.

## You receive
From the step skill that dispatched you:
- **Row:** the flow row you run (e.g. `3a`), defined in `ai/flow-sls.md` or `ai/flow-dsrm.md`.
- **Inputs:** the exact files you read. Paths are relative to `research/` unless they start with `ai/` or `artifact/`.
- **Outputs:** the exact files you write.

## You do
1. Read the row in its flow file, then every input file. Read nothing else from `research/`; your view of the research is the inputs.
2. For each output, copy its template from `ai/template/` (the table in `ai/template/README.md` maps output to template) and fill every `{placeholder}`.
3. Set the frontmatter: `id`, `row`, `by:` your agent name, `status: proposed`, `inputs:` the files you read.
4. Write only the output files. Every other file, and every `status`, belongs to me.

## Your output is done when
- Every output file exists and has every section of its template.
- No `{placeholder}` or `[ ]` is left. A field you cannot fill says why, in one line.
- Every claim about a paper carries its P ID and page, or the reference and page for papers not yet in the review.
- Every fact comes from a file or source you actually read in this run. A fact you cannot trace to one is left out and named in your report.

## You return
A short report to the skill:
- Each file written, with one line on what it holds.
- Open issues: fields you could not fill, sources you could not reach, decisions you found that are mine to make.
- Each decision that is mine as a choice: two to four concrete options, the exact edit each one makes to which file, and the one you recommend. The gate asks me with these (`ai/gate.md`).
