# P73

## Reference
Weinreb, D., Moon, D. (1981). *Lisp Machine Manual*, Fourth Edition, July 1981. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. Read in place of the record screened as R0-127: Weinreb, D., Moon, D. (1981). *The Lisp Machine manual*. ACM SIGART Bulletin no. 78 (October 1981), p. 10. https://doi.org/10.1145/1056737.1056738, which is a one-page notice of the manual, not the manual (see Notes).

## Deepest pass
2 (first pass over title page, preface, both tables of contents and chapter 1; second pass over the sections that serve the form: 10.5.2–10.5.3, 10.10, 14 (pp. 172–183), 20.1–20.6, 20.13–20.14, 21.5.1, 25 (pp. 428–435), 27.1 and 27.3–27.6. The other chapters of the 532-page manual were not read.)

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** System reference manual of an implemented system. It "describes both the language and the 'operating system' of the Lisp Machine" (P73, preface, PDF p. 3) and "is the reference manual for the Zetalisp language. This document is not a tutorial" (P73, p. 1).
- **Context:** The Lisp Machine is "a new computer system designed to provide a high performance and economical implementation of the Lisp language", a "personal computation system" (P73, p. 1); Zetalisp is "closely related to the Maclisp dialect" (P73, p. 1). Its object facility follows "the object oriented programming style used in the Smalltalk and Actor families of languages" (P73, p. 279). No reference list (manual).
- **Correctness:** A manual makes no claims to validate. Its stated assumptions: each user gets "your own processor and memory system for the duration of the session" (P73, p. 1), and "Usually only one process at a time is runnable" (P73, p. 430). Its few performance statements are rough estimates: "the actual speed may vary from these estimates by as much as a factor of two" (P73, p. 484). Parts are said to be in flux: the subprimitives chapter is "considered subject to change without notice" (P73, p. 172); the paging system section reads "[Someday this may discuss how it works.]" (P73, p. 183).
- **Contributions:** Complete documentation of Zetalisp (P73, preface) and of "the stabler parts" of the "operating-system-like parts of the system" (P73, preface); chapter 20 documents flavors, "a language facility to provide generic functions using the paradigm used in Smalltalk and the Actor families of languages, called 'object-oriented programming' or 'message passing'", "widely used by the system programs of the Lisp Machine" (P73, p. 2); chapter 27 documents the instruction set (P73, p. 2).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well indexed (concept, flavor, message, meter indexes; P73, p. ix). It excludes the window system and user interface (P73, preface).

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | Aim stated in one place: "the reference manual for the Zetalisp language" describing the language and the "operating system" (P73, preface; p. 1). |
| Q2 | partly | Format (message name as first argument, a keyword symbol, then arguments; P73, p. 284) and naming of the receiver (the object itself, called as a function; P73, p. 284) are given; delivery is a synchronous call returning values (P73, p. 284); ordering and the busy-receiver case are not stated in the sections read. |
| Q3 | yes | The manual documents a running system ("Everything on the Lisp Machine is written in Lisp, including all system programs", P73, p. 1), though it presents no evaluation. |
| Q4 | no | No measured claim; the run-time estimates (P73, pp. 484–486) name no baseline beyond a qualitative contrast with "a conventional computer such as the pdp-10" (P73, p. 484). |
| Q5 | no | Nothing is measured; the estimates give no workload, configuration or sample (P73, pp. 484–486). |
| Q6 | n/a | The manual has no abstract or conclusions to check against the body. |
| Q7 | no | Causes are asserted (e.g. "in many programs the execution time is determined by paging rather than by CPU run time", P73, p. 484) with no isolating measurement. |
| Q8 | partly | Limits mentioned in passing: implementation restrictions (P73, p. 311), call cost "somewhat higher than it should be" (P73, p. 485), parts "subject to change" (P73, p. 172). |
| Q9 | no | The manual does not evaluate a system; its authors document their own laboratory's system (P73, preface; title page). |

## Extracted fields
| Field | Value | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | Weinreb, D., Moon, D. (1981). *Lisp Machine Manual*, Fourth Edition, July 1981, MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory; P73; screened under I1 (R0-127). Version: scan of the printed manual (Bitsavers, `pdf/mit/cadr/chinual_4thEd_Jul81.pdf`, scanned 2004), 544 PDF pages: title, copyright and preface unnumbered (PDF pp. 1–3), front matter i–ix (PDF pp. 4–12), body pp. 1–532 (PDF pp. 13–544). Offset: printed p. n = PDF p. n + 12. Pages cited here are the printed numbers; the preface is cited by PDF page. The DOI record is a one-page SIGART Bulletin notice (no. 78, p. 10); only its Crossref abstract was read; content from it cites `abstract` | title page; PDF pp. 1–12; abstract |
| Paper type | implementation (a reference manual of an implemented system; the form has no manual type) | p. 1; preface |
| System | Lisp Machine and its language Zetalisp, "developed at the M.I.T. Artificial Intelligence Laboratory" (p. 1); "developed at M.I.T.'s Artificial Intelligence Laboratory over the past 8 years", "implemented with custom hardware and software" as a network of 32-bit personal computers (abstract). Status: running system, all system programs written in Lisp (p. 1); deployed commercially: not stated | p. 1; abstract |
| Levels with message semantics | Hardware: not stated. Microcode: partly, "A message is sent to an instance simply by calling it as a function, with the first argument being the message keyword. The microcode binds self to the object, binds the instance variables ... and calls a dtp-select-method associated with the flavor" (p. 309); other microcoded operations (car/cdr, memory reference, locking, I/O subprimitives) are not message sends (pp. 172, 178–181). Instruction set: no separate send instruction appears in the sections read; a send is an ordinary call of the instance object (inferred from pp. 284, 309, 471, 485). Operating system: partly, processes are flavor instances that receive messages (pp. 429, 435), but processes "communicate in arbitrary ways through shared Lisp objects" (p. 429). Language: partly, "no new features are added to Lisp for message sending; we simply define a convention on the way objects take arguments" (p. 285); flavors are "widely used by the system programs" (p. 2). Between machines: the network (abstract) and Chaosnet packets (p. 432) are not described as a message mechanism in the sections read: not stated. Within a machine: sequence breaks, "a kind of interrupt", reschedule processes (p. 429) and are not messages. Started message-based and later added other paths: not stated; entities predate flavors (p. 311) | pp. 2, 172, 178–181, 284, 285, 309, 429, 432, 435; abstract |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | Receivers are "functional" objects: instances of flavors (dtp-instance, "an 'active object'", p. 173), entities (p. 311), select-methods and closures (p. 144, 285), streams ("A stream is a message-receiving object", p. 338), processes (p. 429). State is held in instance variables, which method bodies read and set (p. 286). Others can read or write it: "Zetalisp makes no attempt to have the language automatically forbid constructs that circumvent the contract. This is intentional" (p. 282); the "outside-accessible instance variables" feature (p. 283); describe prints an instance's variables (pp. 287–288); memory subprimitives read and store any cell (pp. 179–181; applies to instances, inferred) | pp. 144, 173, 179–181, 282–288, 311, 338, 429 |
| Message mechanism | Synchronous: "The sender of the message is simply calling a function with some arguments, and getting some values back" (p. 284). Ordering, delivery guarantees, buffering, busy receiver: not stated. Dispatch: "The two data used to figure out which function to call are the type of the object, and the name of the message" (p. 284); the microcode calls the flavor's select-method, which maps the keyword to a method or to a combined method that "calls the appropriate methods in the right order" (p. 309); a select-method may have a "default handler" (p. 144); streams have a "stream default handler" (p. 338) | pp. 144, 284, 309, 311, 338 |

Locking: %store-conditional, "the basic locking primitive" (p. 178). Interrupt-like: sequence breaks (pp. 429, 432); inhibit-scheduling-flag (p. 430). I/O: %unibus-read/write, %xbus-read/write, %halt (p. 178). Memory: pointer and storage subprimitives (pp. 176–181); invisible pointers handled on every read and write (p. 174). Microcode: subprimitives "are normally hand-coded in microcode" and "take the place of machine language in other systems" (p. 172); miscellaneous instructions are hand-microcoded Lisp functions (p. 471). Reasons for unrestricted access: "the Lisp Machine is an interactive system, and so it is important to be able to examine and alter internal state interactively", and "there is no strong distinction between the 'system' programs and the 'user' programs" (p. 282) | pp. 172, 174, 176–181, 282, 429–432, 471 |
| Self-definition | "Everything on the Lisp Machine is written in Lisp, including all system programs; there is never any need to program in machine language" (p. 1). Outside Lisp: subprimitives and microcoded functions in microcode (pp. 144, 172); function entry services and instance dispatch in microcode (pp. 309, 478, 480). Users can convert some functions to microcode with the micro-compiler (p. 144). ## Reference

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Position or analytical argument with a retrospective of first-generation microkernels (Mach, Chorus) and a short design description of second-generation ones (Exokernel, L4). Magazine article; its numbers are mostly measurements reported from other papers ([6], [8], [16]), not a new evaluation (pp. 70, 73–75).
- **Context:** First-generation microkernels Amoeba, Choices, Ra, V, Chorus, L3 and Mach (p. 71). Mach's external pager [22] (p. 71) and interrupts as IPC messages [17] (p. 72). Measurements by Chen and Bershad [6] and Condict et al. [8] (p. 73). Second-generation Exokernel [9] and L4 [16]; non-microkernel alternatives Spin [2], Synthesis [20], and loadable modules in Solaris and Linux (pp. 74–75).
- **Correctness:** The central claim is that first-generation inefficiency came from "the basic architecture of these kernels", not from inherent IPC cost, because "the hardware-inherited costs of mode and address-space switching are only 3%–7% of the measured costs" (p. 74). The argument rests on the Figure 4 breakdown and on the faster L4 and Exokernel numbers (pp. 74–75). The detailed evidence is deferred to [16] ("A detailed discussion can be found in [16]", p. 74). The author states that "There is no real-life practical experience with second-generation microkernels" (pp. 76–77).
- **Contributions:** A diagnosis of why first-generation microkernels were "inefficient and inflexible" (p. 70): IPC cost (pp. 72–74) and "the policy inside the microkernel" (p. 74). Two evaluation criteria, conservative and progressive (p. 72), and a relative-RPC-overhead model (Fig. 3, p. 73). A description of L4's recursive address spaces (grant, map, demap, with mapping done by IPC) and of the user-level memory servers, pagers, drivers and Unix server built on them (pp. 75–76).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well structured, with figures and FAQ sidebars (pp. 72, 76). The measurement setups are only summarised and depend on cited papers.

# Quality assessment checklist

`n/a` is used only when the source was not read (abstract-only record) or the question cannot apply to the paper's kind, and always with the reason. `no` means the paper fails the question.

| ID | Question asked of each paper | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Does the paper state its aim or contribution explicitly (in the abstract or introduction)? yes: stated in one place as a goal or contribution list; partly: has to be inferred from several places; no: not stated. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q2 | Is the system's communication mechanism described in enough detail to reimplement it: message format, naming or addressing of the receiver, delivery and ordering guarantees, and what happens when the receiver is busy? yes: all four; partly: one to three; no: none. For papers with no system (I3 studies), the studied programs and their communication mechanisms count instead. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q3 | Does the evidence come from a working artefact? yes: silicon, FPGA, or a kernel or system that runs real programs; partly: simulator or emulator; no: design or argument only. For I3 studies: yes: defects taken from real bug trackers or commit histories; partly: from benchmark suites; no: from examples only. Analytical models count as no (design or argument). | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q4 | Is every performance or defect claim measured against a named baseline? yes: each claim names its baseline (system, version, configuration); partly: some claims do; no: none do, or no measured claim is made. A hypothetical baseline counts as partly. For I3 studies: yes if the counts are compared with another named study or population; partly if only some are. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q5 | Is the measurement setup reported: workloads or programs used and why they were chosen, hardware or simulator configuration, number of runs or sample size? yes: all three; partly: one or two; no: none, or nothing measured. For I3 studies: the sampling procedure (sources, search terms, screening) replaces the hardware or simulator configuration. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q6 | Does every quantitative claim in the abstract and conclusions have a table, figure or text passage in the body that reports it? yes: all; partly: some; no: none, or no data in the body. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q7 | Are causes attributed to results (e.g. "the slowdown comes from X") supported by a measurement that isolates that cause, such as an ablation or a breakdown? yes: every attributed cause; partly: some; no: none, or causes only asserted. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q8 | Does the paper discuss limitations or threats to validity? yes: a section or paragraph dedicated to them; partly: mentioned in passing; no: not discussed. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q9 | Is the evaluation independent of the system's designers? yes: no author is listed as a designer or builder of the evaluated system in the paper or its cited design papers; partly: some authors are; no: all authors are, or the paper does not evaluate a system. A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. Programs whose defects are reported as accesses to shared variables count as shared-memory programs even if the paper does not use that term. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

Version: publisher's typeset version (IEEE JSSC layout, printed pages 173–183), as uploaded to ResearchGate by Michael Konow on 1 June 2014 with a one-page ResearchGate cover sheet prepended. Pages cited below are the printed journal pages; PDF page = printed page − 171 (PDF p. 1 is the cover sheet). Dates on p. 173: "Manuscript received April 15, 2010 ... 2

- **Category:** Design and implementation description of a research prototype many-core processor chip, with silicon measurements (power, maximum frequency, two NAS benchmarks) (pp. 173, 179–180).

- **Correctness:** The motivating claim, that "the computational value gained through additional cores will at some point be exceeded by the protocol overhead needed to maintain cache coherency among the cores" (p. 173), is asserted without measurement or citation. - **Contributions:** A 48-core, 24-tile 6×4 2D-mesh chip with no hardware cache coherency; per-tile 16 KB Message Passing Buffer (MPB, "on-die shared memory"); a new cache-line memory type (MPMT) and a new instruction (INVDMB) for software-managed coherency; a 4-stage virtual cut-through router; 4 DDR3 controllers; 8 voltage and 28 frequency islands for DVFS (pp. 173–178).
- **Clarity:** Clearly organised circuits paper; the message-passing protocol is given in one short section (pp. 176–177) and much of its semantics (naming, synchronisation, busy receivers) is left to the cited programmer's-view paper [11]. ## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| new: Message Passing Buffer (MPB) | Per-tile "16 KB of on-die shared memory" in the network interface, "used to increase performance of a message passing programming model whereby cores communicate through local shared memory". | 174 |
| new: Message Passing Memory Type (MPMT) | A cache-line status bit "used to mark the content of the cache line as Message Passing Memory Type"; set from page-table information in the TLB by the OS; addresses "non-coherent shared memory". | 174, 177 |
| new: INVDMB instruction | New IA-32 instruction that "invalidates all MPMT cache lines in a single clock cycle", exposing "the programmer to direct control of cache management while in a message passing environment". | 174 |
| new: software-maintained coherency | "Shared memory coherency is maintained through software in an effort to eliminate the communication and hardware overhead required for a memory coherent 2D-mesh." | 173, 176 |
| new: one-sided put and get | Message-passing protocol "based on one-sided 'put and get' primitives", inspired by SHMEM, MPI and OpenMP. | 176 |
| new: message class (network) | Router packets are split into request and response "message classes"; two reserved virtual channels per class ensure deadlock-free routing. | 175–176 |
| new: voltage and frequency islands (DVFS) | 8 voltage islands and 28 frequency islands allow "independent DVFS of cores and mesh"; voltage commands are sent over the mesh to the VRC. | 173, 177–178 |

## Notes
- **Source read:** full text, publisher's typeset version (IEEE JSSC vol. 46, no. 1, pp. 173–183), ResearchGate upload by Michael Konow (1 June 2014) with a cover sheet, obtained from the mirror https://search.iczhiku.com/paper/WjR2NH8uksdALAbZ.pdf and saved as `papers/P21.pdf` (12 PDF pages). Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar report the paper as closed access; the ResearchGate direct link returned 403; a Semantic Scholar PDF link found by search (pdfs.semanticscholar.org/a768/...) is an unrelated slide deck. Figures were read from rendered page images.
- **Criterion (for gate 3c):** I1 holds only in a qualified way. The paper names "message passing" throughout (title, p. 173) and adds hardware for it, the MPB, MPMT and INVDMB (pp. 174, 176–177), which fits I1(b) "a hardware or microcode mechanism". But the paper itself calls the protocol "a novel message passing based software protocol used to maintain data consistency in shared memory" (p. 173), and data moves by loads and stores into "on-die shared memory" (p. 174); there is no send instruction (p. 174). X2 does not apply as worded, because the instruction set and hardware do have message-specific mechanisms (MPB, MPMT, INVDMB, pp. 174, 177). The paper also plausibly meets I4 for the many-core scaling SQs served by the *Many-core scaling* field (SQ13, SQ14) and for *Model equivalence* (SQ10), since it builds message passing on non-coherent shared memory and argues against hardware coherency at scale (pp. 173, 176) (inferred; I did not read the SQ files). Verdict change, if any, is yours.
- **Hardware messages beyond core-to-core:** voltage change commands are messages to the VRC, a mesh agent "addressable by all cores" (p. 178); every on-die agent communicates by packets (p. 176). This is relevant to SQ1 at the hardware level even though the core-to-core path is shared-memory based.
- **Scope of results:** NAS benchmarks were run only up to 32 (LU) and 36 (BT) cores, not 48, at 533 MHz (p. 179); the paper says the benchmarks "were successfully ported to the processor architecture with minimal effort" (p. 179) without stating what the port involved.
- **Small inconsistencies:** the abstract gives nominal 1.1 V for 1 GHz cores / 2 GHz mesh (p. 173), while the 125 W typical point is at 1.14 V (pp. 180–181); core Fmax starts at 300 MHz at 730 mV (p. 179) while the conclusion and Fig. 14 give 0.7 V and 125 MHz as an operating point (pp. 180–181). The ResearchGate cover gives February 2011; the journal header gives January 2011 (p. 173).
- The programmer's model (synchronisation, receiver naming, what happens when a receiver is not ready) is deferred to Mattson et al. [11], "The Intel 48-core single-chip cloud computer (SCC) processor: Programmer's view" (p. 181); candidate for snowballing.

# Agent contract

What every agent in `.claude/agents/` does, whatever its role. The agent's own file adds only its role.

## You receive
From the step skill that dispatched you:
- **Row:** the flow row you run (e.g. `3a`), defined in `ai/flow-sls.md` or `ai/flow-dsrm.md`.
- **Inputs:** the exact files you read. Paths are relative to `research/` unless they start with `ai/` or `artifact/`.
- **Outputs:** the exact files you write.

1. Read the row in its flow file, then every input file. Read nothing else from `research/`; your view of the research is the inputs.
2. For each output, copy its template from `ai/template/` (the table in `ai/template/README.md` maps output to template) and fill every `{placeholder}`.
3. Set the frontmatter: `id`, `row`, `by:` your agent name, `status: proposed`, `inputs:` the files you read.
4. Write only the output files. Every other file, and every `status`, belongs to me.

## Your output is done when
- Every output file exists and has every section of its template.
- No `{placeholder}` or `[ ]` is left. A field you cannot fill says why, in one line.
- Every claim about a paper carries its P ID and page, or the reference and page for papers not yet in the review.

## You return
A short report to the skill:
- Each file written, with one line on what it holds.
- Open issues: fields you could not fill, sources you could not reach, decisions you found that are mine to make.
- Each decision that is mine as a choice: two to four concrete options, the exact edit each one makes to which file, and the one you recommend. The gate asks me with these (`ai/gate.md`).

# Data extraction form

Fields filled for every included paper (`sls/3-reading/P*.md`). Every SQ is served by at least one field.

- **Applies to:** a field applies to papers included under the criteria in its *Applies to* column; for I4, only the fields serving the SQs the paper answers. A field that does not apply is written `n/a (I3)` (the paper's criterion). `not stated` means the field applies but the paper is silent.
- **Values:** every number in *Cost of message primitives*, *Performance results* and *Scaling* is tagged `measured`, `simulated`, `design figure`, `analytical` or `read off` (estimated from a plot).

| Field | What to record | Serves | Applies to |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reference | Authors, year, title, venue, pages; P ID; criteria that included it (I1–I4). Pages cited in the record are those printed on `papers/P*.pdf` (else its PDF page); say which version it is (publisher, preprint, manuscript, reprint), give the publisher's page range and any offset. Content taken from an abstract only cites `abstract` | SQ1–SQ19 | all |
| Paper type | One or more of: design, implementation, evaluation, retrospective, empirical defect study, position or analytical argument; with page | SQ1–SQ19 | all |
| System | Name of each system the paper describes or evaluates, year built, built by whom; status: design only / simulated / FPGA / silicon / running kernel / deployed commercially; with page | SQ1, SQ5, SQ6 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Levels with message semantics | For each level (hardware, microcode, instruction set, kernel, runtime or virtual machine, language): is a message send the primitive at that level, yes / partly / no / not stated (yes means every state change at that level is caused by a message send, with no other path; partly means a message is a primitive at that level but other paths exist, naming which operations are message-only); for kernels and multicomputers, answered separately between cores or nodes and within a core (traps, interrupts, system calls); whether the system started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages; with page | SQ1 | I1, I2 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | What receives messages (object, actor, process, core, domain, other); whether its state can be read or written by anything other than itself, and how; with page | SQ1, SQ2, SQ7 | I1, I2, I3 |
| Message mechanism | Synchronous or asynchronous; how the receiver is named; ordering and delivery guarantees; buffering; what happens when the receiver is busy; how the receiver selects behaviour (dispatch); with page | SQ1, SQ3 | I1, I2, I3 |
| Non-message primitives | Every mechanism the paper states the system keeps that is not a message send: shared or global memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers, direct memory access, I/O ports, other; at which level; the reason the paper gives for keeping each; with page | SQ2 | I1, I2 |
| Self-definition | Which levels are implemented in the system's own objects and messages, and which in a lower language, microcode or hardware outside the model; whether a running program can inspect or change those levels; what remains outside the system as a base (primitives, a level that is not reflected) and what that base costs or prevents; with page | SQ2, SQ16 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Interposition | Whether a third component can be placed between sender and receiver, or between a program and conventional hardware or kernel (virtual memory, virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management), without changing either (yes / no / not stated); the mechanism; at which level; its cost; with page | SQ3, SQ17 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Operating system functions | For each of protection, scheduling, resource allocation (memory, devices), naming, failure handling: how the system provides it, and whether a central component (a single kernel, master core, global table or lock) is involved, yes / no / not stated (replicated parts that must agree count as coordination); what a decentralised version costs or gives up; with page | SQ4, SQ15 | I1, I4 |
| Cost of message primitives | Measured latency or cycles of one send, one dispatch, one context or actor switch; on what hardware or simulator; with page | SQ5 | I1, I2 |
| Performance results | Each result as: metric, workload, system, baseline (name, version, configuration), value for each, unit; with page | SQ5 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Scaling | Number of cores or nodes measured, metric, result at each count, baseline; with page | SQ5 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Attributed causes | Each cause the authors give for a performance result, quoted or close-paraphrased; who states it (designers or third party); whether it is inherent to the design or due to its implementation; whether a measurement isolates it; with page | SQ5, SQ6, SQ18 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Fate and reasons | What happened to the system (commercial product, research only, abandoned, superseded, still in use) and every reason the paper gives for it; who states it (designers or third party); with page | SQ6 | I1, I2, I4 |

# Quality assessment checklist

`n/a` is used only when the source was not read (abstract-only record) or the question cannot apply to the paper's kind, and always with the reason. `no` means the paper fails the question.

| ID | Question asked of each paper | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Does the paper state its aim or contribution explicitly (in the abstract or introduction)? yes: stated in one place as a goal or contribution list; partly: has to be inferred from several places; no: not stated. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q2 | Is the system's communication mechanism described in enough detail to reimplement it: message format, naming or addressing of the receiver, delivery and ordering guarantees, and what happens when the receiver is busy? yes: all four; partly: one to three; no: none. For papers with no system (I3 studies), the studied programs and their communication mechanisms count instead. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q3 | Does the evidence come from a working artefact? yes: silicon, FPGA, or a kernel or system that runs real programs; partly: simulator or emulator; no: design or argument only. For I3 studies: yes: defects taken from real bug trackers or commit histories; partly: from benchmark suites; no: from examples only. Analytical models count as no (design or argument). | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q4 | Is every performance or defect claim measured against a named baseline? yes: each claim names its baseline (system, version, configuration); partly: some claims do; no: none do, or no measured claim is made. A hypothetical baseline counts as partly. For I3 studies: yes if the counts are compared with another named study or population; partly if only some are. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q5 | Is the measurement setup reported: workloads or programs used and why they were chosen, hardware or simulator configuration, number of runs or sample size? yes: all three; partly: one or two; no: none, or nothing measured. For I3 studies: the sampling procedure (sources, search terms, screening) replaces the hardware or simulator configuration. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q6 | Does every quantitative claim in the abstract and conclusions have a table, figure or text passage in the body that reports it? yes: all; partly: some; no: none, or no data in the body. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q7 | Are causes attributed to results (e.g. "the slowdown comes from X") supported by a measurement that isolates that cause, such as an ablation or a breakdown? yes: every attributed cause; partly: some; no: none, or causes only asserted. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q8 | Does the paper discuss limitations or threats to validity? yes: a section or paragraph dedicated to them; partly: mentioned in passing; no: not discussed. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q9 | Is the evaluation independent of the system's designers? yes: no author is listed as a designer or builder of the evaluated system in the paper or its cited design papers; partly: some authors are; no: all authors are, or the paper does not evaluate a system. For I3 studies: yes if no author developed the studied programs. | yes / partly / no / n/a |

# Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. Programs whose defects are reported as accesses to shared variables count as shared-memory programs even if the paper does not use that term. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

# Protocol change: reading-pilot

Saved as `sls/1-protocol/changes/2026-10-06-reading-pilot.md`.

## What changed
- `extraction-form.md`:
  - New *Applies to* column (I1–I4 per field); a field outside the paper's criteria is `n/a (I3)`, and `not stated` means the field applies but the paper is silent.
  - Values in *Cost of message primitives*, *Performance results* and *Scaling* are tagged measured / simulated / design figure / analytical / read off.
  - *Reference*: pages are those printed on `papers/P*.pdf` (else its PDF page), with the version (publisher, preprint, manuscript, reprint), the publisher's page range and any offset; abstract-only content cites `abstract`. Criteria I1–I4.
  - *Paper type*: one or more types, plus "position or analytical argument".
  - *Levels with message semantics*: adds `partly` (a message is a primitive at the level but other paths exist, naming the message-only operations), and for kernels and multicomputers separate answers between cores or nodes and within a core.
- `quality.md`:
  - Scale adds `n/a`, only for a source not read or a question that cannot apply, with the reason.
  - Q3: analytical models count as no.
  - Q4: a hypothetical baseline counts as partly. For I3, yes if the counts are compared with another named study.
  - Q5: for I3, the sampling procedure replaces the hardware setup.
  - Q9: for I3, yes if no author developed the studied programs.
- `criteria.md`, I3: adds "Programs whose defects are reported as accesses to shared variables count as shared-memory programs even if the paper does not use that term."

## Why
The reading pilot (P5, P8, P9, P10, P12, P13, P22, P33) showed the form and the checklist did not fit most papers:
- most fields did not apply to bug studies or analytical papers;
- readers cited five different kinds of page numbers;
- the strict yes/no on levels hid the differences the review is about;
- abstract-only and I3 records could only answer "no" to quality questions that could not apply.

Lu et al. (2008) met I3 only by inference, because it speaks of shared variables, not shared memory.

## Papers affected
The pilot records P5, P8, P9, P10, P12, P13, P22 and P33 were written under the previous form and are not re-read. Their fields are mapped to the new form at synthesis (4a). P5 meets I3 as changed. Every later record uses the new form.

# Quality assessment checklist

`n/a` is used only when the source was not read (abstract-only record) or the question cannot apply to the paper's kind, and always with the reason. `no` means the paper fails the question.

| ID | Question asked of each paper | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Does the paper state its aim or contribution explicitly (in the abstract or introduction)? yes: stated in one place as a goal or contribution list; partly: has to be inferred from several places; no: not stated. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q2 | Is the system's communication mechanism described in enough detail to reimplement it: message format, naming or addressing of the receiver, delivery and ordering guarantees, and what happens when the receiver is busy? yes: all four; partly: one to three; no: none. For papers with no system (I3 studies), the studied programs and their communication mechanisms count instead. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q3 | Does the evidence come from a working artefact? yes: silicon, FPGA, or a kernel or system that runs real programs; partly: simulator or emulator; no: design or argument only. For I3 studies: yes: defects taken from real bug trackers or commit histories; partly: from benchmark suites; no: from examples only. Analytical models count as no (design or argument). | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q4 | Is every performance or defect claim measured against a named baseline? yes: each claim names its baseline (system, version, configuration); partly: some claims do; no: none do, or no measured claim is made. A hypothetical baseline counts as partly. For I3 studies: yes if the counts are compared with another named study or population; partly if only some are. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q5 | Is the measurement setup reported: workloads or programs used and why they were chosen, hardware or simulator configuration, number of runs or sample size? yes: all three; partly: one or two; no: none, or nothing measured. For I3 studies: the sampling procedure (sources, search terms, screening) replaces the hardware or simulator configuration. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q6 | Does every quantitative claim in the abstract and conclusions have a table, figure or text passage in the body that reports it? yes: all; partly: some; no: none, or no data in the body. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q7 | Are causes attributed to results (e.g. "the slowdown comes from X") supported by a measurement that isolates that cause, such as an ablation or a breakdown? yes: every attributed cause; partly: some; no: none, or causes only asserted. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q8 | Does the paper discuss limitations or threats to validity? yes: a section or paragraph dedicated to them; partly: mentioned in passing; no: not discussed. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q9 | Is the evaluation independent of the system's designers? yes: no author is listed as a designer or builder of the evaluated system in the paper or its cited design papers; partly: some authors are; no: all authors are, or the paper does not evaluate a system. For I3 studies: yes if no author developed the studied programs. | yes / partly / no / n/a |

# Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. Programs whose defects are reported as accesses to shared variables count as shared-memory programs even if the paper does not use that term. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

# P46

## Reference
Jochen Liedtke (1996). *Toward real microkernels*. Communications of the ACM 39(9), 70–77. https://doi.org/10.1145/234215.234473. P46, round-file row R0-063, screened include under I1. Version read: publisher's typeset PDF (ACM), 8 pages. Pages cited below are the printed CACM pages 70–77 (PDF page = printed page − 69).

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Position or analytical argument with a retrospective of first-generation microkernels (Mach, Chorus) and a short design description of second-generation ones (Exokernel, L4). Magazine article; its numbers are mostly measurements reported from other papers ([6], [8], [16]), not a new evaluation (pp. 70, 73–75).
- **Context:** First-generation microkernels Amoeba, Choices, Ra, V, Chorus, L3 and Mach (p. 71). Mach's external pager [22] (p. 71) and interrupts as IPC messages [17] (p. 72). Measurements by Chen and Bershad [6] and Condict et al. [8] (p. 73). Second-generation Exokernel [9] and L4 [16]; non-microkernel alternatives Spin [2], Synthesis [20], and loadable modules in Solaris and Linux (pp. 74–75).
- **Correctness:** The central claim is that first-generation inefficiency came from "the basic architecture of these kernels", not from inherent IPC cost, because "the hardware-inherited costs of mode and address-space switching are only 3%–7% of the measured costs" (p. 74). The argument rests on the Figure 4 breakdown and on the faster L4 and Exokernel numbers (pp. 74–75). The detailed evidence is deferred to [16] ("A detailed discussion can be found in [16]", p. 74). The author states that "There is no real-life practical experience with second-generation microkernels" (pp. 76–77).
- **Contributions:** A diagnosis of why first-generation microkernels were "inefficient and inflexible" (p. 70): IPC cost (pp. 72–74) and "the policy inside the microkernel" (p. 74). Two evaluation criteria, conservative and progressive (p. 72), and a relative-RPC-overhead model (Fig. 3, p. 73). A description of L4's recursive address spaces (grant, map, demap, with mapping done by IPC) and of the user-level memory servers, pagers, drivers and Unix server built on them (pp. 75–76).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well structured, with figures and FAQ sidebars (pp. 72, 76). The measurement setups are only summarised and depend on cited papers.

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | partly | No explicit goal or contribution list. The aim is inferred from the subtitle and the opening paragraph ("Today, we observe radically new approaches…", p. 70) and the conclusion (p. 77). |
| Q2 | partly | Some message content (8- and 512-byte arguments, p. 75; a "map message" naming a virtual address, p. 75) and the receiver learning the sender (`wait for (msg, sender)`, p. 72) are given. Receiver addressing, ordering and delivery guarantees, and busy-receiver behaviour are not stated. |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| microkernel (new) | "minimizing the kernel and implementing servers outside the kernel. Ideally, the kernel implements only address spaces, interprocess communication (IPC), and basic scheduling." | p. 70 |
| first-generation vs second-generation microkernels (new) | The first generation "evolved step by step from monolithic kernels" and was "inefficient and inflexible". The second generation is designed "from scratch", with "a minimal and clean new architecture". | pp. 70, 74 |
| external pager (new) | "the kernel manages physical and virtual memory but forwards page faults to specific user-level tasks"; Mach's external pager was "the first conceptual breakthrough toward real microkernels". | p. 71 |
| interrupts as IPC messages (new) | "The kernel captures the interrupt but does not handle it, instead generating a message for the user-level process currently associated with the interrupt." | p. 72 |
| user-level device drivers (new) | Drivers run in user mode, are "encapsulated in address spaces", and can be "replaced, removed, or added dynamically". | p. 72 |
| conservative and progressive criteria (new) | Conservative: "Applications must not be degraded by the microkernel". Progressive: microkernels "must efficiently support new types of applications" that monolithic kernels cannot. | pp. 72–73 |
| RPC granularity / relative RPC overhead (new) | Overhead against "an ideal system where RPC is free", as a function of user-level cycles between RPCs. "Object-orientation and distribution will cause increased cross-address-space interaction", so "RPC granularity will become finer". | p. 73 |
| reintegration into the kernel (new) | Chorus "supervisor actors" and Mach "kernel-loaded tasks" "run in kernel mode, can freely access kernel space, and can freely interact with each other". This "weakens the microkernel approach". | p. 73 |
| policy inside the microkernel / mechanism, not policy (new) | "the weakness is the policy inside the microkernel". L4 "provides a pure mechanism interface", so "the kernel confines itself to mechanisms. Policies are left completely to user-level servers". | pp. 74–76 |
| processor-dependent microkernel (new) | "microkernels are inherently not portable, although they improve the portability of a whole system". The 486 and the Pentium need "different algorithms and data structures". | p. 74 |
| recursive address spaces: grant, map, demap (new) | Address spaces are built outside the kernel on top of an initial space holding physical memory. Grant and map require consent and are done by IPC; demap removes a page from all spaces that got it from the demapper. | p. 75 |
| protected control transfer (Exokernel) (new) | The "basic communication primitive" of Exokernel; it "crosses address spaces but does not transfer arguments". | p. 74 |
| trusted computing base (new) | "the set of all components whose correct functionality is a precondition for security"; in a microkernel system, hardware, microkernel, disk driver and perhaps a basic file system. | p. 71 |

- **Source read:** the ACM publisher PDF of CACM 39(9):70–77 (8 pages, printed pages 70–77), saved as `research/papers/P46.pdf`. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar list it as bronze open access at https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/234215.234473, but that URL returned HTTP 403 to `curl` on 2026-10-07. The file was taken from the Internet Archive capture of that URL dated 2020-05-31: http://web.archive.org/web/20200531132612id_/https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/234215.234473?download=true. Its first-page footer reads "September 1996/Vol. 39, No. 9 COMMUNICATIONS OF THE ACM", page 70. A 14-page course copy found at cs.fsu.edu is a different paper with a broken font encoding (probably Liedtke's SOSP 1995 paper); it was not used.
- **Page numbers:** printed CACM pages; PDF page = printed page − 69. Figures 2–4 (pp. 73–74) were read from the rendered page images. The Fig. 2 values are printed in the figure; the Fig. 3 values marked (read off) are estimated from the curves.
- **Criterion:** the full text confirms I1(c): IPC is the stated means of communication between the kernel and user-level services, interrupts, pagers and the Unix server (pp. 70, 72, 75–76). X5 does not apply: this is an 8-page ACM magazine article. X9: the title and subtitle do not present it as a survey, and the paper states its own reasons for the first generation's failure (pp. 73–74, 77). It also has content bearing on SQ4/SQ15 (OS functions, p. 75–76), SQ6 (fate, p. 73) and SQ17 (stacked pagers and memory servers, p. 76), so I4 may also apply. I did not read the SQ files, so I cannot say which SQ8–SQ19 it answers. Fields with *Applies to* outside I1 are therefore written `n/a (I1)`.
- **Possible X8:** the L4 numbers (5 µs / 18 µs vs Mach 115 µs / 172 µs, p. 75), the Fig. 4 breakdown (p. 74) and the grant/map/demap concept (p. 75) are taken from Liedtke's "On µ-kernel construction", SOSP 1995 ([16], p. 77), which is longer. If [16] is or becomes an included paper, X8 applies. This paper would then be kept only for what it adds: the first-generation retrospective, the Chen–Bershad and Condict measurements, the conservative and progressive criteria, Fig. 3, and the fate of Chorus and Mach.
- **Secondhand evidence:** most measurements are reported from cited papers ([6], [8], [9], [16]); the setups are not given in this paper. Who measured the 115 µs Mach IPC figure (pp. 72, 74) is not stated.
- **SQ5 / SQ18:** the paper's methodological claim is quoted for synthesis: "Naive, uninterpreted measurements are sometimes misleading. Although early microkernel measurements suggested reducing the frequency of user-to-user IPC, the real problem was the structure and implementation of the kernels" (p. 77).
- **Deepest pass:** pass 2. The whole text, sidebars and figures were read in detail for extraction. Assumptions were not re-derived, and cited sources ([16]) were not checked (no pass 3).

F E A T U R E

Can We Make
Operating Systems
Reliable and Secure?
Andrew S. Tanenbaum, Jorrit N. Herder, and Herbert Bos
Vrije Universiteit, Amsterdam

Microkernels—long discarded as unacceptable because of their lower performance
compared with monolithic kernels—might be making a comeback in operating systems
due to their potentially higher reliability, which many researchers now regard as more
important than performance.

W

hen was the last time your TV set crashed
or implored you to download some emergency software update from the Web? After
all, unless it is an ancient set, it is just a computer with a CPU, a big monitor, some analog electronics for decoding radio signals, a couple of
peculiar I/O devices—a remote control, a built-in VCR
or DVD drive—and a boatload of software in ROM.
This rhetorical question points out a nasty little secret
that we in the computer industry do not like to discuss:
Why are TV sets, DVD recorders, MP3 players, cell
phones, and other software-laden electronic devices reliable and secure but computers are not? Of course there
are many “reasons”—computers are flexible, users can
change the software, the IT industry is immature, and
so on—but as we move to an era in which the vast
majority of computer users are nontechnical people,
increasingly these seem like lame excuses to them.
What consumers expect from a computer is what they
expect from a TV set: You buy it, you plug it in, and it
works perfectly for the next 10 years. As IT professionals, we need to take up this challenge and make computers as reliable and secure as TV sets.
The worst offender when it comes to reliability and
security is the operating system. Although application
programs contain many flaws, if the operating system
were bug free, bugs in application programs could do
only limited damage, so we will focus here on operating systems.

44

Computer

However, before getting into the details, a few words
about the relationship between reliability and security
are in order. Problems with each of these domains often
have the same root cause: bugs in the software. A buffer
overrun error can cause a system crash (reliability problem), but it can also allow a cleverly written virus or
worm to take over the computer (security problem).
Although we focus primarily on reliability, improving
reliability can also improve security.

WHY ARE SYSTEMS UNRELIABLE?
Current operating systems have two characteristics
that make them unreliable and insecure: They are huge
and they have very poor fault isolation. The Linux kernel has more than 2.5 million lines of code; the Windows
XP kernel is more than twice as large.
One study of software reliability showed that code
contains between six and 16 bugs per 1,000 lines of executable code,1 while another study put the fault density
at two to 75 bugs per 1,000 lines of executable code,2
depending on module size. Using a conservative estimate
of six bugs per 1,000 lines of code, the Linux kernel
probably has something like 15,000 bugs; Windows XP
has at least double that.
To make matters worse, typically, about 70 percent
of the operating system consists of device drivers, which
have error rates three to seven times higher than ordinary code,3 so the bug counts cited above are probably

Helios: Heterogeneous Multiprocessing with Satellite Kernels †  Edmund B. Nightingale  Orion Hodson  Ross McIlroy  Microsoft Research  Microsoft Research  University of Glasgow, UK  Chris Hawblitzel  Galen Hunt  Microsoft Research  Microsoft Research  ABSTRACT  1. INTRODUCTION  Helios is an operating system designed to simplify the task of writing, deploying, and tuning applications for heterogeneous platforms. Helios introduces satellite kernels, which export a single, uniform set of OS abstractions across CPUs of disparate architectures and performance characteristics. Access to I/O services such as file systems are made transparent via remote message passing, which extends a standard microkernel message-passing abstraction to a satellite kernel infrastructure. Helios retargets applications to available ISAs by compiling from an intermediate language. To simplify deploying and tuning application performance, Helios exposes an affinity metric to developers. Affinity provides a hint to the operating system about whether a process would benefit from executing on the same platform as a service it depends upon. We developed satellite kernels for an XScale programmable I/O card and for cache-coherent NUMA architectures. We offloaded several applications and operating system components, often by changing only a single line of metadata. We show up to a 28% performance improvement by offloading tasks to the XScale I/O card. On a mail-server benchmark, we show a 39% improvement in performance by automatically splitting the application among multiple NUMA domains.  Operating systems are designed for homogeneous hardware architectures. Within a machine, CPUs are treated as interchangeable parts. Each CPU is assumed to provide equivalent functionality, instruction throughput, and cache-coherent access to memory. At most, an operating system must contend with a cache-coherent non-uniform memory architecture (NUMA), which results in varying access times to different portions of main memory. However, computing environments are no longer homogeneous. Programmable devices, such as GPUs and NICs, fragment the traditional model of computing by introducing “islands of computation” where developers can run arbitrary code to take advantage of device-specific features. For example, GPUs often provide highperformance vector processing, while a programmable NIC provides the opportunity to compute “close to the source” without wasting time communicating over a bus to a general purpose CPU. These devices are not cache-coherent with respect to general purpose CPUs, are programmed with unique instruction sets, and often have dramatically different performance characteristics. Operating systems effectively ignore programmable devices by treating them no differently than traditional, non-programmable I/O devices. Therefore device drivers are the only available method of communicating with a programmable device. Unfortunately, the device driver interface was designed for pushing bits back and forth over a bus, rather than acting as an interface through which applications coordinate and execute. As a result, there often exists little or no support on a programmable device for once straightforward tasks such as accessing other I/O devices (e.g., writing to disk), debugging, or getting user input. A secondary problem is that drivers, which execute in a privileged space within the kernel, become ever more complicated as they take on new tasks such as executing application frameworks. For example, the NVIDIA graphics driver, which supports the CUDA runtime for programming GPUs, contains an entire JIT compiler. Helios is an operating system designed to simplify the task of writing, deploying, and tuning applications for heterogeneous platforms. Helios introduces satellite kernels, which export a single, uniform set of OS abstractions across CPUs of disparate architectures and performance characteristics. Satellite kernels allow developers to write applications ag
ainst familiar operating system APIs and abstractions. In addition, Helios extends satellite kernels to NUMA architectures, treating NUMA as a shared-nothing multiprocessor. Each NUMA domain, which consists of a set of CPUs and co-located memory, runs its own satellite kernel and independently manages its resources. By replicating kernel code and by making performance boundaries between NUMA domains explicit, Helios removes the kernel as a bottleneck to scaling up performance in large multiprocessor systems.
