=== PAGE 1
To appear: "Proceedings of the 20th International Symposium on Computer Architecture," May 1993.

The J-Machine Multicomputer: An Architectural Evaluation
Michael D. Noakes, Deborah A. Wallach, and William J. Dally
Artiﬁcial Intelligence Laboratory and Laboratory for Computer Science
Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Cambridge, Massachusetts 02139
noakes@ai.mit.edu, kerr@ai.mit.edu, billd@ai.mit.edu
Abstract
The MIT J-Machine multicomputer has been constructed to study the role of a set of primitive mechanisms
in providing efﬁcient support for parallel computing. Each
J-Machine node consists of an integrated multicomputer
component, the Message-Driven Processor (MDP), and 1
MByte of DRAM. The MDP provides mechanisms to support efﬁcient communication, synchronization, and naming. A 512 node J-Machine is operational and is due to
be expanded to 1024 nodes in March 1993. In this paper we discuss the design of the J-Machine and evaluate
the effectiveness of the mechanisms incorporated into the
MDP. We measure the performance of the communication
and synchronization mechanisms directly and investigate
the behavior of four complete applications.

1

Introduction

Over the past 40 years, sequential von Neumann processors have evolved a set of mechanisms appropriate for supporting most sequential programming models. It is clear,
however, from efforts to build concurrent machines by
connecting many sequential processors, that these highlyevolved sequential mechanisms are not adequate to support
most parallel models of computation. These mechanisms
do not efﬁciently support synchronization of threads, communication of data, or global naming of objects. As a
result, these functions, inherent to any parallel model of
computation, must be implemented largely in software with
prohibitive overhead.
The J-Machine project [5] was developed to study how
to best apply modern VLSI technology to construct a multicomputer. Each processing node of the J-Machine consists
of a Message-Driven Processor (MDP) and 1 MByte of
DRAM. The MDP incorporates a 36-bit integer processor
(32 bits of data augmented with 4 bits of tag), a memory
 The research described in this paper was supported in part by the De-

fense Advanced Research Projects Agency under contracts N00014-88K0738 and F19628-92C-0045, and by a National Science Foundation Presidential Young Investigator Award, grant MIP-8657531, with matching
funds from General Electric Corporation, IBM Corporation, and AT&T.

management unit, a router for a 3-D mesh network, a network interface, a 4K-word  36-bit SRAM, and an ECC
DRAM controller in a single 1.1M transistor VLSI chip.
Rather than being specialized for a single model of computation, the MDP incorporates primitive mechanisms for
communication, synchronization, and naming that permit
it to efﬁciently support threads with 50 to 150 instructions
which exchange small data objects frequently with lowlatency and synchronize quickly. A 512 node J-Machine is
in daily use at MIT and will be expanded to 1024 nodes in
March 1993.
This paper describes a range of experiments performed
on the J-Machine to study the effectiveness of the selected
mechanisms in supporting parallel applications. These experiments are divided into micro-benchmarks, designed to
isolate the effects of the primitive mechanisms, and macrobenchmarks, to demonstrate the cumulative effect of the
mechanisms on application level codes. We investigate the
sequential performance of the MDP, the message-passing
mechanisms, the performance of the 3D-mesh network,
and the behavior of parallel applications running on the
J-Machine.
We use these studies to critique the effectiveness of
the mechanisms and reﬂect on the impact of these design
decisions in developing programming systems for the JMachine. We contrast the effectiveness of the J-Machine
with comparable multicomputers and consider the impact
of alternative mechanisms to further enhance efﬁciency.

2

The J-Machine

This section describes the architecture of the J-Machine
and the hardware prototype on which the studies were performed.

2.1

Architecture

The instruction set of the MDP includes the usual arithmetic, data movement, and control instructions. The MDP
is unique in providing special support for communication,
synchronization, and naming.

 === PAGE 2
The MDP supports communication using a set of send
instructions for message formatting, a fast network for delivery, automatic message buffering, and task creation upon
message arrival. A series of send instructions is used to
inject messages at a rate of up to 2 words per cycle. The format of a message is arbitrary except that the ﬁrst word must
contain the address of the code to run at the destination and
the length of the message. Messages are routed through the
3D-mesh network using deterministic, e-cube, wormhole
routing [4]. The channel bandwidth is 0.5 words/cycle and
the minimum latency is 1 cycle/hop. Upon arrival, messages are buffered in a hardware queue. When a message
arrives at the head of the queue, a task is dispatched to
handle it in four processor cycles. During these cycles the
Instruction Pointer is loaded from the message header, an
address register is set to point to the new message so that
the thread’s arguments may be accessed, and the thread’s
ﬁrst instruction is fetched and decoded.
Messages may be issued to one of two priorities. Priority
one messages receive preference during channel arbitration,
are buffered in a separate queue at the destination, and are
dispatched before pending priority zero messages. Priority
one threads may interrupt executing priority zero threads.
There is also a background priority that runs whenever
both message queues are empty. Fast interrupt processing
is achieved through the use of three distinct register sets.
Synchronization is provided by the ability to signal
events effectively using the low-latency communication
primitives and by the use of data-tagging in both the register ﬁle and memory. Two of the possible sixteen data types,
cfut and fut, are used to mark slots for values that have
not yet been computed. If a thread attempts to read a slot
before the value has been supplied, the processor will trap
to a system routine to suspend the thread until the value
is delivered. In this event, the arrival of the value is used
to restart the thread. The cfut type provides inexpensive
synchronization on a single slot, much like a full-empty
bit. The fut type may be copied without faulting and
thus supports the more ﬂexible, but more expensive, future
datatype [2]. Futures are ﬁrst-class data objects and references to them may be returned from functions and stored
in arrays, for example.
The MDP supports a global namespace with segmented
memory management and with name translation instructions. Local memory is referenced using indexed accesses
via segment descriptors that specify the base and length of
each memory object. These objects may be relocated at
will, to implement local heap compaction, for example, if
we ensure that only global virtual addresses of objects are
exported from nodes. A hardware name-translation table is
provided to accelerate virtual address to physical segment
descriptor conversion. Virtual-physical pairs are inserted in

the table using the enter instruction and extracted using
xlate. A successful xlate takes three cycles.
The register ﬁle includes four data registers and four
address registers per priority. The instruction set of the
MDP permits most operators to read one of the operands
from memory to help reduce access pressure on the register
ﬁle. The MDP instruction encodes two 17 bit instructions
in each word. Most instructions can operate in one cycle
if both operands are in registers and in two cycles if one
operand is in internal memory. The peak execution rate
is therefore 12.5 million instructions per second. Branch
instructions, prefetching stalls, operands in memory, and
instruction alignment issues reduce this rate to a typical
value of 5.5 million instructions per second if code and
data are in internal memory. This can fall to fewer than 2
million instructions per second if all code and data are in
external memory.

2.2

Prototype

Each processing node of the J-Machine is composed of
a single Message-Driven Processor (MDP) chip and three
1M4 DRAM chips. The resulting node is 2" by 3". Each
J-Machine processor board contains 64 MDP chips along
with their external memories. The board measures 26" by
20.5". Each pair of nodes shares a set of elastomeric conductors to communicate with the corresponding nodes on
the boards above and below in the board stack. A total
of 48 elastomeric connectors held in four connector holders provide 1420 electrical connections between adjacent
boards. Of these connections, 960 are used for signalling
and the remaining 460 are ground returns. The use of
elastomeric conductors enables the J-Machine to achieve a
very high network bisection bandwidth (a peak rate of 14.4
Gbits/sec) in a very small cross sectional area (2 ft2 ) and at
the same time keep the length of the longest channel wire in
a 1024-node machine under four inches. A stack of sixteen
processor boards contains 1024 processing nodes (12,500
MIPS peak) and 1Gbyte of DRAM memory in a volume of
4 ft3 , and dissipates 1500W (1.5W per node).
Figure 1 shows a pair of J-Machine cabinets. The cover
has been removed from the cabinet on the left to reveal a
partial processor board stack at the top and a pair of peripheral interface cards below. Cards will soon be available to
connect to SCSI devices, a Sun Sparc host, and a distributed
graphics frame-buffer. The maximum possible bandwidth
into this peripheral stack is 3.2 Gbyte/sec using just one
of the faces of the cube. The base of the cabinet holds an
array of up to 80 3.5-inch disk-drives, power supplies, and
the host.
The experiments reported in this paper were run on a
512-node machine arranged as an 8  8  8 mesh, operating
at a processor clock rate of 12.5Mhz (derived from a 25Mhz
input clock).

Micro-Benchmark performance
To characterize the performance of the J-Machine’s
communication and synchronization mechanisms, we have
written a number of small, synthetic programs designed to
measure various aspects of J-Machine performance. Our
studies focus on the tight coupling between the processor
core and the network to support ﬁne-grained communication, the impact of the differing communication bandwidths
among the modules of the MDP, and the variation of message latency with network load.
Communication performance is characterized by
throughput, which is the number of messages per unit time
that can be delivered, and latency, which is the end-to-end
time required to deliver one message. Throughput limits the performance of communication intensive programs
with large amounts of parallelism. Latency adds to the
length of the critical path through a program with limited
parallelism. Both latency and throughput depend on the
end-to-end performance of the communication system, not
just on network performance. The performance of the network interface and the coupling between the processor and
the network interface are key factors in determining overall
communication performance.
Network latency Figure 2 shows the round-trip latency
of a null remote procedure call (RPC) as a function of
the distance traversed and the data transferred. These measurements are taken on an unloaded network. The indicated
data points show measured values for a 512 node machine.
Each line corresponds to a different type and size of
data transfer. The line labeled Ping gives the latency for
sending a two-word request message to the remote node and
waiting for and receiving a single word acknowledgment.
The remaining lines give the latencies for remote reads of 1
or 6 words from either the on-chip memory (Imem) or the
off-chip memory (Emem). The remote read is performed
by sending a three-word request message to a remote node.
That node reads the speciﬁed address and replies with a 2
or 7 word message containing the requested data.

a sense of the reduction in overhead that can be achieved
when the programming model matches the available hardware more closely. We observe that the J-Machine reduces

the overhead per message by up to two orders of magnitude. This is a striking difference whose repercussions have
a dramatic impact on communication costs in the machine.
Network latency vs load The latency statistics reported
above were measured on an unloaded network. In a loaded
network there is an additional component of latency due
to contention. We developed an experiment to evaluate
the total one-way message latency for messages of different lengths at different average network loads. In this
experiment, every node in the 512 node machine repeats a
simple loop in which it selects a random destination, sends
a message of length N to the target, waits for an N word acknowledgment, and then idles for L cycles. The idle phase
simulates computation and its duration has an inverse relation to the average trafﬁc load placed on the network.
We run this loop for between 15 and 30 seconds, and then
compute the average message rate and thereby the bisection trafﬁc. We establish a base case in which no messages
are transmitted in order to determine the number of cycles
that execute in the loop itself. This allows us to measure
the total number of cycles for the round-trip exchange. We
divide this by two to obtain the one-way message latency.
The left-hand side of Figure 3 shows the one-way message latency in a 512 node machine as a function of network
bisection trafﬁc. A family of four curves represent messages of length 2, 4, 8, and 16 words, respectively. Again,
the difference in latencies for the zero load case is due to

idle time L is varied to generate the full range of possible loads. The basic loop of the application takes 45 cycles

and tend to communicate mainly with neighboring nodes,

overhead is traditionally amortized by ensuring that remote

and effective load-balancing particularly difﬁcult. The efﬁcient communication mechanisms of the J-Machine enable us to approach the effective terminal bandwidth of the
network using small messages.

To characterize the performance of the J-Machine’s
communication and synchronization mechanisms, we have
written a number of small, synthetic programs designed to

core and the network to support ﬁne-grained communication, the impact of the differing communication bandwidths

Communication performance is characterized by
throughput, which is the number of messages per unit time
that can be delivered, and latency, which is the end-to-end
time required to deliver one message. Throughput limits the performance of communication intensive programs
with large amounts of parallelism. Latency adds to the
length of the critical path through a program with limited
parallelism. Both latency and throughput depend on the
end-to-end performance of the communication system, not
just on network performance. The performance of the network interface and the coupling between the processor and

communication performance.

two source strings, where a subsequence is the string remaining after removing arbitrary characters from a source
string. In this implementation, one string is distributed
evenly across the nodes of the machine; the other string
is placed on Node 0 and the characters are passed across
the nodes in a systolic fashion. We studied the application
for the case where the ﬁrst string is 1024 characters long
and the second 4096. This program was written directly in
Radix Sort This application sorts a set of integer keys.
The keys are sorted one digit at a time, with digits represented by b-bits, from the least-signiﬁcant to the mostsigniﬁcant digit. A stable, three-phase counting sort was
used to sort each digit. In the ﬁrst phase, a single scan of
the source array determines the number of keys that hash to
each of the digits (0 to 2b 1). These keys will appear consecutively in the destination array at the end of the iteration.
The counts are used to compute the initial offset for each
key in the destination array. Finally, the array is scanned
again and the data is reordered. In the parallel version, the
data is distributed evenly across the machine. The counts
computed by each node are combined and the initial offsets
are generated using a binary combining/distributing tree.
This program is written in Tuned J and sorts a set of 65,536
28-bit integers 4 bits at a time. This data set is small enough

one node to serve as a challenging base case.

A task is deﬁned as a unique subpath of a given length;
the tasks are initially distributed evenly over all the nodes.
To process a task, a node explores all possible tours containing the subpath in depth-ﬁrst order, while maintaining
the shortest tour seen so far. If the length of the task’s
subpath is larger than the current bound, the node does not
explore the subpath. This program is written in Concurrent

The SLS has five steps (`ai/flow-sls.md`). You're in step 3.

1. **Protocol** (done, frozen). Fixes the rules before any reading starts: the need for the review, the 19 SQs, the inclusion and exclusion criteria, the quality checklist and the extraction form.
   - 1a: an agent drafts them.
   - 1b: a skeptic adds counter-evidence SQs.
   - 1c: you freeze them. Later changes go in `changes/` (e.g. the pilot change).
2. **Search** (round R0 done). Finds candidate papers and decides which ones enter.
   - 2a: the search string and the start set R0.
   - 2b: you decide include or exclude, and P IDs are assigned.
   - 2c and 2d: snowballing rounds R1, R2… (backward through references, forward through citations), each with your gate.
3. **Reading** (in progress: the pilot plus batch 1). Turns each included paper into a checked record.
   - 3a: a reader drafts the record (five Cs, quality, extracted fields, concepts, all with pages).
   - 3b: a citation checker verifies every claim against the paper.
   - 3c: you accept, change or reject each record and read your key papers in full. The PDFs are then published.
4. **Synthesis.** Builds concepts across papers.
   - 4a: an agent merges the records into concept files (C{n}).
   - 4b: you accept, merge or split them.
   - **Stop rule:** if the last round included new papers, go back to step 2 for another snowballing round. If not, go to step 5.
5. **Gap.** Answers the questions and states what's missing.
   - 5a: an agent drafts an answer per SQ, the gap, existing solutions, the history and the limitations.
   - 5b: a skeptic attacks the gap.
   - 5c: you accept the gap. Then the DSRM starts (row 6a).

So steps 2–4 form a loop: each snowballing round's papers are read and synthesised before the next round. The SLS ends when a round finds nothing new.

The TSP algorithm, like the N-Queens algorithm, is a
graph-searching problem. The main difference between
them is that TSP can prune the amount of work that needs
to be done based on the work already done: a shortest
path cannot be longer than any already calculated path.
Pruning dominates the behavior of the TSP application, as
can be seen in the speedup curve shown in Figure 5. The
multi-node version happens to ﬁnd better paths using less
total work than the sequential one for this particular city
conﬁguration, and therefore exhibits super-linear speedup
for the smaller machines. The TSP application’s use of
dynamic task balancing results in an idle time of only 3.8%
as compared to 15% in N-Queens (Figure 6).
The TSP application, also like N-Queens, is very coarsegrained in its current implementation. There are three main
types of threads: task-processing, bounds-distributing, and
work-requesting. A task-processing thread can run as a
single 32,000 instruction task; however, it must be interrupted periodically so that the messages that propagate updated bounds can be processed. These messages could,
in principle, be handled using priority one threads but
CST/COSMOS does not currently support this. Instead,
we cause the path-tracing thread to suspend periodically
by performing a null procedure call. Sixteen percent (the
synchronization overhead from Figure 6) of the time that
TSP runs is currently spent in this operation.
The xlate instruction is used to translate global object
names into local physical addresses. The name is generally
stored in the current context frame, and xlate places the
physical address in the speciﬁed address register. Because
the instruction takes only three cycles if the name is found in
the name-cache, it is also used to reload an address register
after a spill. This accounts, in part, for the large number

1. Performance results (HLLESF row), p. 101:

2. Fate and reasons (direct execution row), p. 100:
   `The reason given is that programs must first be checked for syntax errors, "tantamount to compiling".`
   →
   `The principal reason given is that programs must first be checked "for syntax or detectable semantic errors", steps that "account for most of the phases of a compiler"; and retaining intermediate information to avoid retranslation "is tantamount to compiling".`

3. Hardware–language trade-off (cost row), p. 98:
   `Cost: HLLCs "require more logic for their implementation than their contemporary counterparts" (p. 98).`
   →
   `Cost: the paper names as the "first inference" of Axiom 3 that HLLCs "require more logic for their implementation than their contemporary counterparts", extra hardware that proponents justify with "the cliche of the falling cost of hardware" (p. 98).`

4. Concepts (transparent reversibility row), pp. 102–103:
   `Errors are reported at source level by decompiling the object program, using an address map, a copy of the source and a symbol table.`
   →
   `Errors are reported at source level from three data structures stored with each load module: an address map, a copy of the source and a symbol table. A decompiled version of the failing statement is then pattern-matched against the original to find the operator or operand at fault. Decompiling the whole program is "not recommended", because "it is not possible to recreate the original source line exactly".`

In step 3 the agents do the reading and checking. Your part is gate **3c**, where nothing counts as evidence until you've decided it.

## What happens before you

1. **3a, reader:** one agent per paper writes `P{n}.md`. It holds the five Cs (category, context, correctness, contributions, clarity), the nine quality answers, the extraction-form fields and the paper's concepts, each with a page number.
2. **3b, citation checker:** a second agent opens the paper and checks every claim in the record. It quotes the passage, marks the claim *found*, *differs* or *not found*, and writes an exact fix for each problem in `P{n}.citations.md`.

## What you do at 3c

For each paper:

1. **Look at the flags.** I show you the record's path, one line on what it holds, the citation counts, the suggested fixes, and any question the reader raised. Open the files whenever you want to see more than my summary.
2. **Decide the record:**
   - **Accept** it as written.
   - **Change** it: pick which suggested fixes to apply, or give your own edits.
   - **Reject** it.
3. **Decide the criterion questions.** The readers can't settle these; only you can. For batch 1:
   - **Wrong or extra criterion:** P21 and P67 may not meet I1. P72, P65 and P70 may also meet I2, and several papers may also meet I4.
   - **Duplicates (X8):** P64 and P69 against P12; P66 against its journal version; P46 against Liedtke's 1995 paper.
   - **Unobtainable text:** P74 is abstract-only. You can try the library, exclude it (X7), or keep it as is.
   - **Reference fixes:** P73 should cite the manual, not the SIGART notice; R0-072 has the wrong author name.
4. **Read your key papers in full yourself.** These are the papers your argument depends on. The rule exists because a thesis can't rest on an agent's summary: you must be able to defend those papers at your defense. P8, P9, P10 and P12 from the pilot are still waiting on this. From batch 1, I'd suggest P65 (J-machine evaluation), P72 (Intel 432), P280 (Ditzel & Patterson), P46 (Liedtke) and P48 (L3 to seL4).

## What I do after you decide

- Apply exactly the edits you chose, and set each status (`accepted`, `changed` or `rejected`).
- Write one decision file per record in `research/ai-log/decisions/`.
- Publish the PDFs with `just papers-push`.
- Run `just check`.

## How to make it manageable

The gate goes in batches, through multiple-choice questions, up to four per round:
- **Clean records:** grouped into one "accept these" question.
- **Criterion and duplicate questions:** asked one by one, with a recommended option.
- **Citation fixes:** offered per record. You can take all of them, pick some, or write your own.

Batch 1 will be roughly 22 records with about 15 real decisions; the rest are fix approvals. The 4 remaining citation checks and the P11 reader finish first, then I'll open the gate.

last_assistant_message:
You decide. The rule comes from step 3's own file: "Papers my argument depends on are read in full by me." The reading skill asks me only to tell you which ones those are at gate 3c, so I propose a list and you settle it. Batch 1 is the first time I've proposed one, and you should know how I build it, because it's a judgement, not a calculation.

## How I pick them

A paper is key if your thesis would be **weaker or wrong** without it. I use four tests:

1. **Sole or main evidence.** It's the only paper, or one of very few, answering an SQ your argument needs. Example: P65 is the main measured evaluation of a machine with message sends in hardware (SQ1, SQ5).
2. **Load-bearing claim.** The gap or the problem statement will quote it directly. Example: P280 and P29 for "language-directed machines failed because…" (SQ6, SQ9).
3. **Strongest counter-evidence.** A paper that argues against you is key, because the defense will ask about it. Examples: P22 (cache coherence is here to stay) and P17 (the RISC case).
4. **Seed of your observation.** The papers in `0-start/seeds.md` that started the idea. Examples: P8 (Multikernel), P10 (Intel 432).

A paper that only adds one more data point to a pattern several others show is not key, and its record is enough.

## The limit

At gate 3c this can only be a **provisional** guess, because the argument doesn't exist yet. It takes shape at synthesis (4a, where the concepts show which papers each one rests on) and at the gap (5a, where the claims are written). A better point to settle the list is **after 4a**, when each concept file lists its papers. A paper that carries a concept alone is key by test 1, and that becomes visible in the files, not from my reading of summaries.

## What I'd suggest

- **At 3c:** I mark my provisional candidates with the test each one passes. You accept them or not; nothing blocks on it.
- **After 4a:** we fix the list from the concept files, and you read those papers in full before the gap gate (5c).

So for P8, P9, P10 and P12, which are waiting on you now, you don't have to read them before deciding the rest of the batch. You can accept their records as provisional and read them before 5c.

Abstract

The Smalltalk-80™ system makes it possible to write programs quickly by providing
object-oriented programming, incremental compilation, run-time type checking,
user-extensible data types and control structures, and an interactive graphical interface.
However, the potential savings in programming effort have been curtailed by poor perfor-
mance in widely available computers or high processor cost. Smalltalk-80 systems pose
tough challenges for implementors: dynamic data typing, a high-level inszuction set, fre-

quent and expensive procedure calls, and object-oriented storage management.

To solve these problems, a group of researchers at U. C. Berkeley has designed and
built the SOAR (Smalltaik On A RISC) microprocessor. In order to determine the perfor-
mance of Smalltalk-80 on SOAR and to evaluate the importance of each of the ideas, simu-

lations of five representative benchmarks have been anaiyzed. The results suggest that:

set, multiple windows of on-chip registers, caching the target of a call instruction in the
instruction itseif, byte insert and extract instructions, instructions for arithmetic and
comparison operations on tagged integers, and our storage management algorithm,

Generation Scavenging.

lines: ## Rules
- Every extracted value and concept has a page.
-- Papers my argument depends on are read in full by me.
+- Papers my argument depends on (key papers) are read in full by me. A paper is key if it passes at least one test:
+  1. **Sole or main evidence:** it is the only paper, or one of very few, answering an SQ.
+  2. **Load-bearing claim:** the problem or the gap rests on a claim it makes.
+  3. **Strongest counter-evidence:** it argues most strongly against the observation.
+  4. **Seed:** it is in `0-start/seeds.md`.
+- Key papers are proposed, with the test each passes, at 3c (provisional), fixed at 4b from the papers each accepted concept rests on, and read in full before the gap gate (5c).
## Produces
Template in `ai/template/sls/3-reading/`. Flow rows 3a–3c (`ai/flow-sls.md`).

# AI log

Everything the AI does is recorded, not only the decisions. Two parts in `research/ai-log/`.

## 1. Raw log
`raw/<session>.jsonl`: every action, written automatically.
- Written by the hooks in `.claude/settings.json`, which call `ai/tools/log_hook.py`, not by the agents, so no agent can forget or leave out an entry.
- One entry per hook event, as Claude Code sends it, plus a timestamp: session start and end, my prompts, every tool call before it runs and after (full input and full output), every agent stop, every compaction.
- Skill calls and agent dispatches are tool calls (`Skill`, `Agent`), so the skill, the agent and the row it was given are in their logged input. Subagents' own tool calls are logged too.
- `raw/<session>.transcript.jsonl` is a copy of the session transcript, refreshed at every stop and at session end. It also holds the model's own messages, which tool hooks do not see.
- At session start the hook gives the model the session ID, so gates can write it into decision files.
- Append only. Never edited by hand.

## 2. Decisions
`decisions/{date}-{row}-{id}.md`: one file per gate.
```
---
row: 3c
target: sls/3-reading/P12.md
decision: accepted          # accepted | changed | rejected
---
Proposed by: reader, citation-checker
What I changed and why:
Raw log entries: <session> <first>–<last>
```

The raw log shows what the AI did. The decisions show what I did with it. Each decision points to the raw entries behind it.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Raw AI log: append every Claude Code hook event to research/ai-log/raw/<session>.jsonl.

Wired in .claude/settings.json. Never blocks or fails a session: every error is swallowed.
See ai/ai-log.md.
"""
import json
import os
import shutil
import sys
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path


def main() -> None:
    raw = sys.stdin.read()
    event = json.loads(raw)
    root = Path(os.environ.get("CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR") or event.get("cwd") or ".")
    session = event.get("session_id", "unknown")
    log_dir = root / "research" / "ai-log" / "raw"
    log_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    entry = {"ts": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(), **event}
    with open(log_dir / f"{session}.jsonl", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(entry, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")

    name = event.get("hook_event_name")
    if name in ("Stop", "SubagentStop", "SessionEnd", "PreCompact"):
        transcript = event.get("transcript_path")
        if transcript and Path(transcript).is_file():
            shutil.copyfile(transcript, log_dir / f"{session}.transcript.jsonl")
    if name == "SessionStart":
        # Stdout of SessionStart is added to the model's context: the gate needs the session ID.
        print(f"Raw AI log session: {session} (research/ai-log/raw/{session}.jsonl)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        main()
    except Exception:
        pass
    sys.exit(0)

# P11

## Reference
David Michael Ungar (1986, dated "February, 1986" on the cover). *The Design and Evaluation of a High Performance Smalltalk System*. PhD dissertation, Computer Science, University of California, Berkeley. Published as UC Berkeley technical report UCB/CSD-86-287 and later as a book by MIT Press (ACM Distinguished Dissertation, 1987). The report number and the MIT Press edition come from the reference line given to me; neither is printed on the scanned pages I read. P11, screened in under I2 (row R0-011). Pages cited below are the printed arabic page numbers of the dissertation scan in `papers/P11.pdf`. Printed p. *n* is PDF page *n* + 18 (e.g. Chapter 1 starts on printed p. 1, PDF p. 19). The front matter has no printed numbers, so the abstract is cited by its PDF pages (pp. 7–8). This is not the MIT Press edition, whose page numbers will differ.

## Deepest pass

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Design and evaluation of a processor architecture and its run-time software, SOAR ("Smalltalk On A RISC"). It also contains a survey of earlier high-level-language machines (Ch. 2) and a new garbage collector, Generation Scavenging (Ch. 5) (pp. 1–5).
- **Context:** Smalltalk-80 runs poorly on widely available hardware. The only machine that "has demonstrated universally acceptable Smalltalk-80 performance" is the $120,000 ECL Xerox Dorado (p. 11). Earlier language machines (R-2, Burroughs B5700/B6700, Scheme-79, Symbolics 3600, Katana-32) "closely coupled the source language semantics to the hardware" (p. 14). RISC work (IBM 801, RISC I/II, MIPS) and the Deutsch-Schiffman software techniques for the 68010 are the other context (pp. 12–14, 24–28).
- **Correctness:** The premise is that a RISC with a few Smalltalk-specific additions can match microcoded or high-level-instruction machines. It is tested by instruction-level simulation of Xerox's official benchmarks (pp. 61–66). The NMOS chip exists and ran diagnostics, but Smalltalk-80 had not yet run on it (pp. 2, 127). The value of each feature is an omission cost measured in cycles under the current compiler. The author says this neglects cycle-time effects and compiler interaction (pp. 64–65, 67, 72).
- **Contributions:** (1) The SOAR instruction set, with tagged integer arithmetic, register windows, in-line call-target caching, fast shuffle, trap mechanisms and direct object pointers (Ch. 3). (2) A feature-by-feature evaluation that sorts features into "winners", "questionable" and "losers" (Tables 4.4–4.5, pp. 68–69). (3) Generation Scavenging, which reclaims storage with about 3% CPU overhead and no object table (Ch. 5, p. 126). (4) The "architect's trap" lesson (p. 70).
- **Clarity:** Clearly written and organised, with summary tables per chapter. The scan is legible but OCR-noisy, and a few table cells were checked against page images (pp. 66, 71).

| new: in-line caching (call-target cache in the instruction stream) | After a lookup the call is overwritten with a call to the target. A prologue checks the receiver's type and traps on a miss. It requires non-reentrant code and a process-switch-enable bit. | pp. 13, 45–47 |
| new: compilation to a low-level (reduced) instruction set vs. a high-level (bytecode) instruction set | SOAR "abandoned the Smalltalk virtual machine instruction set"; omission cost ~100% | pp. 35, 68 |
| new: tags trap bad guesses (tagged arithmetic in parallel with the operation) | "SOAR assumes that the operands are integers ... simultaneously checking the tags", trapping if wrong | p. 31 |
| new: register windows for frequent calls | "SOAR would run 46% slower without them", because Smalltalk's compilation produces many calls | pp. 43, 67, 70 |
| new: architect's trap | Clever features that speed one operation and add design time without improving overall performance. | pp. 70, 72, 126 |
| new: Generation Scavenging | Two generations, scavenge only new objects; "young objects die young"; 3% CPU, no object table, no hardware support | pp. 50, 86, 110, 126 |
| new: migrating functionality between levels of abstraction | "viewing the system as a whole rather than as a collection of layers"; microcoded instructions replaced by software trap handlers | p. 126 |
| new: exploratory programming environment (EPE) | A software system in which programming is viewed as exploration. EPEs "remain largely experimental" because of poor cost-performance. | pp. 6, 10 |

## Notes
- **Source read:** `research/papers/P11.pdf` (249-page image scan; Acrobat image conversion, 2002). It has no text layer, so I OCR'd all pages with tesseract 5.5.2 at 200 dpi and checked key table pages (pp. 66, 71, 127, cover) against the page images. Version: the UC Berkeley dissertation, February 1986. The front matter includes a technical-report-style abstract page with DARPA contract numbers (PDF p. 1). This is not the MIT Press 1987 edition.
- **Chapters read:** front matter and abstract; Ch. 1 (pp. 1–5); Ch. 2 (pp. 6–29); Ch. 3 (pp. 30–60); Ch. 4 (pp. 61–73); Ch. 5 §5.1–5.2, §5.9.3–5.11 (pp. 74–75, 101–110); Ch. 7 (pp. 125–129); Appendix A §A.4.4–A.4.5 (pp. 185–192). Not read: Ch. 5 §5.3–5.9.2 (algorithm survey and detailed GS evaluation), Ch. 6 (medium-lifetime objects, analytical), and the rest of Appendices A and B (raw data).
- **Criterion:** the full text supports I2 as screened. SOAR is described as an architecture for the Smalltalk-80 language, with simulated performance and stated reasons (pp. 2, 61–73). It does not meet I1: SOAR has no send or message instruction or mechanism (Table 3.2 p. 37), and sends are compiled to `call` plus software lookup (pp. 46–47). No verdict change proposed.
- **Discrepancy (Q6):** the abstract (PDF p. 8) says the language-specific hardware "doubles its performance over a RISC II with the same cycle time". Table 4.6 and p. 71 give a ratio of 1.6. Elsewhere the paper says the language-specific features "approximately double performance" (p. 4), and that register windows and tagged integers "nearly double SOAR's performance" (p. 125). These may measure different things. I record them as stated.
- **Evidence status:** most performance figures are cycle counts from simulation multiplied by 400 ns. The chips' effective cycle is 510 ns, and the chip ran diagnostics at 800 ns actual system cycle time (Table 3.8 p. 59; p. 127). So the "as fast as a Dorado" claim is a prediction: "the 400 ns NMOS SOAR chips that have been fabricated should run just as fast" (p. 73).
- **Process model:** process switches are deferred to safe calls and jumps through a software interrupt. All Smalltalk processes share one address space (pp. 45–46). This is relevant to SQ2 as a non-message, shared-memory base beneath the object model.

- **Context:** Smalltalk-80 runs poorly on widely available hardware. The only machine that "has demonstrated universally acceptable Smalltalk-80 performance" is the $120,000 ECL Xerox Dorado (p. 11). Earlier language machines (R-2, Burroughs B5700/B6700, Scheme-79, Symbolics 3600, Katana-32) "closely coupled the source language semantics to the hardware" (p. 14). It is tested by instruction-level simulation of Xerox's official benchmarks (pp. 61–66). The NMOS chip exists and ran diagnostics, but Smalltalk-80 had not yet run on it (pp. 2, 127). #!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Raw AI log: append every Claude Code hook event to research/ai-log/raw/<session>.jsonl.

Wired in .claude/settings.json. Never blocks or fails a session: every error is swallowed.
See ai/ai-log.md.
"""
import json
import os
import shutil
import sys
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path


def main() -> None:
    raw = sys.stdin.read()
    event = json.loads(raw)
    root = Path(os.environ.get("CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR") or event.get("cwd") or ".")
    session = event.get("session_id", "unknown")
    log_dir = root / "research" / "ai-log" / "raw"
    log_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    entry = {"ts": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(), **event}
    with open(log_dir / f"{session}.jsonl", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(entry, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")

    name = event.get("hook_event_name")
    if name in ("Stop", "SubagentStop", "SessionEnd", "PreCompact"):
        transcript = event.get("transcript_path")
        if transcript and Path(transcript).is_file():
            shutil.copyfile(transcript, log_dir / f"{session}.transcript.jsonl")
    if name == "SessionStart":
        # Stdout of SessionStart is added to the model's context: the gate needs the session ID.
        print(f"Raw AI log session: {session} (research/ai-log/raw/{session}.jsonl)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        main()
    except Exception:
        pass
    sys.exit(0)
